title: Optimal Dynamic Quantizers for Periodically Time-Varying Systems via Cyclic Reformulation
abstract: This paper addresses the design of optimal dynamic quantizers for discrete-time linear periodically time-varying (LPTV) plants with discrete-valued inputs. Optimal dynamic quantizers, which minimize the worst-case output error caused by quantization, are well established for linear time-invariant (LTI) plants, whereas the corresponding design for plants with periodically time-varying dynamics has not been addressed. For square LPTV plants having relative degree one at every time phase, this paper derives an optimal periodic dynamic quantizer in closed form. The quantizer is constructed by applying the LTI theory to the cycled plant obtained by cyclic reformulation and reading off its periodic coefficient matrices block by block; its optimality is then verified directly, showing that it attains a performance lower bound determined by the largest instantaneous input-to-output gain over the time phases. The worst-case output error of general periodic dynamic quantizers is also characterized. The optimal quantizer is shown to be stable if and only if all invariant zeros of the cycled plant lie in the open unit disk, which is the condition that governs stable causal inversion of LPTV plants. A numerical example with comparisons to conventional quantizers illustrates the results.

title: Lieb-Robinson Bounds for Electric Quantum Walks
abstract: We derive Lieb-Robinson type bounds with optimal propagation velocity for shift-coin and split-step quantum walks in rational electric fields. The velocity decays exponentially fast in the period of the field, showing long intervals of suppressed spreading. The proof rests on bounds for the imaginary part of the analytically continued dispersion relation of the electric walk. We show that the infimal Lieb-Robinson velocity coincides with the asymptotic velocity for these walks, while a nonhomogeneous example demonstrates that the two types of velocity need not agree in general. We also obtain an exponential tail estimate on the probability of a walk to lie outside the effective light cone.

title: Postselection on Halting and Reductions to the Halting Problem
abstract: A probabilistic Turing machine is an ordinary Turing machine that may also toss fair coins, with no limit on its running time or memory. If it always halts, it decides only computable problems. Aaronson et al. studied machines that may run forever on some coin tosses, with the answer read only from the runs that halt. Suppose the correct answer must be more than twice as likely as the wrong one. They showed that these machines decide exactly the problems solvable with a fixed list of questions about the halting problem. They asked what happens when the correct answer need only be the more likely one. We show that the machines then decide exactly the problems solvable by asking such questions one after another, each chosen after the earlier answers. We also show that the factor two can be replaced by any fixed factor greater than one. A machine may promise two numbers: a lower bound on its probability of halting, and a lower bound on its probability of being right when it halts. From these two numbers we compute exactly how many questions fixed in advance the machine can replace. The main idea is that probability acts as a budget for how often a computable guess may change its mind. The results extend to oracle machines and to machines nested inside each other. Quantum machines decide the same problems.

title: What the Averages Hide: Monocular Metric Depth Models Still Fail in Everyday Scenes, Mostly on Scale
abstract: Zero-shot monocular metric depth models are evaluated by averaging metric and scale-aligned scores across datasets. Averages cannot show how many images still have severely wrong metric depth, whether depth is under- or overestimated, or whether different models fail on the same images. We propose an evaluation built on per-image results: the failure rate (metric $δ_1$ < 0.5); scale-aligned metrics for structure, and the bias, dispersion and absolute error of the alignment scale for scale; and a cross-model comparison that separates shared from model-specific failures. We apply it to 11 recent architectures with and without ground-truth intrinsics (18 model evaluations) on the 7 everyday-scene benchmarks (4,406 images) used by MoGe-2. Metric depth estimation is not solved in everyday scenes, and the remaining difficulty is mainly scale: the best of the 18 evaluations still has a failure rate of 7.7% (datasets weighted equally); pooled over all failures, 78.8% have intact structure, and after scale correction 98.3% no longer fail. Images failed by at least 6 architectures make up 7.3% of the data, concentrated on HAMMER and DIODE; even when selected only by architectures of other families, they hold 34% to 40% of the error of the top 6 models, against 14% to 18% for as many random images from the same datasets. Adding objects reduces the scale error of most models; ground-truth intrinsics and, in most families, larger models reduce the failures but do not remove them. We recommend reporting failure rates, structure and scale separately, and results stratified by how many models fail. We will release the code, the per-image results with shared-failure labels, and two diagnostic sets built from TUM RGB-D.

title: AI Tool Adoption and Loyalty among Product, Industrial, and UX/UI Designers across the Double Diamond
abstract: Designers share many AI tools, yet their roles produce different work. This survey compared 337 Product, Industrial and UX/UI Designers from 40 countries and regions across the four phases of the Double Diamond. It measured AI adoption, breadth and frequency, tool function and the number of tools named per phase. A tool was loyal when a role picked it in all four phases. Industrial Designers adopted AI less often (73.9% against 88.2% and 87.9%), a gap that went with physical projects once project type and country were held constant. Of 60 AI tools, 25 were common to all three roles and carried at least 90% of each role's picks. Tool function differed by role, most of all in Develop. A few loyal tools carried about half of the picks, led by ChatGPT. Tool counts fell across the phases in every role. A hurdle model found a Phase x Role interaction for using AI in a phase (p = 0.041), which was not shown for the number of tools (p = 0.080). Predicted adoption among UX/UI Designers fell from 87.2% in Define to 43.9% in Develop. Support for designers needs one shared core, role-specific tools and most attention in Develop.

title: Towards Inter-satellite Laser Metrology for Formation Flying Interferometry
abstract: Context. The direct detection and atmospheric characterization of terrestrial exoplanets has been highlighted as a key science focus by the US ASTRO2020 Decadal survey and the ESA Voyage 2050 plan. This will require a new generation of telescope which is able to meet the contrast requirements necessary to image a planet many orders of magnitude fainter than its host star - a technological feat which currently limits our observation capabilities. In the mid-infrared, the most viable solution has been shown to be a formation-flying nulling space interferometer. Aims. In this work, we present the initial prototype for an inter-spacecraft metrology system. This system is a sub-system of the Pyxis/SEIRIOS interferometer, a formation-flying interferometer which serves as a technology demonstrator for the LIFE mission. Methods. We have designed a multi-stage metrology system using three interferometric measurement techniques, covering varying distance resolution ranges. Digital Interferometric (DI) ranging provides the coarsest measurement, while a differential phase read-out provides sub-nm precision. Multi-wavelength interferometry is employed to overcome the phase ambiguity associated with the differential phase readout. Results. A single-wavelength electronic noise floor below 20 pm RMS over 10 s was measured by applying a common photodetector signal to both readout channels, a factor of 28 below the 560 pm requirement. For the multi-wavelength readout, the obtained electronic noise RMS was 556 nm at 10 second integration, decreasing to 200 nm below 3 second integration. The full optical measurement in laboratory air is currently limited by environmental path fluctuations. Conclusions. We demonstrate an initial prototype system for precision ranging between satellites for formation-flying nulling interferometers.

title: LINK: Lightweight and Inductive Node-to-Node Propagation Rule Learning for Traffic Kriging
abstract: Spatio-temporal traffic kriging aims to reconstruct traffic time series at unobserved locations with no historical traffic observations by leveraging spatial and temporal dependencies across the road network. Existing Graph Neural Network (GNN)-based approaches primarily rely on neighborhood aggregation to capture spatial dependencies, thereby modeling traffic interactions implicitly and making it difficult to accurately recover traffic magnitudes at locations without historical observations. To address this limitation, we propose LINK, a Lightweight and Inductive Node-to-node propagation rule learning paradigm for traffic Kriging. LINK introduces three key designs: 1) a propagation-centric traffic kriging paradigm that explicitly learns a shared node-to-node transition rule; 2) a context-aware Spectral Propagation Network that performs traffic-state propagation in both the spectral and time domains; and 3) TraffiKrig, a realistic traffic kriging benchmark that preserves heterogeneous road-segment characteristics and road-specific metadata while enabling systematic comparison of representative kriging methods under a unified metadata-enhanced setting. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LINK achieves strong reconstruction accuracy and computational efficiency. Compared with the strongest baseline on each subset, LINK achieves an average MAE reduction of 54.7% over original baselines. LINK also achieves substantial efficiency improvements, reducing training time by 66.5% and inference time by 86.6% compared with the fastest competing methods. Zero-shot experiments further demonstrate the transferability of the learned propagation rule across regions.

title: AFRNet: Adaptive Frequency Redistribution Network for Image Deraining
abstract: Image deraining aims to recover rain-free images from rain-degraded observations. Recent frequency-aware deraining methods have demonstrated promising performance by removing rain artifacts in the spectral domain. However, since rain artifacts and background textures often appear in several correlated subbands, prior frequency-domain deraining models still enhance frequency subbands separately. Such band-wise processing limits information exchange across subbands. Without context from other subbands, rain and clean content that appear together in one subband cannot be separated. This leads to either residual rain streaks or over-smoothing of fine details. To address this limitation, we propose AFRNet, an Adaptive Frequency Redistribution Network for image deraining. First, we introduce an Adaptive Frequency Recombination Module (AFRM) that performs cross-band modulation among wavelet subbands, enabling information interaction and adaptive recombination of degraded frequency components. We then develop a Subband Compensation Block (SCB) that compensates for decoder subband degradation by leveraging encoder subband features through inter-subband attention in the wavelet domain, alleviating detail loss during reconstruction. Extensive experiments demonstrate that AFRNet achieves competitive performance and consistent results across diverse deraining benchmarks.

title: Degenerate Preconditioned Proximal Point Algorithms as Forward Methods for Nonmonotone Inclusions
abstract: We study degenerate preconditioned proximal point algorithms (PPPA) for finding zeros of nonmonotone set-valued operators in Hilbert spaces under solution-relative $(U,V)$-semimonotonicity, with possibly indefinite $U$ and $V$. With a closed-range preconditioner $P$, the reduced PPPA dynamics admit a forward representation through the complementary resolvent of a parallel composition, without requiring monotonicity or admissibility. Relative semimonotonicity of the range-restricted operator transfers to the reduced forward map, allowing our forward theory for possibly set-valued mappings to yield Fejér estimates and residual rates. Under suitable conditions, including demiclosedness of the reduced map at zero, the projected PPPA iterates and shadows converge weakly to a common projected zero. Without demiclosedness, a counterexample shows that the projected sequences may converge to a point outside the projected zero set, even when the original operator is continuous. Bounded recovery condition yields weak convergence of the full (non-projected) shadows. The monotonicity modulus $U$ yields additional results: under suitable conditions, $U\succeqτP$ with $τ>0$ gives strong and linear convergence of the projected PPPA sequences, while $U\succeq-σP$ with $0\leσ<1/2$ still permits local linear rates under metric subregularity. These strong convergence and linear rate guarantees extend to the full shadows when a Lipschitz recovery estimate holds, such as when $U$ is strongly monotone on $\ker P$. For Chambolle--Pock and Douglas--Rachford splitting, we establish Lipschitz recovery even when $U=0$ by exploiting the primal--dual structure. Under suitable parameter conditions, full-shadow convergence guarantees, including $R$-linear rates, extend to the original PPPA iterates.

title: GaugeRoPE: RoPE-Compatible Executable Latent Attention
abstract: Latent KV cache compression reduces memory footprint by mapping historical keys and values into compact representations. However, generic compressed key states require reconstruction to native dimension before applying RoPE and computing attention scores, adding sequence-scaling overhead to the decode path. We characterize when a latent KV representation can serve directly as the execution state of pretrained RoPE. For RoPE-based transformers, exact static linear execution of the rotary key path requires the latent-to-native map to preserve the pretrained RoPE action through an intertwining relation, restricting exact mixing to coordinates that share the same RoPE frequency. Guided by this characterization, we build GaugeRoPE, a training-free executable latent KV representation. It combines a RoPE-compatible carrier that preserves the rotary action with an approximate position-independent residual key--value (RKV) correction for complementary key and value information, both evaluated without per-token dense historical K/V reconstruction. On Mistral-7B, GaugeRoPE achieves $5.85\times$ KV compression while maintaining quality close to the full-cache baseline. Additional MHA results validate the construction beyond GQA. GaugeRoPE achieves up to $2.48\times$ the decode throughput of the vanilla uncompressed baseline through direct latent execution.

title: Effects of elasticity on the stability of viscoelastic boundary layers
abstract: The elastic effect on the stability of boundary layers is studied for incompressible elastic fluids in the half-plane. It is known from [33] that if the deformation tensor matrix is nonsingular near the boundary, elasticity can prevent the formation of a boundary layer. In this paper, we prove stability properties when the deformation tensor degenerates. Our results are twofold: (1) when the first row of the deformation tensor has a non-degenerate projection onto a fixed direction, the initial-boundary value problem for the two-dimensional viscoelastic Prandtl boundary layer equations in the half-plane admits local well-posedness in Sobolev spaces, without any monotonicity condition on the velocity profile; (2) when the first row of the deformation tensor vanishes simultaneously at one point, the linearized Prandtl boundary layer system is ill-posed. The first result reveals the stabilizing effect of elasticity against the classical Prandtl instability. The second result shows that elastic effects cannot suppress the Prandtl-type instability associated with a non-degenerate critical point of the velocity profile.

title: Compositional Data-Driven Small-Signal Stability Assessment of Power Systems via Output Differential Passivity
abstract: This paper proposes a compositional data-driven small-signal stability assessment framework for interconnected power systems based on output differential passivity (ODP). Without requiring explicit device models, local ODP matrices and scalar indices are estimated directly from measurement trajectories. When internal states are available, trajectory-based linear matrix inequalities (LMIs) are constructed from input-state measurements to estimate the local ODP matrices and scalar indices. When internal states are unavailable, an extended-state representation is constructed from input-output measurements, enabling the same assessment using only external signals. The estimated ODP matrices are combined with the network coupling matrix for compositional assessment of power system stability, while their scalar indices enable decentralized assessment. To address the computational and numerical challenges of trajectory-based LMIs, we introduce right-inverse whitening (RIW) to remove redundant behavioral coordinates and improve computational efficiency, and apply instrumental-variable (IV) preprocessing to alleviate numerical ill-conditioning and mitigate noise effects. Case studies on a modified IEEE 39-bus power system show that ambient measurements satisfy the required informativity conditions and that both formulations yield estimates close to model-based references under the tested noise levels. The reusable local ODP estimates also enable modular stability reassessment after controller updates.

title: Recurrent losers: A network approach to cover-bidding patterns in public procurement
abstract: We develop and apply a network-based method to examine patterns consistent with cover bidding within procurement markets, using only bidder participation and winner identities. A statistical test identifies relationships in which firms win unusually often when particular competitors also bid. These relationships form a directed graph with links from recurrent losers to recurrent winners. We use maximum $k$-core to classify possible organizational forms of cover bidding and propose tender exposure -- the share of contested tenders involving a reported relationship -- as a market-level indicator of potential cover-bidding risk. Applied to 200,065 contracts procured by district engineering offices of the Philippine Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) from 2017 to 2025, covering three congressional terms, the method identifies 8,728 directed relationships across 407 of 564 markets. The $k$-core classes differ in network breadth, relationship depth, and bidder roles. In simpler networks, each recurrent loser is usually tied to a single winner, while highly interconnected networks involve multiple recurrent winners and broader groups of bidders that rarely win. Some of the deepest relationships and highest levels of tender exposure occur in intermediate networks, showing how relationships can reach much of a market without extensive interconnectedness. Offices named in official investigations more often contain highly interconnected networks than other offices. Two of the three offices referred for bid rigging are among the twelve in our ranking with the highest exposure in 2023-2025.

title: ReconPotBench: Evaluating LLM Honeypots in Multi-Round Linux Reconnaissance
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to build interactive honeypots, yet existing evaluations mainly assess isolated command outputs and cannot determine whether a system remains believable when later commands depend on earlier results. We present ReconPotBench, a multi-round benchmark for Linux reconnaissance honeypots. It contains 1{,}032 three-round reconnaissance interactions across eight reconnaissance categories, with reference outputs collected from a real Linux environment. Under a unified testing protocol, we compare Cowrie, open-source LLMs, and closed-source LLMs along three dimensions: round-level authenticity, cross-round contextual consistency, and hacker-oriented reconnaissance value. Results show that multi-round evaluation exposes failures hidden by single-round testing, as authenticity declines with interaction depth and both open-source and closed-source LLMs struggle to maintain coherent state across rounds. LLM-based honeypots nevertheless outperform Cowrie in authenticity and reconnaissance value, while Cowrie remains more consistent because of its rigid templated behavior. Category-level analysis further shows that tasks requiring systems to preserve network relationships across rounds are harder than tasks centered on explicit entities such as ports. ReconPotBench enables reproducible evaluation of LLM honeypots across authenticity, entity consistency, and hacker-perspective utility in dependent multi-round interactions. The dataset is available at: https://github.com/qianli-wang/ReconPotBench

title: Harmonic branches of Einstein--ModMax--scalar field gravity: exact solutions and regularity II
abstract: We integrate harmonic solution branches of Einstein--ModMax--Scalar field gravity, keeping the electromagnetic phase \(\tanΘ=\mathcal{G}/\mathcal{F}\) non-constant. For each family we first solve the field equations $(a(\s),b(\s),c(\s))$ and reconstruct the physical functions $f,ω,k,A_t,A_φ,ϕ$. In the same section we then select the Schwarzschild or Coulomb harmonic function, impose the regular horizon conditions, identify the ModMax solution, and state its Maxwell limit. Two theorems distinguish a constant electromagnetic phase from an exact static charge rescaling and show how twist prevents constant diagonal rescalings of the electromagnetic potentials at fixed metric and scalar. The catalogue covers known RN and charged Taub--NUT solutions, single-charge configurations, explicit static dyons with scalar-dependent couplings, and a restricted stationary family with an active scalar. We distinguish new explicit ModMax extensions of known Maxwell profiles from the nonfrozen stationary integration. The axial LWP reconstruction recovers the known Melvin--swirling background and gives an exact ModMax Schwarzschild exterior within that background. At its horizon, smooth metric and electromagnetic limits are distinguished from the constitutive continuation at a null equatorial circle. Uncharged configurations and earlier Maxwell fields are traced back to the preceding harmonic catalogue.

title: Freidlin-Wentzell exit-laws for a stochastic Cucker-Smale model
abstract: This paper investigates the exit-time asymptotics, at a vanishing noise limit, related to a stochastic particles system in mean-field interaction subjected to frictions, confining potential and flocking forces. The dynamics are governed by a kinetic Langevin-type SDE with an idiosyncratic noise acting solely on the velocity coordinates. Using the seminal large deviations principles of Freidlin and Wentzell [20], and their extension by Azencott [4] to the framework of non-elliptic diffusions, we establish the Arrhenius' law and Kramers' type law related to the first exit-time of the system from an energy level set $\mathcal O^γ_N(R)$ of interest.

title: First observation of the decay $D_{s1}(2460)^{+} \to D_{s}^{*+}γ$ and measurement of the branching-fraction ratio $\mathcal{B}[D_{s1}(2460)^{+} \to D_{s}^{*+} γ]/\mathcal{B}[D_{s1}(2460)^{+} \to D_{s}^{+} γ]$
abstract: We report the first observation of the radiative decay $D_{s1}(2460)^{+} \to D_{s}^{*+} γ$ with a significance greater than 10 standard deviations. The signal is found in $e^{+}e^{-} \to c\bar{c}$ production using data samples with integrated luminosities of 980 and 572~$\mathrm{fb}^{-1}$ collected by the Belle and Belle~II detectors operating at the KEKB and SuperKEKB asymmetric-energy $e^{+}e^{-}$ colliders, respectively. The branching-fraction ratio $\mathcal{B}[D_{s1}(2460)^{+} \to D_{s}^{*+} γ]/\mathcal{B}[D_{s1}(2460)^{+} \to D_{s}^{+} γ]$ is measured to be $0.74 \pm 0.05 ({\rm stat.}) \pm 0.06 ({\rm syst.)}$. This result helps discriminate between different theoretical models regarding the internal structure of the charm-strange meson $D_{s1}(2460)^{+}$.

title: Global existence of an initial boundary value problem for the Einstein equation via a Hamiltonian approach
abstract: The global existence of the initial boundary value problem for the Einstein equation in \((2+1)\)-dimension with totally geodesic timelike boundary is proved by a Hamiltonian approach. The initial boundary value problem is formulated within the framework of the ADM formalism, and the ADM reduction is carried out under the constant mean curvature spatial harmonic gauge. Deriving energy estimates for the flows in the reduced phase space shows the global existence.

title: RemeshingAgent: An Iterative Agent for Repair-Based Decimation of Generated Building Meshes
abstract: Aggressively simplifying a generated high-poly building mesh to 0.5-1% of its faces confronts a hard limit. The surface looks complete, yet the mesh is topologically shattered: 10^3-10^4 connected components and non-manifold thin walls. Below a certain budget, every practical decimator "melts": it deletes parts, welds thin walls, or breaks the error tolerance. We attribute this to instance-specific pathology: which components are significant and where the cliff sits vary from mesh to mesh, so no single fixed algorithm suffices, and decimation becomes an iterative loop of cleaning, simplifying, and verifying. We present RemeshingAgent, an agent that turns this loop into a validated process. The melting follows from a triangle-budget decomposition into curvature, crease, component, and genus terms: below the component floor, no output satisfies the repair contract, and cleaning first is the theory-mandated response. At a 0.5% budget the agent stays topology-clean where QEM and vertex clustering melt, matches a commercial remesher on 20 unseen city buildings, and on the 24 training buildings a nine-participant single-workstation blind study prefers our outputs 168:48 (p = 0.0195, subject-level sign test). The trained skill deploys as retrieval replay: 11.7 seconds per mesh on CPU, with no LLM calls.

title: Social Welfare and Equilibrium in Distributed Microgrid Prosumer Coordination Under a Mixed Competitive-Cooperative Setting
abstract: Price-based distributed prosumer coordination in distribution networks is fundamentally challenging when the aggregator pursues grid-level goals that couple prosumers' decisions, because the Lagrangian fails to separate and nodal prices are undefined under conventional dual decomposition. This paper develops a novel method that embeds mixed competitive-cooperative objectives exactly into prices, which are split into energy, congestion, and grid-objective components, closing the gap between the social welfare optimum and the competitive equilibrium. To compute the equilibrium, a distributed optimization algorithm is developed based on the projected Arrow-Hurwicz-Uzawa scheme. Explicit step-size rules are developed for the algorithm to guarantee $\mathcal{O}(1/\sqrt{L})$ and $\mathcal{O}(1/L)$ ergodic convergence rates. Simulations on an IEEE 33-bus feeder that is connected to prosumers and electric vehicle fleets validate the accuracy and efficacy of the proposed methods.

title: VAHBench: A Harness Benchmark for Agentic Long-Video Generation
abstract: AI agents are commonly used for everyday information retrieval and coding. We ask whether they can also interpret human requests and turn them into complete videos. We introduce VAHBench, a benchmark that tests this ability through five short-drama briefs specifying story, characters, dialogue and duration. Agents plan and carry out production using shared generation tools. Evaluation combines video completeness and basic quality with checks of production reliability and reporting accuracy. Across 240 runs covering 48 configurations of general-purpose and video-specific agents, higher quality scores do not necessarily mean more complete delivery. Missing episodes, repeated footage and static filler reveal gaps between producing a video file and fulfilling the brief. Added composition tools help some agents but do not consistently improve performance. VAHBench measures how well agents translate user intent into finished video content and helps identify where that process breaks down.

title: Uniqueness for an inverse problem of determining orders and coefficients for multi-term time-fractional diffusion equation
abstract: This paper investigates a uniqueness problem for determining all fractional orders and their corresponding coefficients in multi-term time-fractional diffusion equations with Caputo derivatives in an abstract Hilbert space. The main result establishes that these parameters can be uniquely identified from a single scalar observation of the solution, of the form (u(t), phi), by comparing the solutions of two evolution equations governed by possibly different positive self-adjoint operators A and B. In contrast to existing results that rely on local space-time measurements and, in particular, may require the initial data to satisfy sign conditions and strong spatial regularity assumptions, our approach uses only the minimal assumption that a belongs to H, without imposing any sign or additional smoothness conditions on the initial value. The proof combines spectral representations of the solutions with a recursive asymptotic comparison method based on fundamental identities for the multinomial Mittag-Leffler function. This approach enables the successive identification of all fractional orders and their associated coefficients, even when the two equations involve different operators. Furthermore, the uniqueness argument extends to multi-term time-fractional wave equations with orders in the interval (1,2).

title: SmoothShift: Disrupting Visual Adversarial Attacks on LVLMs at Test Time
abstract: Visual adversarial perturbations can substantially impair large vision-language models (LVLMs) despite introducing only subtle input changes. To understand how these small changes cause substantial errors, we investigate their optimization and propagation through the model, revealing two key findings. First, stronger attacks rely on finer iterative optimization, while subtle input perturbations induce representation discrepancies that are amplified layer by layer through the vision encoder and persist in the language model. Second, disrupting the alignment between within-patch input patterns and the model's computation reduces clean-adversarial representation discrepancies and substantially weakens attacks. Together, these findings suggest that adversarial effectiveness depends on both fine-grained perturbation patterns and their coupling with the model's computation. Motivated by these findings, we propose SmoothShift, a lightweight, training-free defense that combines local smoothing and spatial transformations. Smoothing weakens fine-grained perturbation patterns, while spatial transformations disrupt their alignment with the encoder's patch grid. SmoothShift requires no model updates, auxiliary networks, or additional model inference. Experiments cover three LVLM families on four datasets and robustly fine-tuned Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP) models on eight classification datasets. Evaluations across eight attack methods and multiple perturbation budgets demonstrate improved robustness while largely preserving clean performance. SmoothShift also provides robustness gains under defense-aware attacks using mixed-gradient BPDA with EOT.

title: Effective and Efficient Rumor Assertion Over Large-Scale Social Networks (Technical Report)
abstract: Nowadays, social networks, like Facebook, X, Reddit, YouTube, and so on, have become essential online platforms for users to connect with friends daily, post/share news, and express their opinions/comments. Meanwhile, however, the rapid and widespread dissemination of rumors and misinformation across social networks has become a serious concern. Such misleading information can distort public opinion and potentially cause significant social and economic consequences in real-world scenarios, including product promotion, elections and voting, and even cyberbullying. Therefore, accurately and efficiently verifying whether news spread on social networks is rumor or truth has become an increasingly important yet challenging problem. While previous works usually identified rumors by their contents, in this paper, we propose a novel \textit{user behavior model} to capture the users' judgment/discriminative abilities, which is learned via our well-designed evidence-aware probability reconstructor. We develop a general framework for tackling \textit{rumor assertion over large-scale social networks} (RA-SN), which can efficiently and effectively determine whether a given news item is a rumor with high confidence, based on users' behaviors, in a scalable manner. Extensive experiments demonstrate the efficiency and effectiveness of our proposed RA-SN approach on both real-world and synthetic graphs.

title: Graph Intersections and Hypergraph Discrepancy
abstract: Let $G$ and $H$ be graphs on $n$ vertices with $e(G)=p\binom{n}{2}$ and $e(H)=q\binom{n}{2}$, where $p,q\in(0,1)$ are fixed. Bollobás and Scott studied intersections of two graphs under random relabelling and asked for the minimum $L^2$ norm of the deviation of their intersection size from its expected value. We answer this question by proving that, for graphs of order $n$ with fixed edge densities $p,q\in(0,1)$, the minimum is \begin{equation*} \left(\sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)q(1-q)}{2}\cdot\frac{1-\sqrt R}{1+\sqrt R}}\right)n+o(n), \end{equation*} where $R=\max\{p,1-p,q,1-q\}$. The coefficient of the linear term is best possible. Bollobás and Scott defined the positive and negative discrepancies of two hypergraphs as the largest deviations of their intersection size above and below its expected value under relabelling, respectively. They asked for the minimum product of the positive and negative discrepancies of two $(n/2)$-uniform hypergraphs on $n$ vertices with $\frac{1}{2}\binom{n}{n/2}$ edges. We answer this question by proving that the minimum product of these discrepancies is $0$ if $4\mid\binom{n}{n/2}$ and $1/4$ otherwise.

title: Changing a View Is Not Amending a Record: Timing and Visibility in a Model of Public Correction
abstract: An accusation may remain on the public record after its author has changed their mind. Observers can respond either to what a person says now or to an earlier statement that has never been explicitly amended. We examine the consequences of these two signals with a generative agent-based model that separates private evidence updates, current expression, and revisions linked to a specific declaration. In paired worlds, evidence, prehistory, and opportunities to revisit that declaration remain fixed. When expression and amendment are synchronized and fully observed, the feedback channels produce identical trajectories. With sparse review, record-based feedback leaves 19.44 percentage points more eligible accusations unamended after 24 rounds (paired-world 95 percent bootstrap interval 13.89 to 25.31). The comparison averages 50 eligible worlds, containing 556 agents, from 128 newly generated worlds. Event traces show how a persistent public cue changes subsequent amendment propensity; an exact small-state calculation independently establishes the timing boundary. Reducing record salience can erase or reverse the increment, and a generic held-state process reproduces the dynamics. The findings show when current expression ceases to track correction of a particular public statement.

title: Scale-aware composite forcing enhances forward energy transfer in lattice Boltzmann simulations of forced homogeneous isotropic turbulence
abstract: In forced homogeneous isotropic turbulence (FHIT), conventional large-scale forcing sustains statistical stationarity but offers limited control over energy at intermediate scales. We propose a scale-aware composite forcing strategy for the lattice Boltzmann method, combining large-scale random forcing with feedback aligned with an intermediate-scale velocity field extracted by composite filtering. The magnitude of the cross-power spectrum between feedback and filtered velocity is concentrated in the target band, with a time-averaged fraction of 72.26%-74.56%. Feedback increases energy in both target and high-wavenumber bands, with larger relative gains at high wavenumbers. At feedback strengths $α$ = 1%, 3%, 5%, and 7%, the target-band energy fraction increases by 6.29%, 11.65%, 18.99%, and 19.89% relative to the baseline. The mean forward nonlinear energy flux across K = 12 rises to 1.18, 1.54, 2.32, and 3.06 times its baseline value, with larger relative increases than across K = 4. As $α$ increases from 0% to 7%, the mean Taylor-microscale Reynolds number rises from 73.94 to 97.86 and enstrophy increases by 181.98%, while longitudinal velocity-gradient skewness shifts toward zero and standardized velocity and normalized Q'-R' distributions largely retain their shapes. Mean $k_{\max}η$ values of 1.01 and 0.90 at 5% and 7% feedback indicate an approaching resolution limit and a risk of under-resolution, respectively. At approximately matched dissipation rates, 5% feedback gives a target-band energy fraction of 32.36%, versus 27.55% under enhanced large-scale forcing, and a post-transient forward flux across K = 12 generally 2.17-2.39 times larger. The strategy thus enables targeted control of energy distribution and nonlinear transfer, with feedback strength constrained by small-scale resolution.

title: PeV Gamma-Ray Emitters: Observations and Implications
abstract: The origin of Galactic cosmic rays (CRs) around and beyond the knee remains an open problem. Gamma rays extending to the PeV range provide direct evidence for extreme particle acceleration. LHAASO has greatly expanded the observational sample of such sources. In this review, we use the term "PeV gamma-ray emitter" for a source whose measured spectrum extends to, or approaches, 1 PeV, rather than restricting it to sources detected above 1 PeV at more than $5σ$. We review LHAASO observations of six PeV gamma-ray emitters (i.e., the Crab Nebula, the Aquila Booster, the Cygnus Bubble, Cygnus X-3, V4641 Sgr, and GRS 1915+105) together with relevant multiwavelength observations and on-going theoretical studies. Together, these sources show that PeV particle acceleration can occur in different environments and on spatial scales ranging from compact pulsar-wind nebulae and binary-scale jets to large-scale jet--environment interaction regions and extended star-forming complexes. Their spectra, morphologies, variability, magnetic fields, and surrounding gas provide important constraints on particle acceleration and transport mechanisms. We also discuss the implications of these observations for the origin of Galactic PeV CRs and future observational prospects for clarifying this problem.

title: Limit theorems and bias correction for the initial-noise-adjusted SIML estimator
abstract: We propose a sine-based modification of the separating information maximum likelihood (SIML) estimator for integrated volatility and covariance under equidistant sampling with microstructure noise. The estimator allows for nonzero initial observation noise. We establish consistency under moment assumptions and asymptotic normality under first-order Malliavin regularity of the diffusion coefficients. We also construct a feasible noise-bias correction using an estimator of the unknown noise covariance. This correction permits wider spectral bandwidths for consistency and stable asymptotic normality.

title: Hyperspectral imaging from diffractograms
abstract: We consider an optical system with a periodic point spread function, such as a camera with a periodic diffractive filter array placed near the sensor. Such systems produce a monochrome image that we call ``diffractogram'', and that multiplexes the spatial and spectral information about the scene. We present a method to efficiently invert this forward model and recover the hyperspectral scene. The inverse problem is formulated as a large scale $\ell_1$-penalized least squares problem that is solved iteratively with the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM). A Krylov subspace solver, such as LSQR, may require tens to hundreds of iterations to approximatively solve the augmented least-squares problem required in each ADMM iteration. Here we present an exact direct solver for the augmented least-squares problems that exploits the periodicity of the point spread function. Each direct solve costs roughly as much as three LSQR iterations, eliminating inner iterations entirely. We validate the method on both synthetic and experimental datasets.

title: Dynamic infrared thermography and computed tomography angiography fusion for DIEP flap perforator selection: a novel measurement system
abstract: Accurate perforator selection is critical for successful deep inferior epigastric artery perforator (DIEP) flap breast reconstruction. While computed tomography angiography (CTA) provides high-resolution anatomical detail, it lacks functional perfusion assessment. Dynamic infrared thermography (DIRT), in contrast, captures superficial rewarming dynamics but lacks objective anatomical validation. This study presents a standardized multimodal measurement system enabling automated fusion of DIRT with CTA-derived perforator coordinates. The framework integrates controlled thermographic acquisition, real-time hotspot detection, metric spatial calibration, and global one-to-one assignment of thermal hotspots to CTA perforators within a predefined periumbilical region of interest. The workflow was evaluated in 12 patients. Of 46 CTA perforators within the region of interest, 84.8% were successfully linked to thermographic hotspots, with a median spatial offset of 14.74 mm. Automated assignment excluded 76.1% of detected hotspots due to lack of anatomical correspondence, thereby reducing subjective interpretation. The proposed system enables quantitative multimodal validation of functional and anatomical imaging and provides objective support for perforator selection in clinical practice.

title: A Gaussian Primitive Data Management Framework for Efficient 3DGS Trajectory Rendering
abstract: Trajectory rendering, which renders novel views of a reconstructed 3D scene along a camera path, is a core operation in digital twins and autonomous inspection. Structured 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) renders a single view in real time by decoding sparse anchors into Gaussians on demand, but it renders a trajectory view by view: every view projects all anchors to select them, re-decodes anchors already requested by neighboring views, and runs all steps on the GPU while the CPU idles. We treat this as a spatial data management problem, where anchors are spatial objects, views are range queries, and decoded Gaussians are shared derived data, and propose GDM-GS, which removes redundancy at three levels. Within a view, an anchor index and an occluder index answer each view as a holed-frustum range query, so out-of-view and provably hidden anchors are never decoded. Across views, shared materialization decodes each requested anchor once per group of consecutive views while preserving each view's selection. Across processors, a hybrid pipeline balances selections between the CPU and the GPU before grouped decoding under bounded memory. Experiments on large-scale public scenes show that GDM-GS substantially reduces trajectory rendering latency while preserving image quality.

title: Klein four slices of the representation suspensions of $H\underline{\mathbb{F}_2}$
abstract: We study the regular slice filtration of representation spheres $S^V\wedge H\underline{M}$. For every finite group $G$, we locate all slices in an explicit interval $[n(V),k(V)]$ and show that both endpoints occur. We introduce a \emph{defect vector} to measure a slice's failure. For the Klein four-group with $\underline{\mathbb F}_2$-coefficients, a balanced defect allows us to move $S^V\wedge H\underline{\mathbb F}_2$ by certain $RO(G)$-graded cohomology classes to its $\dim V$-slice, which is again a representation sphere, while an odd defect obstructs any spherical slice. As an application, we obtain closed formulas for the bottom slice of $Σ^nH\underline{\mathbb{F}}_2$ for every $n$, recovering the computation of Guillou and Yarnall by a different method. Along the way, we determine the complete slice tower of $S^{\inftyα_i}\wedge H\underline{\mathbb F}_2$ and consequently, the partial tower for $S^{nα_i}\wedge H\underline{\mathbb F}_2$.

title: ECPack.wl: A Mathematica Package for Elliptic Curves over the Rationals and Finite Fields
abstract: We present a Mathematica package entitled ECPack.wl, where we implement many important properties and commands relevant to the study of elliptic curves over the rationals and finite fields, namely $\mathbb{Q}$ and $\mathbb{F}_q$, where $q=p^r$ and $p$ is prime. By streamlining the analysis of general elliptic curves and their transformations, ECPack.wl offers foundational computational tools for applications in high-energy physics, including elliptic Feynman integrals. This package significantly extends the functionalities of a package due to McGee in so far as we are able to study all versions of elliptic curves, such as the long Weierstrass, quartic and Legendre forms. We implement suitable transformations that are required for the general case, as well as those associated with fields of characteristic 2 and 3. Furthermore, the package computes many curve properties, such as point arithmetic, minimality checks, rank bounds and analytic rank, group structure, invariants, and the Weil and Tate pairings, over both $\mathbb{Q}$ and $\mathbb{F}_p$, as well as the Kodaira classification of the singular fibres of one-parameter families of elliptic curves, with the associated F-theory data. The package and its accompanying notebooks are available at https://github.com/DhamakedarDarsh/Mathematica-Code-and-worked-out-notebooks-for-Elliptic-Curves

title: RoShift: Lazy Shift and Weight-aware Rotation for Activation Sparsity in LLM Inference
abstract: Activation sparsity accelerates LLM decoding by skipping unnecessary weight reads and computation. However, SiLU-based LLMs exhibit little natural sparsity, and imposing high sparsity can substantially degrade accuracy. We propose RoShift, a training-free method that transforms activations into sparsity-friendly representations. RoShift introduces lazy shift, which recenters SiLU activation distributions around zero and defers correction to the end of the FFN to obtain additional sparsity. It also reduces sparsification-induced output error through rotation that jointly accounts for activation and weight information. By fusing the corrections required for shifting and rotation, RoShift translates these gains into decoding speedup. At 50% and 60% sparsity, RoShift improves average accuracy over TEAL by 1.60 and 3.29 percentage points, respectively, across five models. It achieves up to $1.72\times$ decoding speedup over the dense model on an RTX 5090 at 50% sparsity and yields a better accuracy-speedup Pareto frontier than TEAL. Code is available at https://github.com/hulahula3247/RoShift

title: Mollification Regularization and Asymptotic Correction for Analytical Expansion of BSDEs with Non-Smooth Terminal Conditions. I. Theory
abstract: The analytical expansion method for BSDEs of Zhang (2017) breaks down when the terminal condition psi has kinks or discontinuities. We replace psi by psi_epsilon = psi * rho_epsilon and derive a joint error decomposition whose expansion constants explicitly track the derivative blow-up as epsilon tends to 0. For symmetric mollifiers the leading weak bias cancels. The associated balanced rates are conditional on an explicitly stated uniform local-to-global Taylor-propagation assumption: under that assumption the benchmark (l, m, alpha) = (0, 2, 1) gives epsilon* ~ delta_t^{1/3} and weak rate 2/3. Without it, the rigorous additive bound gives no decay when m - 2l = 2; an unconditional positive rate is obtained only for m - 2l > 2. Asymptotic corrections cancel the weak bias through order epsilon^{2J}; their faster exponents are formal targets unless the auxiliary expansion errors and the Picard defect satisfy additional rate conditions, which we state explicitly. For the driver-free fixed-center scheme we identify an n-independent terminal-representation error and show that it depends on the expansion center and on the terminal representative; change-of-basis invariance does not imply centering independence. A Gaussian moment-compression layer combines whitening, a Stein recursion, and knapsack truncation with a jet-conditioned error certificate. This Part I contains the theory, with all proofs self-contained; numerical evidence and implementation measurements are reported separately in the companion paper (Part II).

title: GranularGPT: Natural-Language-Driven End-to-End Discrete Element Method Simulations
abstract: Discrete element method (DEM) simulations are widely used to investigate granular and particulate systems, but their application often requires specialized expertise in particle physics, numerical modelling, and simulation post-processing. Large language models (LLMs) offer new opportunities to simplify these workflows by enabling users to interact with simulation tools through natural language. This study offers GranularGPT, an LLM-assisted agentic framework for end-to-end DEM simulation workflows, from natural-language problem descriptions to simulation execution and automated post-processing. The framework enables users to generate DEM simulation cases, execute and monitor simulations, and automatically extract and report physical and process-level metrics. Evaluation across 60 normal-condition cases covering 12 DEM scenarios and parameter variations achieve a simulation success rate of 91.7%. In the error-handling evaluation, all 10 repairable errors are detected and 9 are successfully resolved, while all 5 non-repairable cases are correctly identified and reported. The framework automatically extracts a range of DEM-relevant metrics, including particle size distributions, packing and density measures, velocity profiles, discharge rates, mixing indices, contact force characteristics, and thermal quantities. GranularGPT provides a foundation for improving the accessibility and efficiency of DEM simulation workflows while reducing the specialized expertise required for their operation.

title: A compact non-Kähler shrinking Ricci soliton
abstract: We construct a gradient shrinking Ricci soliton on the simply-connected eight-manifold $\mathsf{SU}(3)\times_{\mathsf T^2}\mathbb{CP}^1$. This Riemannian manifold is not Einstein, is nowhere locally Kähler, is locally irreducible, and is invariant under the effective cohomogeneity one action of $\mathsf{PSU}(3)\times S^1$. This new gradient Ricci soliton is found by first constructing an approximate solution, certifying the residual, and applying a fixed-point theorem.

title: Learning a Task-Adaptive Low-Dimensional Semantic Space for Improved Visual Classification
abstract: Semantic visual classification commonly aligns visual embeddings with semantic spaces induced by pretrained text encoders. However, such spaces are typically high-dimensional, weakly aligned with visual feature geometry, and insufficiently discriminative for downstream classification tasks. We propose TaSS, a framework for learning a task-adaptive low-dimensional semantic space that preserves semantic structure while explicitly optimizing class separability. TaSS is constructed through a parameterized geometry transformation of pretrained text embeddings that enlarges inter-class margins via distance reshaping and improves intra-class compactness through prototype-preserving semantic constraints. The resulting semantic space maintains meaningful semantic relationships while producing a discriminative geometry tailored for classification. Frozen visual encoder features are subsequently aligned to TaSS using a lightweight MLP, enabling improved discriminative learning without fine-tuning pretrained backbones. We further provide theoretical analysis showing that TaSS preserves semantic consistency while enforcing enhanced inter-class separation and controlled intra-class variance. Extensive experiments on skeleton-based human action recognition, video classification, and image classification benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements over existing semantic alignment approaches, with gains exceeding 3 percentage points on average and up to 8.5 points on challenging datasets.

title: $L$-systems on the large Witt design
abstract: Let $L=\{0,1,2,3,4,8\}$, associated with the large Witt design $S(5,8,24)$, and let $m(n,24,L)$ be the maximum size of a family of $24$-element subsets of an $n$-element set whose distinct members have intersection sizes in $L$. We prove that there are positive constants $c,C,n_0$ such that, for every $n\geq n_0$, \[ cn^{316/63}\leq m(n,24,L)\leq Cn^{169/29}. \] We also obtain similar results for the systems associated with $S(4,7,23)$, $S(3,6,22)$, and $S(3,4,14)$. The upper bounds follow from a non-Shannon information inequality and disprove conjectures of Kupavskii and Terekhov. The lower bounds follow from an algebraic construction for arbitrary Steiner systems.

title: Bending Rigidity of Smectic Filaments
abstract: Many biological and engineered filaments exhibit internal structure or fluidity that alters their elastic behavior. We study the elasticity of microscale filamentous smectic condensates, grown during liquid-liquid crystal phase separation. We use a Fourier analysis of their thermal bend fluctuations to measure their persistence length, which follows a non-classic linear scaling with their cross-sectional area, in contrast to the classic quadratic scaling for elastic filaments. We rationalize this scaling using the Helfrich energy to compute the free energy of bending a filament with internal smectic fluid ordering. Our analysis then provides a direct method to measure the bend modulus K, which quantifies the rigidity of smectic layers; providing the first method to directly measure K for dispersed smectic phases. We quantify the softening of filaments in the presence of shorter alkyl-tail mesogen dopants, decreasing K by up to ~35%. Out results suggest how nanoscale smectic organization and molecular composition determine filament-scale elasticity, informing the control of filament mechanics and self-assembly in biomimetic and engineered materials.

title: A Staggered Discontinuous Galerkin Neural Network Method with a Computable Error Decomposition
abstract: We develop a staggered discontinuous Galerkin neural network (SDGNN) method for scalar elliptic problems with a computable error decomposition. The staggered discontinuous Galerkin (SDG) method requires only local continuity of its trial functions and gives a square, inf-sup stable system without stabilization parameters; we carry this structure over to neural networks. Networks defined on the patches of a staggered mesh satisfy the SDG continuity conditions for all values of the network parameters, and the loss is the squared dual norm of the SDG weak residual. We show that the loss is equivalent, with computable constants, to the square of the training error, the distance between the SDG projection of the network and the SDG finite element approximation, so that the full error is bounded by the discretization error, a multiple of the square root of the loss, and the network projection error. The weak residual requires no derivatives of the networks, the boundary and convection terms carry no penalty or stabilization weights, and the scalar trial functions may jump across the midlines of the primal cells. Numerical experiments show that the square root of the loss tracks the error during the training, that prescribed jumps across a square and a circular interface are captured consistently over the initializations, and that the method is more accurate than physics-informed neural networks at the same parameter counts.

title: AsymEEF: Bimanual Manipulation with Asymmetric End Effectors
abstract: Teleoperated demonstrations are costly to collect and rarely reusable across end-effectors with different kinematics and action spaces. This burden grows in bimanual manipulation, where each end-effector pair may require new data. We present AsymEEF, a framework for executable cross-end-effector demonstration generation and unified bimanual policy learning. Given a small source dataset, AsymEEF transfers demonstrations to heterogeneous combinations of two-, three-, and five-fingered end-effectors without additional teleoperation. Kinematic teacher anchors provide geometric supervision, while sparse real-world X-Calib anchors correct discrepancies in grasp execution. A shared encoder maps wrist poses and actuator states to a morphology-agnostic latent space, and a morphology-conditioned decoder reconstructs target commands. Generated trajectories undergo replay filtering for task-level executability. The representation also supports a unified bimanual visuomotor policy trained across multiple pairs. Across four simulated and six real-world tasks, AsymEEF improves replay success over adapted transfer baselines, achieves a mean replay-valid expansion gain of 16.6 times in simulation, and is evaluated through downstream policy training on real robots. Project website: https://asymeef.vercel.app/.

title: Vision-Language Grounded Semantic Navigation for Autonomous Mobile Robots
abstract: Language-guided navigation enables mobile robots to interpret natural language commands and navigate toward user-specified targets in unstructured environments. However, integrating open-vocabulary visual perception with classical robotics pipelines for mapping and navigation remains a challenging problem. In this work, we present a complete ROS2-based system that combines frontier-based exploration, open-vocabulary object detection using Grounding DINO, depth-based 3D localization, and semantic mapping to enable end-to-end vision-language grounded navigation in simulation. The system accepts natural language commands such as ``go to the yellow box,'' detects candidate objects from RGB images using text prompts, estimates their positions in the world frame, and generates navigation goals executed by the Nav2 stack. In a Gazebo-based indoor environment with a TurtleBot3 robot, the system autonomously explored the room, detected three of the five target objects, and successfully executed both natural language navigation commands tested, without task-specific training. The results indicate that open-vocabulary grounding models can be integrated into classical navigation pipelines, though performance is limited by detection uncertainty, depth-based localization error, and incomplete exploration coverage. These findings highlight both the feasibility and current limitations of deploying vision-language grounded navigation systems using lightweight, CPU-only architectures.

title: Schauder bases and local unconditional structure in Hardy spaces of Dirichlet series
abstract: We prove that among the Hardy spaces $\mathcal{H}^p$ of Dirichlet series with $1\le p<\infty$, only $\mathcal{H}^2$ has local unconditional structure. Consequently, $\mathcal{H}^p$ admits an unconditional basis exactly when $p=2$. At the endpoint $p=1$, we also construct a Schauder basis of Dirichlet polynomials and give an explicit formula for each basis vector. Together, these results answer the basis questions posed by Aleman, Olsen and Saksman, as well as the question of Saksman and Seip concerning an unconditional basis for $\mathcal{H}^1$.

title: Inversion of magnetization anisotropy in low magnetic fields for textured Bi2223 superconductor due to magnetic responses from superconducting crystallites and intercrystalline boundaries
abstract: A detailed study of the magnetic anisotropy of a bulk textured high-temperature superconductor Bi2223 has been carried out. In the range of moderate and high fields (up to 1 kOe), the difference ΔM between the upper and lower branches of the magnetization hysteresis loop is larger when the external magnetic field H is parallel to the normal of the texturing plane (H||NTP) than when H is parallel to the texturing plane (H {\perp} NTP). This magnetic anisotropy is typical for such textured superconductors. However, at small values of the maximum applied field Hmax (up to 15 Oe at a temperature T = 78 K), an anomalous inversion of anisotropy has been found: ΔM(H||NTP) < ΔM(H {\perp} NTP). It has been established that in the field range up to ~30 Oe (the first penetration field into Bi2223 crystallites is about 30 Oe at T = 78 K), the magnetic hysteresis is determined only by the magnetic flux trapped in the intercrystallite boundary subsystem. The pronounced platelet shape of the Bi2223 crystallites leads to partial screening of the external field inside the sample when the field is oriented parallel to the crystallite c-axis. The observed inverse anisotropy ΔM(H||NTP) < ΔM(H {\perp} NTP) has been explained by the fact that the effective magnetic field into the intercrystallite boundaries is smaller for the H||NTP orientation than for H {\perp} NTP. Therefore, when the field is oriented H||NTP, a larger external field is required for magnetic flux to penetrate into the sample inner than for the H {\perp} NTP orientation.

title: When Better Artificial Intelligence Widens the Adoption Gap in Health Care
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) can assist healthcare providers in clinical practice or replace services for which they are paid. We model how provider influence shapes two policy choices. The first is adoption, the share of cases in which coverage is switched to care using AI. The second is the review requirement, the number of paid reviews that must accompany AI when it is used in clinical care. Assistance can lower providers' costs and increase their profits while leaving paid reviews unaffected. However, increasingly capable AI may support autonomous use that can replace reviews and reduce providers' profits. Provider gains from adoption first rise and subsequently fall as AI capability improves. Hence, providers oppose sufficiently autonomous AI if their lost income from reviews exceeds savings from better assistance. Opposition to AI adoption arises earlier for AI that displaces more reviews. When providers can influence adoption but not the review requirement, their opposition causes under-adoption. The patient value forgone at the margin grows as AI improves. At interior policies, provider influence over both decisions widens adoption and raises review requirements above the patient optimum.

title: One-Shot Calibration via Model Editing
abstract: Model editing aims to correct errors in large, pretrained models by replacing model generations with user-provided responses. Existing editors assume a single target answer for each edit. However, many real tasks inherently entail uncertainty, resulting in multiple plausible answers with varying likelihoods in user feedback. Such feedback forms a target distribution to not only correct but also calibrate model generations. We therefore propose SoftEdit, the first model editor to leverage uncertainty in user responses and perform one-shot calibration during editing. To generalize calibration to unseen samples, SoftEdit uses co-plausibility relationships between answers while preserving real distributional shifts, balancing the new distributional generality-locality tradeoff. Across three language models, three vision-language models, and two large datasets, SoftEdit achieves state-of-the-art performance, ultimately showing that uncertainty in user responses enables generalizable calibration of pretrained models beyond single-answer corrections.

title: Structure-Preserving Neural Time-Stepping for Gradient-Flow PDEs via Onsager's Variational Principle
abstract: We propose a unified Onsager-based neural time-stepping (ONTS) framework for solving gradient-flow partial differential equations with conserved and nonconserved dynamics. Unlike conventional neural time-stepping methods that directly parameterize the evolving state, the proposed framework employs spatial neural networks to approximate the Onsager process variables, namely, the rates in nonconserved systems and the fluxes in conserved systems. Within this Eulerian framework, we develop three complementary schemes: an explicit least-squares scheme (E-ONTS), an implicit variational scheme (I-ONTS), and a predictor--corrector scheme (PC-ONTS) that combines explicit prediction with safeguarded implicit correction. For conserved systems, the flux-based formulation guarantees discrete mass conservation under periodic or no-flux boundary conditions. Furthermore, we rigorously establish unconditional discrete energy stability for the implicit schemes, provided that a suitable descent criterion is satisfied, without requiring global minimization of the neural variational objective. Numerical experiments for the heat, Allen--Cahn, Cahn--Hilliard, Fokker--Planck, and coupled Poisson--Nernst--Planck equations demonstrate the accuracy, robustness, and structure-preserving properties of the proposed framework.

title: Strict Capabilities with a PNVI Escape Hatch
abstract: Capability systems enforce memory safety by tying pointers to their originating allocations, preventing forgery, use-after-free, and out-of-bounds accesses. Yet conventional capabilities are simultaneously too strict and not strict enough for C: they reject common low-level idioms involving integer casts or raw pointer bytes, while failing to enforce type correctness and sub-object bounds. Proposed Provenance Not Via Integers (PNVI) semantics expose this tension by permitting representation-level manipulation while retaining strict rules for ordinary pointer operations. We argue that these requirements call for two interoperable abstractions rather than a compromise within one. Strict capabilities enforce provenance, liveness, type correctness, and (sub-)object bounds; ordinary capability operations preserve these invariants. Exposed representations are non-dereferenceable, integer-like values that support arbitrary integer and byte-level manipulation under PNVI semantics while retaining unforgeability guarantees. They carry no directly usable memory-access authority: converting an exposed representation back to a strict capability reconstructs provenance under PNVI rules and validates type and bounds before access. Thus, low-level C idioms can use an explicit escape hatch without weakening ordinary capability derivation. We realize this design using Fully Randomized Pointers (FRP) and dynamic type metadata. Evaluation on low-level pointer idioms, Juliet tests, and existing C benchmarks shows that strict type and sub-object safety can coexist with low-level pointer manipulation.

title: Memory-Efficient Speculative Decoding with Quantized Draft KV Cache
abstract: Speculative decoding reduces generation cost, but it stores two KV caches: one for the target model and one for the draft model. We reduce this extra memory by quantizing the draft cache. The target cache and verifier remain in BF16, so that compression cannot change the target model's final correction rule. We first study how to divide precision between keys and values. A naive per-token quantizer makes keys appear much more sensitive: splitting a 12-bit budget, K8V4 beats K4V8 in acceptance by 10.87pp. However, with grouped per-channel keys, the gap becomes -0.25pp. A controlled Qwen test confirms that changing only the key quantizer can erase or reverse the preferred bit split. Hence, following KIVI, we propose K4V4 quantization with per-channel keys and per-token values. Across six model pairs, our method reduces draft cache memory by 66.20%, and combined memory across both caches by 23.95%. Mean acceptance drops from 57.93% to 57.14%, only 1.36% relative. Overall, quantized draft caches can make speculative decoding more memory efficient; as a predictive principle for efficient AI design, key and value precision must be co-designed with the quantizer layout.

title: Weight-Space Programming Changes How an LLM Uses Python for Computational Biology
abstract: Weight-space programming allows a language model to edit another model's weights without gradient-based training. We used Claude Opus 5.5 to edit Qwen3.5-0.8B and investigated how the edits changed its use of Python on computational biology problems. We compared four initial edited checkpoints with the original model on 50 test problems across three test seeds, yielding 600 paired evaluations. Strictly correct answers increased from 44 to 77, and technically correct answers, which included correct final values rejected for formatting, increased from 64 to 100. Repeated Python calls decreased from 1,834 to 1,044. Among the 64 pairs in which only the edited response was technically correct, the original model had already computed the correct value in 36 but did not submit a technically correct final answer. The edited model corrected the computation in 13 of the 64 pairs. With six additional checkpoints on the same 50 problems, technically correct answers rose from 96 to 154 across 900 pairs. We explored three selected problems with ten test seeds for each of ten checkpoints. On the melting-temperature problem, correct Python outputs decreased from 60 to 22 while technically correct final answers increased from 0 to 18. Weight editing changed both the calculations Qwen ran and whether it submitted a correct answer.

title: Calibrated Functional Prediction from Overlapping Nonlinear Observations
abstract: We study prediction of nonlinear audit functionals from scalar observations of a shared hidden table state. For Schur-rational operators, local Gaussian projections yield a common sparse kernel for overlapping tasks, repeated row identities, and cross-row dependence. Shared-state residual samples extend this kernel through a positive-semidefinite feature representation. Positive matrix integration and sample-value enclosures connect the original inputs to the actual saved hybrid prediction. A sorted calibration-role perturbation bound then certifies its complete finite-pool pinball risk. Independent complete-loss selection chooses the ridge, score scale, and residual weight, while task-rank calibration supplies an upper endpoint. Evaluation uses twenty new reference contexts per dataset at two task sizes, giving 400 conditions across ten benchmark populations. The mean dataset complete-loss ratios are 0.9977 to the degree-two kernel, 0.9961 to matched complete-MC shrinkage, and 0.9911 to the retrospective minimum over 174 public configurations. The last ratio has a paired reference-bootstrap interval of [0.9898,0.9927]. On 40 profiles at coefficient tolerance $10^{-7}$, Gamma quadrature has a geometric mean cold-time ratio of .0646 to strengthened Arb/Petras integration.

title: sqrtVINS-Based 360 Visual-Inertial SLAM Systems: Hilti-Trimble SLAM Challenge 2026 Entry
abstract: This report describes our submission to the 2026 Hilti-Trimble SLAM Challenge. The system is a 360-camera visual-inertial pipeline that uses only the provided dual-fisheye image streams and IMU measurements. First, raw images are preprocessed with low-light enhancement and static/dynamic masking, and then fed into a $\sqrt{\text{VINS}}$ frontend as the local odometry, with deep learning-based SuperPoint features, ELSED line segments, and LightGlue matching. The resulting trajectory is refined using a GTSAM-based backend that performs tightly-coupled factor graph optimization with SALAD global descriptor and visual bundle adjustment (BA). The backend performs local-to-global structureless BA, tightly regularized intrinsic and extrinsic refinement, and global scale adjustment supported by the known inter-camera baseline and cross-view constraints. The design targets long indoor sequences with dark regions, repetitive corridors, dynamic objects, and limited geometric parallax, while keeping the pipeline reproducible in the provided ROS2 workspace. Fig. 1 demonstrates that our proposed method aligns well with the floorplan across several indoor sequences.

title: ToolGraph as a Q-Function for Test-Time Scaling of Tool-Use Agents
abstract: Tool-use agents must chain interdependent calls, yet which outputs satisfy which later inputs in a deployed catalog is not something a general-purpose language model reliably infers from tool descriptions alone. We compile that structure once into a reusable external representation. ToolGraph is a directed, weighted dependency graph over a tool catalog: parameter matching and interventional probes, which execute a candidate chain with and without its proposed predecessor, propose edges whose evidence is combined into an edge confidence. Prior work uses such graphs to retrieve tools, search for tool paths, or score the next call. We ask instead whether the same structure can supply a \emph{multi-step} value by composing graph paths into a goal-conditioned action value \(Q(s,a,g)\). We study three estimators (dynamic programming over entity sets, a GraphSAGE estimator distilled from it, and an LLM scorer conditioned on graph evidence) plus a verbalizer that returns action--goal feedback to the agent, which keeps final action selection. Across two tool-use benchmarks and three backbones, we compare value ranking against personalized-PageRank retrieval over the identical graph, and against direct and reflective agents. Composition pays off only when the estimator also reads the concrete state: the LLM estimator improves on PageRank in every benchmark--backbone setting, by \(8.3\) points on average, while the two purely structural estimators fall below it, because a value defined over tool types cannot separate a correct tool called with a wrong argument. Graph construction is a one-time cost; we report it separately rather than assume it amortized away (at our scale it is comparable to request-time cost) and sweep four knobs controlling how much graph evidence to expose against success and tokens.

title: OrthoMark: Place Recognition with Point-Anchored Orthographic Height Mark
abstract: LiDAR place recognition provides the loop closures of Simultaneous Localization and Mapping(SLAM). Perspective from Z-axis, a gravity-aligned scan is an orthographic map of the scene, and a revisit from another position and heading moves this map rigidly in the plane, a motion that a polar Fourier spectrum ignores and phase correlation recovers. Along the vertical, the heights of the returns describe the structures, but which heights are observed depends on the range, because the sensor's vertical field of view cuts nearby structures low; height thus misleads a global key, yet is decisive once two scans are aligned and compared cell by cell where they overlap. We present \method, a training-free method built on one principle: two LiDAR scans can only be compared through features computed from the same geometric surfaces in both scans. \method retrieves candidates with a translation- and rotation-invariant polar spectrum of the bird's-eye view (BEV), 1.9,KB per keyframe, and verifies each candidate by estimating its planar pose through phase correlation and scoring it with \emph{point-anchored height columns}: every BEV cell keeps a 16-bit mask of the heights of its own returns; within a session, the score is weighted by the expected overlap of the two scans' sensing ranges, computed from their distance. We show that this vertical link pays off in verification but hurts in retrieval, where what a height slice contains depends on the range to the structure. For single robot, \method has the highest AP of the training-free methods without 3D registration on the KITTI development sequences; across robots, on all multi-robot sequences, it matches or exceeds RING++ at 1/350 of its descriptor size and closes more inter-robot loops than the learned BEVPlace++ on all tests.

title: Stability threshold of Couette flow for two-dimensional MHD equations on the infinite channel
abstract: In this paper, we study the stability threshold of the two-dimensional incompressible MHD equations near Couette flow and a constant horizontal magnetic field \((β,0)\) on \(\mathbb T\times\mathbb R\). For \(N>10\), \(0<ν,μ\le1\) and \(|β|\ge(ν+μ)/(3\sqrt{νμ})\), we prove global stability for initial perturbations of size \(δ_N\min\{ν,μ\}^{1/3}\) in \(H^N\), where \(δ_N>0\) is independent of \(ν,μ,β\). We also obtain enhanced dissipation of the nonzero horizontal modes on the time scale \(\min\{ν,μ\}^{-1/3}\), together with inviscid damping of the vertical components. The proof combines time-dependent Fourier multipliers with an energy correction constructed using the Alfvén oscillations. By combining the nonlinear terms arising from this correction, we obtain the cancellation needed to close the energy estimates at the $1/3$ scale.

title: Nonsense rank correlations between independent random walks
abstract: Yule's nonsense correlation persists for Spearman's rho and Kendall's tau between independent random walks. Neither coefficient concentrates at zero as the sample size grows. For centred random walks with finite increment variances, we derive a universal joint limit expressed through Brownian occupation functionals. Integral formulas give limiting variances of approximately 0.222 and 0.108, respectively, below the Pearson value of 0.241. Rank correlations thus reduce the limiting dispersion on their respective coefficient scales. We prove that both marginal limits have symmetric densities and represent them exactly as limits of polynomial densities determined by Gaussian moment integrals. Spearman's conventional t test and Kendall's normal approximation are asymptotically invalid, with rejection probabilities tending to one under process independence.

title: Dynamic Shaping: Acquiring Interfaces and Constructing Execution over Frozen Pretrained Components
abstract: We introduce Dynamic Shaping, a method for constructing executable neural arrangements through acquired response and partial-derivative interfaces over frozen pretrained components. The method learns local descriptions of available computation, ranks component rebindings using task-gradient alignment, transports the current interface across a rebinding, and retains changes through behavioral feedback. Continuous interface acquisition uses proximal policy optimization; the source coefficients remain fixed. We derive an exact identity relating transport error in component responses and partials to changes in action logits and their sensitivities. A pixels-only ViZDoom Basic study evaluates first task acquisition without a competent reference controller, demonstrations or intact response targets.
