The widespread use of large language models (LLMs) further intensifies this problem by making hateful content easier and cheaper to generate at scale. Although stronger hate speech detectors continue to be proposed, their performance remains uneven across target identity groups and different forms of hateful expression, partly because existing training data provides only limited coverage of these cases. Thus, we introduce PersonaHate, a scalable persona-driven data synthesis pipeline for constructing diverse hate speech datasets. PersonaHate begins with a large persona pool of 457K personas drawn from two real-world sources. Conditioned on selected personas from this pool, it prompts eight LLMs to generate hate speech across 34 identity groups and performs multi-judge annotation to obtain reliable labels. The resulting corpus contains 791K samples, from which we curate a 67K group-balanced training set. Our modular design also supports extension to new identity groups, generators, and emerging hate targets. Built upon this dataset, we evaluate two detector training strategies: training from scratch and further fine-tuning. Results show that all trained models achieve competitive performance across four widely used external benchmarks. Notably, a 184M-parameter DeBERTa-v3 model trained on PersonaHate reaches 77.5% average F1 and 79.4% average accuracy, outperforming OpenAI's Moderation API on HateBenchSet and MHS. Furthermore, fine-tuning Llama-3.1-8B raises its average F1 from 70.7% to 78.4%, a gain of 7.7 percentage points, surpassing LlamaGuard-3, Meta's official safety model based on the same Llama-3.1-8B architecture, on three of four benchmarks. These results show that PersonaHate can substantially improve the robustness and cross-dataset generalization of hate speech detectors.

title: A Log-Timescale Perturbation Bound for Selective State Space Models at Every Sequence Length
abstract: Mamba models deployed on streaming data, such as limit order book updates, run far past the sequence lengths they were trained on. A guarantee on how much a small change of input can move the hidden state therefore has to hold at every length. The closest existing bound we know of measures the change of the timescale additively, and it grows linearly with the sequence length unless the timescale is bounded away from zero. In this paper, we measure the change on a log scale instead. The key observation is that the decay factor of each step then moves by at most a fixed fraction of that step's input weight, so the per-step errors cannot pile up. Using this, we prove that two runs of a selective-scan cell from a common start stay within a bound that holds at every length, shrinks to zero with the size of the change and needs no lower bound on the timescale. We give a construction showing that, for small changes, this bound is within a factor of about 2 of the best possible, and we extend it to the update used in Mamba's released code when the timescale is bounded above. We then evaluate block-level bounds built from the theorem on two small models trained on one day of order book data. With a bounded timescale, a bound built on the existing analysis is tighter than ours for at most the first 8 steps. With Mamba's softplus timescale, whose certified lower bound is as small as $10^{-21}$, it is looser at every length. Our bounds hold for every input to a block, but they remain more than five orders of magnitude above the changes that gradient attacks find.

title: Robust Decision Curve Analysis for Survival Risk Prediction Models in the Presence of Informative Censoring
abstract: Decision curve analysis (DCA) is recommended for evaluating the clinical utility of prediction models by quantifying net benefit (NB). Conventional NB estimators for survival outcomes rely on the assumption that censoring is non-informative, potentially yielding biased estimates and misleading decisions when this assumption is violated. We propose a robust estimator of survival NB using conditional inverse probability of censoring weighting (CIPCW). In simulation studies, we compared its performance against the conventional approach across censoring mechanisms, censoring model specifications, censoring rates, and decision thresholds, in terms of relative bias, relative root mean squared error (RMSE), and 90% confidence interval coverage. Under non-informative censoring, both estimators performed comparably, with relative bias below 1% and coverage close to the nominal level. Under informative censoring, conventional estimators underestimated the true NB by up to 58% with coverage as low as 1%, whereas the CIPCW estimator had a relative bias of at most 4%, coverage of at least 78% and consistently lower relative RMSE. As a case study, we illustrated its use in validating a breast cancer recurrence-free survival model to guide intensified adjuvant therapy in the German Breast Cancer Study Group (GBSG) cohort. Using the model was the best strategy at some clinically relevant thresholds, but accounting for potential informative censoring changed the best strategy to treating all patients, showing that informative censoring can change the conclusions drawn from DCA. When censoring may be informative, we recommend CIPCW-based NB estimation in DCA for survival outcomes.

title: ThermLeT: Transformer-based Temperature Prediction for 2.5D Chiplet Architecture
abstract: The drive toward heterogeneous 2.5D chiplet packages promises unmatched performance and customization, yet the resulting density amplifies thermal challenges. To facilitate rapid design space exploration, we present ThermLeT, a multimodal transformer-based, scale invariant surrogate that integrates power density maps, spatial coordinate embeddings, material properties and heat transfer rate to predict steady state temperature in 13 ms, about four orders of magnitude faster than conventional finite element solvers such as ANSYS. To train the transformer model, we also create a dataset of 6,221 chiplet layouts perturbed from three representative architectures. On a 150 sample test set, ThermLeT achieves an RMSE of 3.16°C and an MAE of 2.24°C, improving accuracy by 35% over ThermEDGe and by 71% over HotSpot, while running approximately 6x and 11x lower inference latencies respectively. Ablation studies confirm robust generalization to unseen floorplans. Code and dataset available at https://github.com/MicroSystemsDesignLab/ThermLeT

title: SCAN: Site-Aware Collaborative Privacy-Preserving Adaptation of Vision-Language Models for Neurological Disease Classification
abstract: Worldwide neuroimaging data could strengthen diagnostic foundation models, but privacy rules often prevent centralizing brain MRI scans. We present SCAN, a site-aware collaborative adaptation framework for Neurological Disease Classification that lets new sites adapt a 3D medical vision-language model (VLM) without retraining or sharing patient scans. Each site keeps exact class prototypes for local prediction and can share privacy-protected class summaries: norm-bounded sums and counts perturbed once with calibrated noise. Using 7,641 scans from 67 sites across 12 countries, covering Alzheimer's disease (AD), stroke, epilepsy and controls, we assess local adaptation, cross-site benefits, and effects on existing sites. At seven unseen sites, the frozen VLM's zero-shot AUCs were 0.833-0.945 for AD and stroke. Training-free local prototypes improved epilepsy AUC at three sites from 0.598/0.625/0.508 to 0.684/0.729/0.762 and AD AUC at one site from 0.833 to 0.863, nearly matching a classifier trained at each site (mean AUC 0.757 vs. 0.759). With differential privacy ($ε$ = 4), new sites contributed without materially reducing accuracy at existing sites (AUC change $\leq$0.2%), although gains from sharing were limited, and membership attacks performed near chance. SCAN offers hospitals a worldwide framework to adapt and share brain MRI VLMs without exchanging scans or retraining.

title: Eight in Ten LLMs Leak System-Prompt Secrets: Nevan, an Agentic Capture-the-Flag Study
abstract: We audit instruction-hierarchy enforcement across 363 text-in/text-out models from the OpenRouter catalog. The research question we answer with this experiment is which models disclose a protected secret embedded in the system prompt, and through which techniques. Each model guards a secret 16-character flag set in its system prompt, while an artificial intelligence (AI) agent (OpenCode, powered by DeepSeek V4.1 Flash), steered by a human researcher, tries to persuade it to emit the flag. The flag was exfiltrated from 296 of the 363 models, plus four models released after the initial catalog freeze, for 300 captures in total. Of these, 170 involved a non-English language pivot, most often French. Each capture shows that a model ranked a user request above its system instruction at least once. It does not show that the model provably resists untested attacks, nor that it would consistently leak semantically sensitive data, nor that it is vulnerable to harmful-content jailbreaks. For practitioners, we draw three lessons: do not store secrets in system prompts, enforce critical behavior outside the model with output validation and deterministic checks, and do not let a large language model (LLM) judge be the sole decider of consequential outcomes.

title: Operating an Agent-Driven Dataset Factory: Discovery, Construction, and Public Release
abstract: Turning public data into prediction datasets requires connecting source discovery, task definition, construction, and distribution. We deployed Dataset Factory to perform these steps continuously under a standing release policy. Bounded language-model tasks interpret sources, write construction code, and review task meaning; deterministic software manages state, workers, retries, and publication. Over 81.53 hours, the factory published 14 datasets at an estimated recurring operating expenditure of about \$2.74 per publication. The accounting includes failed attempts, inference, workers, and hosting. Separate agents completed prediction experiments on all twelve evaluated releases. Source review nevertheless identified a task whose construction filters contradicted its population declaration. The original reviewer accepted later-record exclusions without reconciling them with the published selection rule. This experience documents an operating source-to-release workflow and shows why successful execution and consumer use need separate checks of task meaning.

title: Weight-space programming for tractor guidance controller: large language models natively write neural network weights that steer a real tractor
abstract: Weight-space programming is a process where a large language model reads and writes the weights of a neural network directly, guided by a natural language specification, without an optimiser or gradient descent. This study applies it to automatic tractor guidance, where a 253-parameter neural network steers along paths of lines and arcs and must be adapted when the machine changes, such as a slower steering actuator. GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1 (also 5.2) edited the network for our research tractor using a small budget of simulated evaluations to repair a network trained for another tractor and write a controller into a network with zero weights. We compared them with an evolution strategy, gradient descent and pure pursuit in simulation and on the real tractor. Both models read the network and analysed the closed loop with control theory correctly, and Fable's repair without simulation succeeded only occasionally. With simulated feedback, both models repaired the trained network in single sessions and wrote a working controller from zero weights, whereas from zero the evolution strategy found none. The controllers written from zero were sparse and in a classical cascaded structure; one model edited the trained network while the other replaced it. Gradient descent reached higher accuracy with far more simulation, and all language model controllers steered the real tractor without intervention, with errors of the same order as pure pursuit. Language models can program the weights of a neural controller directly, much as control engineers design one. We call this Weight-Space Engineering.

title: OCCAM: Improved Single-Cell Representation Learning and Perturbation Effect Prediction
abstract: Predicting the effects of genetic perturbations requires models that generalize beyond observed cell contexts and gene combinations. We introduce Occam, a multilayer perceptron (MLP) framework for representation learning and perturbation-effect prediction. Occam combines cell representations learned through denoising with gene interaction, text, and protein-sequence features. It achieves the highest aggregate representation scores for perturbation information and cell-type preservation with batch integration. In cross-context few-shot prediction, a perturbation and a cell context are each observed during training, but never together. Occam better captures the measured response patterns for these unobserved combinations than four retrained competitors or direct transfer of the same perturbation's measured effects from other training cell lines. Without fine-tuning, Occam best distinguishes perturbations among the evaluated models and simple baselines in cell lines held out from predictor training, across seen and unseen assays. Predicting expression levels accurately in these settings remains challenging. For double perturbations, which target two genes simultaneously, Occam composes learned single-gene responses to better capture the combined response and reduce expression error compared with competing models and summed single-gene effects. These gains extend to both strongly additive and weakly additive responses. Together, these results support simple MLPs for cell representation learning and perturbation-effect prediction across contexts and gene combinations.

title: Convergence of discrete exterior calculus for the Hodge-Dirac and Hodge-Laplace problems on surfaces
abstract: We prove that discrete exterior calculus converges for the Hodge-Dirac and Hodge-Laplace problems on every closed oriented Riemannian surface. The proof applies the error bounds of a companion paper on finite element exterior calculus. We prove and use that every closed oriented surface, with any metric, carries uniformly regular families of triangulations that are acute with a uniform margin.

title: Forbidden Substructures Preserved by the Blob Graph Operation
abstract: The blob graph $G^\circ$ of a graph $G$ has a vertex for each non-empty connected vertex subset of $G$, with two distinct subsets adjacent whenever they intersect or are joined by an edge of $G$. This construction has been used in reductions from induced subgraph optimisation problems to maximum-weight independent set, where the preservation of forbidden substructures is essential. We completely characterise the graphs $H$ for which excluding $H$ from $G$ guarantees that $G^\circ$ also excludes $H$, under six containment relations. For subgraphs, minors, and topological minors, preservation holds exactly when $H$ has at most two vertices. For induced subgraphs, it holds exactly when $H$ is a linear forest. For induced topological minors, it holds exactly when $H$ is triangle-free and has maximum degree at most two. For induced minors, it holds exactly when $H$ is triangle-free and every neighbour of a vertex of degree at least three has degree exactly two. These classifications unify and extend preservation results previously established for particular forbidden graphs in algorithmic applications.

title: A Catalog of Young Stellar Objects in the Lagoon Nebula
abstract: M8, the Lagoon Nebula, has been known for more than 100 years as a region forming stars. It is (in projection) very close to if not in the Galactic Bulge. As a result, the source surface density is very high and source confusion is a substantial challenge. Because of the location, there have been many surveys that serendipitously observed M8, in addition to studies specifically targeting it. But to this point, there has been no effort to resolve source confusion across all the existing catalogs, spanning many different wavelengths, sensitivities, and spatial resolutions. We have done all of this source reconciliation, and present the merged catalog here. The net result is 3019 YSOs with largely photometric data and/or YSO selection from ~50 different origins, primarily ranging from $g$-band through 25 um, but with a significant number of X-ray sources, and some data of limited sensitivity out through 70-450 um. The catalog includes several flags that enable users to select, e.g., the YSOs that have been identified as young by the most studies, or the YSOs with the most multi-wavelength counterparts, or the ones with the clearest IR excesses. We use this catalog in a companion paper; it will also be of use in, e.g., future SPHEREx and Roman work.

title: Structural balance in complex networks: from measurement to dynamics, emergence and implications
abstract: Structural balance theory, introduced in social psychology to describe how friendly and hostile ties organize into consistent patterns, has been reinterpreted through statistical physics and complex networks. In the classical formulation, a triad with positive or negative links, representing friendship and hostility, is balanced when the product of its signs is positive; a balanced network splits into at most two internally friendly, mutually hostile groups. This review synthesizes how the triadic formulation has been extended to a statistical-ensemble perspective in which balance is encoded by immanent three-body interactions described by a proper Hamiltonian, balanced configurations correspond to low-energy states, and balance measures serve as order parameters for transitions between consensus, polarization, and disorder. We organize the field into three sections: Measurement, Dynamics and Emergence, and Implications. In Measurement, we compare measures of structural balance and null models, and show that conclusions for a given system depend on the chosen measure and null model. In Dynamics and Emergence, we review deterministic and stochastic systems, including the gradient, Hamiltonian, and local triad models, and examine how noise, topology, and competing mechanisms determine whether balance emerges. In Implications, we survey consequences for belief formation, opinion contagion dynamics, polarization, international relations, and markets. Across domains, the evidence is strongest for local triadic stability and weakest for system-wide balance. Balance is not synonymous with harmony: balanced structures can reflect cohesion, polarization, or persistent conflict. Its empirical relevance is well supported in some reciprocal social systems, but remains less settled in biological and other complex networks.

title: Solver to System: LLM Reasoning Across Representations and Execution in Scientific Simulation
abstract: Simulators based on partial differential equations (PDEs) are widely used to model physical systems, but generating and interpreting PDE solver code with large language models (LLMs) remains challenging. Scientific simulation code is a useful testbed for LLM scientific reasoning because (1) one system can be represented by code, equations, natural language, and numerical trajectories and (2) code can execute successfully while implementing invalid physics. We introduce Solver2System, a dataset of PDE solvers with multiple representations, controlled corruptions, and lexical perturbations, to evaluate whether LLMs can recover the underlying physical system through (1) cross-representation consistency and (2) static and agentic detection of physical invalidity. Across eight open-weight models, LLMs systematically favor some representations when evidence conflicts, and lexical perturbations to code alter interpretation of other unchanged representations. Execution improves physical-validity judgments, but weaker agents can judge correctly without identifying the causal defect. Thus, LLMs may reach correct judgments despite inconsistent representation reconciliation or causal misdiagnosis.

title: Learning Effects in Concept Association: A Study with Multidimensional Scaling
abstract: This work presents a study designed to investigate learning effects in the association of scientific concepts. In the experiment, high school students worked with advance organizers, as proposed by Ausubel, and with an Arduino board to play songs they had programmed. Numerical Association of Concepts Tests (TANC), administered before and after the instructional intervention, were analyzed using ALSCAL, a multidimensional scaling program available in the SPSS statistical package. The results strongly suggest that TANC is sensitive to changes in students' cognitive structures and that AlSCAL is capable of extracting structural information from the tests.

title: Supersaturation and reconfiguration diameter of independent transversals
abstract: Consider the collection of independent transversals of a vertex-partitioned graph of maximum degree $Δ$. It is a classic result that when all parts have size at least $2Δ$, the collection is nonempty. Recently, it was found that if the parts have size at least $2Δ+1$, then every pair of independent transversals is connected, within the collection, by a sequence of one-vertex reconfigurations. We prove, among other results, that there are exponentially many independent transversals when the parts have size at least $2Δ$, and that the reconfiguration diameter is at most linear in the number of parts when the parts have size at least $4Δ$.

title: Exotic smooth structures on nonorientable 4-manifolds
abstract: We construct closed nonorientable aspherical 4-manifolds with an arbitrarily large number of distinct smooth structures. This uses the reflection trick of Davis-Hayden-Huang-Ruberman-Sunukjian. Our examples become mutually diffeomorphic after either type of stabilization: taking a product with the real line, or taking a connected sum with sufficiently many copies of S^2 x S^2.

title: Shifted Hankel determinants via Hankel continued fractions
abstract: The Hankel determinants $H_n(F)$ of a power series $F(x)$, as well as the shifted ones $H_n^{(1)}(F)$ and $H_n^{(2)}(F)$, can be read off from its Jacobi continued fraction, provided that all $H_n(F)$ are nonzero. Without any condition on $F$, the Hankel continued fraction ($H$-fraction) still yields all $H_n(F)$. We show that the $H$-fraction of $F$ also determines the shifted Hankel determinants $H_n^{(1)}(F)$, $H_n^{(2)}(F)$ and the backward shifted ones $H_n^{(-1)}(F)$, and we give explicit formulas for them. As applications, we provide simple proofs of Hankel determinant evaluations that were previously established by means of complicated explicit $H$-fractions.

title: It's My Turn! Interpretable Methods Reveal Developmental Differences from Mother-Child Conversational Dynamics
abstract: Understanding conversational interactions between mothers and children is an important challenge for computational behavioral modeling. Existing methods use traditional statistical approaches and subjective measures of conversational dynamics, without incorporating temporal or probabilistic modeling. We developed an interpretable computational framework that combines sequence analysis, information-theoretic measures, and Bayesian hierarchical modeling to characterize temporal conversational dynamics in parent-child play. We applied this framework to interactions from 94 mother-child dyads with two-year-old children. Sequence analysis revealed that dyads with lower language development (as defined by scores on the Bayley developmental test) exhibited more heterogeneous conversational organization and fewer serve-and-return exchanges than higher-development dyads, a reciprocal turn-taking pattern in which one partner initiates communication and the other responds. Mutual information analyses suggested differences in conversational predictability between lower- and higher-development dyads, although the bootstrap confidence intervals overlapped. Bayesian hierarchical models estimated temporal trajectories for maternal consecutive turns, child responses following maternal speech, and overlapping responses; HDIs showed that trajectories differed in whether they excluded 0, but there were no statistically credible differences between the Bayley groups. Overall, these results indicate that children with higher developmental scores have more organized and predictable communication styles, with more ``serve-and-return" patterns with their mothers. These results demonstrate that interpretable computational representations of conversational dynamics capture developmental differences beyond simple measures of speech quantity.

title: Hierarchical Personalized Federated Learning for Fine-Grained Intrusion Detection: A Multi-Class Analysis in Heterogeneous Attack Environments
abstract: Intrusion Detection Systems (IDS) play a vital role in protecting modern network infrastructures. Although Federated Learning (FL) enables collaborative training without sharing raw network traffic, global models struggle with non-IID attack distributions. Moreover, practical security operations require fine-grained attack classification for targeted threat responses. To address these challenges, this paper investigates the convergence dynamics and performance of Hierarchical Personalized Federated Learning (HPFL), which combines multi-tier aggregation with client-level personalization, for 8-class, 6-class, and 4-class intrusion detection using Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) models implemented in NVIDIA FLARE on the CICIDS2017 dataset. Experimental results show that personalized HPFL models achieve micro F1-scores up to 0.9911 in the 6-class task, while the overall local accuracy reaches 0.9975 in the 8-class task. On 8-class local test sets, HPFL achieves a micro F1-score of 0.9901 and a macro F1-score of 0.8324, outperforming FedAvg (0.7176) and FedProx (0.5624) in macro F1. Cross-client evaluations demonstrate out-of-distribution generalization, with HPFL achieving a 4-class micro F1-score of 0.9294 compared with 0.9140 for standalone local models. Furthermore, distance-weighted network analysis estimates a 48.9% reduction in transmission overhead compared with conventional FL (194.4 MB vs. 380.3 MB for the 8-class task). These findings demonstrate HPFLs potential as an accurate, privacy-preserving, and communication-efficient approach to fine-grained intrusion detection in heterogeneous networks.

title: Remarks on thin sets in potential theory for sub-Laplacians
abstract: In contrast to Euclidean cases, we observe that, there are sets in Heisenberg groups that are thin at the origin and block all geodesics from the origin. However, in polarizable Carnot groups, using horizontal radial curves constructed for polar coordinates by Balogh and Tyson, we show that sets, that are thin at the origin, cannot block all horizontal curves. Consequently, we are able to use the asymptotic behavior with respect to the fine topology to estimate the Hausdorff dimension of singularities of potentials for sub-Laplacians and obtain geometric applications.

title: Photonic Maxwells demon as an energy resource
abstract: We propose a new realization of Maxwells demon for photons and its use as an energy resource. The starting point is a multilayer dielectric mirror that transmits photons within a certain wavelength band but reflects photons at longer wavelengths, followed by a material that irreversibly converts the wavelength. A 3D box constructed from these one-way mirrors is a self-acting Maxwells demon for photons. The first case considered is a one-way mirror for visible photons, converting blue to red as an example. The next case is a one-way mirror that transmits visible light but reflects infrared light, followed by a perfect blackbody. We analyze a 3D box with such mirrors as walls to accumulate and store blackbody radiation. Applications include solar-powered thermal energy and solar-powered thermophotovoltaics. The latter case would combine the 3D box with an ultra-low bandgap semiconductor photovoltaic cell inside. In the ideal optical limit, radiation can enter the box but cannot return through the entrance channel after conversion, allowing repeated photon recycling and nearly complete optical utilization. This can in principle move the conversion efficiency toward the thermodynamic limit for solar-energy conversion, the Landsberg limit of 93.3%.

title: How Many Persistent Features Does a Biometric Need? A Law Linking Equal Error Rate to Feature Count and Persistence
abstract: A biometric designer controls the number of features and their temporal persistence. Earlier empirical work linked the equal error rate (EER) to persistence and to the required number of features by straight lines. We derive the law behind these regularities. For $N$ independent standardized Gaussian features with test-retest correlation $ρ$, scored by cosine similarity, Fisher's $z$-transform turns the genuine and impostor scores into two normals, giving $\mathrm{EER}=Φ(-\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{N}\,\operatorname{atanh}ρ)$ and, inversely, $N=(2q/\operatorname{atanh}ρ)^2$ with $q=Φ^{-1}(1-\mathrm{EER})$; intercorrelated features enter through an effective count $N_{\mathrm{eff}}$. The central extension lets persistence vary across comparisons with spread $τ$ on Fisher's scale: $\mathrm{EER}=Φ(-m/(\sqrt{τ^2+v}+\sqrt{v}))$ with $v=1/(N_{\mathrm{eff}}-2)$, which for a normal spread has a floor $Φ(-m/τ)$ that no number of features can lower. With no fitted parameter the simple law reproduces published simulations and the EER-ICC line, and predicts the KCC-EER relation of eye-movement embeddings on GazeBase ($R^2=0.88$), though less well on GazeBaseVR ($0.63$). Read from the genuine and impostor scores, the general form matches the EER of eye movements, keystroke dynamics, the ECG and face embeddings over 101 conditions with $R^2=0.98$ and a median error of $0.6$ points, against $0.87$ and $1.9$ points for the simple law. The 61 eye-movement, keystroke and ECG conditions check consistency on the same scores; the 40 face conditions use held-out subjects, with the same accuracy. The product $τ\sqrt{N_{\mathrm{eff}}-2}$ gives a design rule: adding or decorrelating features pays fully while it is well below one and little once it exceeds about three, where only higher or more uniform persistence helps.

title: Beyond Bitwidth: Deployment-Constrained Mixed-Precision Quantization for Multilingual LLM Inference on NVIDIA Blackwell
abstract: Low-bit LLM quantization is useful only if a model preserves service-relevant accuracy, executes through supported GPU kernels, and meets measured memory and latency limits. We study Qwen3-8B on NVIDIA B200 with vLLM, including INT2/INT3, GPTQ, NVFP4, and mixed-precision configurations. We verify native packed execution and precision on all 144 fused linear modules and evaluate Korean, English, numerical, and reasoning quality under preregistered gates. Packed INT2 and INT3 execute, but all seven tested INT2 grids degenerate on generation. Isolated module-restoration effects are strongly non-additive; Korean and reasoning sensitivity rankings disagree, and a promising INT4/INT8 development candidate fails independent final evaluation. A configuration with 16-bit activations, 98 NVFP4 weight-only modules, 46 INT8 modules, and an INT8 output head passes all gates on the untouched FINAL-81 set (5,168 items): 5.917 GiB of weight-loading memory (limit 5.98), Korean teacher-correct retention 0.904 (gate 0.90), and TPOT ratio 0.939 relative to BF16. It improves paired accuracy over NVFP4 W4A4 by +1.4 percentage points (Bonferroni-adjusted interval [+0.2, +2.6]), compared with +3.4 points on the selection set. This comparison changes both activation precision and INT8 protection; exploratory analyses suggest that the activation change contributes substantially, but the isolated allocation effect is not established. Final checkpoints were not retained, and bitwise rebuild reproducibility remains unverified.

title: Pathology Randomization for Synthetic Priors and Zero-Shot Detection
abstract: Hospital brain imaging archives hold a diverse array of pathology at sample sizes beyond prospective studies, particularly for underrepresented populations and diseases. To unlock uncurated clinical data and scale analysis, methods are needed to detect abnormalities across contrasts and resolutions. Synthetic data has provided robust, contrast-agnostic models for a variety of human neuroimaging tasks in healthy anatomy, but pathology detection and other tasks in clinical settings still require real patient data, contrast-specific models, or disease-specific generators. We propose PathoDraw, a generative model of brain MRI with pathology. A conditional distribution of lesions given the healthy anatomy is drawn into the label map before contrast-agnostic rendering, and a single network estimates healthy anatomy with exact signed intensity deviation of any input scan. The contrast-agnostic 3D UNet learns the healthy labels under the lesion and the signed deviation directly and identifies pathology via robust tissue statistics and learned features, despite no training on real pathology. We show zero-shot detection on public stroke, tumor, and white matter hyperintensity datasets as well as archived clinical data, spanning $T_1$w, FLAIR and $T_2$w at various resolutions under a recent unsupervised anomaly detection benchmark protocol. Our single model exceeds or performs comparably to contrast-specific anomaly detectors trained on real scans and keeps healthy anatomy intact. The same generator trains networks for super-resolution and for registration in the presence of pathology. Our model, robust across acquisition and disease, enables the use of uncurated, archived data for clinical analysis. Our code is available at https://github.com/agr78/Pathology-Randomizer.

title: Sparse Integer Fourier Transform and Its Application In Machine Learning
abstract: The Discrete Fourier transform, mainly implemented by Fast Fourier Transform (FFT), has been essential for numerous domains, such as digital signal processing and feature extraction in materials design. However, current FFT methods suffer from extensive non-trivial multiplications and twiddle-factor operations in the big data era. To improve the computational efficiency of FFT, this study proposes Sparse Integer Fourier Transform (SIFT), a method that leverages the fast computing of sparsity and small integers, and applies the Radix-n method to derive an FFT. The 2N-point DFT matrix in Radix-n FFT is decomposed into four sparse integer matrices. A diagonal matrix containing complex twiddle factors is efficiently approximated using an optimization strategy while the remaining matrices retain sparsity and integer entries. For radix-32 FFT, SIFT reduces the estimated arithmetic cost by 75%, with RMSE below $2.3765\times10^{-8}$ and MAPE below 0.01089%. We evaluate frequency extraction in a numerical test and an engineering case. In the numerical test, MAPE and RMSE are below 2.016% and $2.536\times10^{-6}$, respectively. For wind turbine fault diagnosis, SIFT extracts compact spectral features that retain fault information while reducing the classifier's input dimensionality relative to the full time series.

title: Synchrony, Affect, and Perceived Autonomy in Virtual Robot-Facilitated Anxiety Support Groups
abstract: Socially assistive robots could expand access to group-based mental health support when skilled human facilitators are unavailable. However, their effectiveness will depend on whether they foster productive interactions among participants. We examined dyadic head-movement synchrony among 96 participants across 18 virtual robot-facilitated anxiety support group sessions. A human-controlled virtual robot, via a Wizard-of-Oz (WoZ) system, facilitated all sessions. We found that stronger peak synchrony predicted lower post-session negative affect. In contrast, speakers who more often followed listeners' movements reported higher negative affect and state anxiety, demonstrating that synchrony strength and direction capture distinct interpersonal processes. Participants who believed the robot was autonomous showed more genuine synchrony and stronger peaks than those who believed it was human-operated; more negative attitudes toward robots also predicted greater synchrony. These findings support synchrony as an objective, behaviorally grounded measure for evaluating robot-facilitated groups and a potential signal for guiding future autonomous facilitators.

title: WebAgents: Unbundling Agent Creation, Hosting, and Execution for an Agent-Native Web
abstract: Large language models are moving from isolated assistants toward autonomous agents that can plan, use tools, and coordinate with others, motivating an emerging Agentic Web of independently developed agents and services. Realizing this vision requires agent behavior to move across creators, hosts, and runtimes without coupling publication to a particular execution environment or transferring authority over user resources. We introduce WebAgents, which unbundles these roles through a signed agent.pkg that carries portable workflows, skills, schemas, and resource requirements. An OpenClaw-based agent-native browser/runtime verifies the package, obtains authorization, and binds it at run time to user-controlled models, tools, permissions, and budgets, while hosts distribute the public program and may retain private services server-side. We demonstrate this contract with three unrelated workflows executed unchanged under local and API-backed models, including literature review with live services and a website-published travel agent using semantic tools and user-selected personal resources. In a controlled suite, WebAgents explicitly blocks all 716 injected contract violations while accepting all 295 matched benign controls, with median automated pre-execution processing below 0.5 s for all three packages. We conclude by outlining a path toward NANDA-based discovery and interoperable package ecosystems while retaining execution authority in the user's runtime.

title: Laplacian Eigenvectors of Generically Weighted Graphs Have Pairwise Distinct Coordinates
abstract: Poignard, Pereira and Pade conjectured that, for a generic choice of the nonzero weights of a given graph, the Fiedler vector of the weighted Laplacian has pairwise distinct coordinates. We give a proof that also covers every nonconstant eigenvector. For each connected graph on n vertices we construct a nonzero homogeneous polynomial with integer coefficients in the edge weights, of degree n(n-1)(n^2-n+2)/4, which vanishes at a positive weighting exactly when the Laplacian has a repeated eigenvalue, an eigenvector with a zero coordinate, or a nonconstant eigenvector with two equal coordinates. The exceptional weights therefore lie in an algebraic hypersurface, which gives structural genericity in the sense of Poignard, Pereira and Pade; algebraically independent weights are never exceptional, and there are good integer weights not exceeding the degree plus one. The polynomial is a product of Krylov determinants. Its nonvanishing follows by induction on trees: when a leaf is attached with a small weight, a cut identity gives the first-order profile of the new eigenvector and separates the coordinates that coincide in the limit. Exact small cases show that exceptional weightings need not be symmetric.

title: Modeling Document and Section Hierarchies in Embedding Space
abstract: Embedded topic models integrate word embeddings into the topic generation process, producing coherent topics and robust performance on large vocabularies. However, each document is represented by a single topic distribution, ignoring its internal structure. Many real world collections, including legal documents, company and government reports, and online discussion forums, exhibit hierarchical organization in which documents consist of multiple sections that often address distinct subtopics. We introduce the Hierarchical Embedded Topic Model (hETM), a structured topic model that couples the topic distribution of a document and those of its sections through a hierarchical prior in the embedding space. We derive an amortized variational inference procedure for hETM and evaluate it on structured collections from each of these domains. Experimental results show that hETM achieves the lowest or near-lowest held-out perplexity among flat and hierarchical topic model baselines, along with comparable or higher topic quality. It also performs strongly on a downstream clustering task, achieving the best clustering performance on most of the collections.

title: Who Gets the Grid Capacity? Allocating Dynamic Access Among Multiple Virtual Power Plants
abstract: Virtual power plants (VPPs) trade in the same wholesale market and share distribution lines and transformers, and uncoordinated, profit-maximizing VPPs can push a shared transformer past its thermal limit or drive a feeder voltage out of band. The utility, which only observes the front-of-the-meter net injection at each bus, must keep the network safe from that net injection alone. We allocate a 24-hour active and reactive operating envelope to each VPP by a Benders decomposition: the utility sets a trial envelope, each VPP solves its private convex portfolio problem, and the returned value and dual gradient become supporting cuts that rebuild its value function while its schedule, state, and cost stay private. The envelope carries the transformer's thermal state across hours, bounds a joint conditional value-at-risk over forecast uncertainty, and is re-optimized each hour with the current hour committed. On a reduced IEEE-13 feeder with real load and prices, an active-power-only implementation lowers the transformer's peak-temperature CVaR from 254 to 97\,$^\circ$C at a 28\% value give-up and holds the transformer below its limit where nameplate access breaches it.

title: Emerging Vertical Power Delivery in AI Data Centers: Challenges and Solutions
abstract: The rapid growth of artificial intelligence (AI) workloads is increasing power demand in AI data centers, and processor current is projected to reach 2000 A and beyond. This trend is exposing the limitations of lateral power delivery (LPD) to processors and has motivated growing interest in vertical power delivery (VPD). This paper reviews the power delivery network (PDN) of AI data centers and the upcoming transition from LPD to VPD. First, the 800 VDC power delivery architecture, the impedance behavior of the PDN, and the limitations of LPD are discussed. Then, VPD implementation approaches, reported converter designs, and packaging technologies are examined, together with integrated voltage regulators (IVRs) and embedded passive components. In addition, power integrity simulations are presented to compare regulator and plane positions, from which a set of PDN design guidelines is derived. The results show that moving a voltage regulator module (VRM) from 50 mm away to directly below the die reduces the loop inductance by nearly half. In a complete PDN, this relocation lowers the low-frequency anti-resonant peak, whereas the mid- and high-frequency impedance depends on the decoupling stages and the position of the power and ground planes. This paper also shows that achieving practical VPD remains closely tied to challenges such as regulator height, passive-component embedding, and thermal management.

title: Large Language Models as Nonlinear Dynamical Systems: The Three Clocks of Depth, Training, and Generation
abstract: Language models are dynamical systems. A transformer is iterated over its layers, over the steps of its training and over the tokens it generates, and on each of these three clocks it shows behavior that nonlinear dynamics has studied for a century: fixed points, bifurcations, synchronization, chaos and noise-driven escape from potential wells. The two communities rarely meet, so this behavior is often rediscovered under new names. We build a bridge between them. To describe, we condense about 200 papers into the Three-Clock Dictionary, which maps fifteen concepts of nonlinear dynamics onto each clock and marks every correspondence as proved, measured or conjectured, and we show each concept in a mechanical system and in a language model side by side. To explain, we derive reduced-order models: the softmax is a Boltzmann distribution, gradient descent an Euler step on a nonlinear spring, a loss spike a ball thrown out of a stiff valley, attention on the circle a Kuramoto model, and a repetition loop a well that deepens while it is occupied. We then test these explanations on open language models, on a laptop CPU. Escape from repetition loops in GPT-2 and Pythia follows the Arrhenius law with the logit gap as the barrier, and the barrier deepens and then saturates, so the temperature needed to leave a loop falls like $1/\ln N$ with the generation length $N$ and rises with model size. Coherent text lives in a narrow window of temperatures, which a small reasoning model shares at its recommended temperature. Training makes each Pythia layer more expansive, and a small transformer trains at a multi-mode edge of stability. The third step, solving problems of language models, is still ahead: controllers derived from the escape analysis remove loops but do not yet beat the best fixed temperature. We state twelve open problems where nonlinear dynamics could get there.

title: From Apology to Action: Apologies, Compensation, and Cooperation in LLM Agents
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can make decisions that affect other agents, but what happens after a harmful or unsuccessful interaction remains poorly understood. We investigate whether apologies by LLM agents are associated with subsequent cooperative behaviour, using controlled Prisoner's Dilemma experiments with four commercial models (Claude Opus 4.8, GPT-5.5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, and Mistral Large 3). Across payoff conditions, we examine when agents apologise, the reasons they provide, and the actions that follow. We also examine how access to one round of interaction history affects behaviour and, in a second experiment, whether and how agents offer compensation alongside their apologies. Apology behaviour differed substantially across models and preceding interaction outcomes, and verbal expressions of cooperation did not always align with subsequent actions. Notably, Claude Opus 4.8 apologised even after mutual cooperation, while Mistral Large 3 apologised after being exploited but continued to defect even when its opponent cooperated. After unilateral defection, positively compensated apologies from GPT-5.5 and Gemini 3.1 Pro were followed by mutual cooperation, unlike those from Claude and Mistral. Our findings suggest that apologies, compensation, and strategic behaviour are distinct: conciliatory messages may precede continued defection, while costly apologies may go unanswered. This has important implications for the study of machine behaviour and human-AI interactions, as verbal signals alone may not reliably reflect an AI system's subsequent actions.

title: First-Order Model-Free Policy Gradient for Undiscounted LQR with Global Optimality and Convergence Guarantees
abstract: We provide a first-order model-free policy gradient (PG) framework for learning undiscounted infinite-horizon linear quadratic regulator (LQR) policies with global optimality and convergence guarantees. We first construct a stochastic wrapper policy class parameterized by the LQR gain to enable exploration around a deterministic linear control law. We analyze the additional cost induced by exploration over infinite-horizon, and establish a weak gradient dominance condition that characterizes global optimality under exploration. We then construct a model-free first-order PG algorithm using sampled trajectory information, without identifying the dynamics or approximating a value function. Finally, we establish finite-time convergence guarantees, providing the sufficient number of samples required for near-global optimality with our proposed PG algorithms.

title: Unveiling the infrared excess of SIPS J2045-6332 II: SPHEREx spectral decomposition supports a young unresolved binary interpretation
abstract: SIPS J2045-6332 is an unusual low-mass object previously identified by its infrared excess and possible signatures of youth and unresolved multiplicity. Earlier work suggested that it is relatively young and may host a mid-L companion. Here we reassess the system using low-resolution 0.75-5 micron spectroscopy from SPHEREx. We perform single- and binary-template spectral decomposition with field-gravity and intermediate-gravity (beta) templates spanning M8-L4. Binary-template models consistently outperform single-template models, most strongly for the beta templates. The preferred solution, an L0beta + L1beta combination (reduced chi^2 = 10.72), best matches the combined-light spectrum, although M9beta + L1beta and M9beta + L2beta give comparably good fits. Combining bolometric luminosities from gravity-dependent bolometric corrections (log L/Lsun = -3.42 +/- 0.08 and -3.85 +/- 0.09) with the Sonora evolutionary models, we estimate component masses of ~0.015 and ~0.011 Msun at 25 Myr and >~0.043-0.046 and ~0.038-0.043 Msun at 200-250 Myr for the primary and secondary (primary values are lower limits), implying a mass ratio q <~ 0.7-0.9, i.e. a companion of comparable but not necessarily equal mass. These results independently reinforce previous interpretations that SIPS J2045-6332 is a relatively young unresolved binary, and demonstrate the capability of SPHEREx spectroscopy to characterise young low-mass binaries through spectral decomposition.

title: Safe Reinforcement Learning with Hard Constraints: Policy Gradient Methods with Intersample Guarantees
abstract: We develop a policy-gradient (PG) reinforcement learning (RL) framework with hard inter-sample control barrier function (CBF)-based safety constraints for nonlinear sampled-data systems. We first design a class of stochastic policies with support truncated to sampling-period-dependent safe control sets, that guarantee safety-by-construction at sampling instants. We then propose a model-free PG algorithm that searches over the class of safe-by-design policies and establish sufficient conditions on sampling-period such that any action sampled from safe control sets remains safe throughout the sampling interval, providing inter-sample guarantees. We further establish finite-time convergence and sample complexity guarantees for the proposed PG algorithm and characterize its global optimality under gradient dominance. Finally, we illustrate inter-sample safety guarantees on a safe quadrotor navigation environment.

title: Deep Learning Models for Fractional Option Pricing
abstract: This paper investigates whether neural networks can infer fractional option prices and the Hurst parameter directly from sequences of fractional Gaussian returns, without separately estimating the latent parameters for each new sequence. Feedforward neural networks (FNNs) and long short-term memory (LSTM) networks are trained to jointly predict European call prices, put prices, and the Hurst parameter from 252-return sequences. A controlled simulation varies the total sample size from 5,000 to 500,000 sequences and evaluates point prediction, empirical residual-based prediction intervals, and computational performance. The neural-network models are also compared on a common simulated test set with Bayesian joint estimation and exact Gaussian maximum likelihood estimation. In that four-method comparison, the LSTM achieves the lowest Hurst-parameter root mean squared error (0.033) and option-price root mean squared error (1.305). After training, neural-network predictions are substantially faster than repeated parameter estimation, although the methods quantify uncertainty in different ways. Applications to five financial return series illustrate differences between data-driven and model-based fractional price estimates. The results support sequence-based learning as a computationally efficient complement to statistical inference under the assumed fractional model; they do not establish out-of-distribution accuracy or accuracy against observed traded-option prices.

title: Orbital Stability and Instability of Slow and Fast Solitary Waves of gILW
abstract: We study the solitary waves of the generalized Intermediate Long Wave equation (gILW), for a power-type nonlinearity of order $p\geq1$. Using concentration-compactness and symmetric rearrangement, we prove existence of suitable (even, strictly positive and radially decreasing) solitary waves of gILW for every $p\geq1$, and show that, as the depth parameter tends to infinity, they converge in the energy space and in $L^q$, $q\in[2,\infty]$, to the solitary waves of the generalized Benjamin-Ono equation (gBO), while, as the depth parameter tends to zero, after a suitable rescaling, they converge in $L^q$, $q\in[2,\infty]$, to the solitary waves of the generalized Korteweg-de Vries equation (gKdV). Our main results concern the orbital stability of slow and fast solitary waves of gILW, that is, of those for which the product $δc$ of the depth parameter and the velocity is small or large, respectively. For slow waves we obtain stability for $p=1,2,3$ and instability for $p\geq5$ (the same threshold as for gKdV), while for fast waves we obtain stability for $p=1$ and instability for $p\geq3$ (the same threshold as for gBO). In particular, for $p=3$ the stability of the solitary waves changes from one regime to the other. These results extend to $p>1$ the classical result of Albert, Bona and Henry for the Intermediate Long Wave equation ($p=1$). The proof proceeds by perturbation theory, transferring spectral information from gKdV and gBO to gILW through the convergence of the corresponding solitary-wave operators, and in particular avoids any use of an explicit formula for the solitary wave profile, none being available for $p>1$.

title: Hyperkähler Periods in Families of Parabolic Higgs Bundle Moduli Spaces
abstract: We consider the period map on families of parabolic Higgs bundle moduli spaces with varying parabolic weights $α$ and Higgs field eigenvalues $σ$. We assemble the moduli spaces into a smooth family $π:\mathscr M\toΛ$ where $Λ$ encodes $(α,σ)$, and define parallel transport for homology along paths in an open dense subset $Λ_0\subsetΛ$. By generalizing a classical theorem of Duistermaat and Heckman, we prove that the period map is affine linear in $(α,σ)$, with slope governed by the curvature class of a principal torus bundle over $\mathscr M$. For the four-dimensional moduli spaces of types $E_6,E_7,E_8$, we compute these classes to get explicit formulas for the period maps.

title: High-Order Regularization for Singular and Nearly Singular Laplace and Stokes Layer Potentials in Two Dimensions
abstract: Layer potentials represent the solutions of many elliptic boundary value problems, but their kernels have the singularity of the fundamental solution, so standard quadrature loses accuracy at targets on or near the boundary. In two dimensions, Gaussian regularization of the logarithmic kernel gives a smooth kernel involving the exponential integral $E_1$, but for the single layer its regularization error is only first order in the smoothing radius $δ$. We construct modified kernels for two-dimensional Laplace and Stokes single- and double-layer potentials that achieve regularization error $O(δ^p)$, $p=3,5,7$, uniformly for targets on and near the curve. The resulting method is both high-order accurate and easy to implement: the integrals are evaluated directly by the periodic trapezoidal rule on a single fixed set of boundary nodes for all targets. Choosing $δ=c h^q$ with $q<1$, where $h$ is the node spacing, keeps the discretization error smaller than the regularization error as $h\to0$, and numerical experiments confirm the predicted $O(h^{pq})$ convergence. Finally, we combine the near-curve evaluation with a fast Poisson solver to compute the potentials on the entire Cartesian grid.

title: Accelerating auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo with mixed-precision random propagators
abstract: We develop an algorithm to propagate auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo (AFQMC) wavefunctions in mixed precision. We target NVIDIA Tensor Cores using the TensorFloat-32 (TF32) format. We approximate each full-precision array by a TF32 leading term and a TF32 residual, and each full-precision matrix product by three TF32 products accumulated in full precision. Benchmarks on hydrogen chains show that mixed-precision propagation is consistently faster than double-precision GPU propagation, with an increasing advantage as the system size grows. The resulting local-energy deviations remain small over the propagation windows considered here. These results identify the stochastic two-body propagator as a particularly effective target for reduced precision, while our method allows higher precision to be retained for accuracy-sensitive operations. Hence, our algorithm provides a practical way to speed up AFQMC calculations and demonstrates where reduced precision can be applied without adverse effects on the method's accuracy.

title: DEFTS: Data-Efficient, Training-Free Few-Shot Learning for CLIP in the Text Subspace
abstract: Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP) achieves impressive zero-shot image classification performance by comparing image embeddings against class-specific text embeddings. While recent few-shot methods leverage labeled training samples to improve upon this zero-shot baseline, they often predominantly rely on image embeddings and underutilize the semantic structure of the text embeddings. In this paper, we introduce DEFTS, a data-efficient, training-free few-shot classification method strictly in the text subspace. We first demonstrate empirically that while raw text embeddings can be suboptimal as direct classifiers, the linear subspace they span remains highly discriminative. DEFTS therefore proposes to reduce the image-text modality gap by projecting estimated image prototypes directly into this subspace. Importantly, by expressing these prototypes as linear combinations of text embeddings, DEFTS reduces a high-dimensional estimation problem to the derivation of just a few coefficients. These coefficients are then computed via a Bayesian posterior mean, using a prior naturally centered on the original text embedding coordinates. Extensive experiments across 12 image classification benchmarks demonstrate that DEFTS significantly improves upon existing training-free methods.

title: An alternate proof of the QMA lower bound for set-size estimation
abstract: In the set-size estimation query task, a query algorithm decides whether an $N$-bit input has Hamming weight $\ge B$ or $\le A$ (with $\ge B$ as the yes instances and $\le A$ as the no instances). When $B = 2A$, this is sometimes called approximate counting. The query complexity for this problem with a quantum witness (i.e., $\mathsf{QMA}$ query bounds) was resolved by Aaronson, Kothari, Kretschmer, and Thaler (CCC 2020) and proved using Laurent polynomials. Here we give a morally similar but distinct proof of the lower bound using the polynomial method.

title: Deciding Without Pointing: A Case Study of Whether a Decision Model Localizes the Anomalies It Detects
abstract: Decision models can answer a typed question about an image with a probability per option, without generating text. In our case study of Clef-flash (post-trained Qwen3.5-9B backbone) on industrial inspection benchmarks, we ask whether it localizes the anomalies it detects. We obtained uneven results with zero-shot detection: per-category image AUROC 0.924 on MVTec AD and 0.668 on MVTec AD 2. On the former, the decision head's routing attention produces 0.391 mean per-image pixel AUROC, and hiding the image tokens from it leaves detection unchanged. The multimodal LLM's backbone attention does point at the defect, however it falls below a center prior when we change question. It falls below chance if we remove textual context in the question, partly due to backbone attention leaving the object, while the head's map hardly changes. The backbone's states carry the location when probed with normal images, on the test-split images, however, the decision depends on the defect region. A larger model, Clef, that comes with a post-trained Qwen3.8-27B backbone, gives no useful map in the decision head either. We found that it's possible to recover anomaly location by asking question specifically on an image region, retraining the head or reading the backbone, but none matches dedicated few-shot localizers.

title: Beyond Appearance: Where Forest Visual Place Recognition Actually Fails
abstract: Visual place recognition (VPR) in forest environments remains challenging because repetitive vegetation, and changes in illumination, season, and viewpoint can make distinct places appear similar and revisited places appear substantially different. In this paper, we investigate whether temporal, linguistic, structural, and geometric context can improve on an appearance-only descriptor, and what limits each representation when it does not. Using MegaLoc as the appearance-based baseline on the WildCross benchmark, we evaluate score-space and descriptor-space sequence matching, vision-language captions and reranking, scene-graph representations, and depth-derived stem graphs across same-direction revisits, extended routes, and reverse traversals. On a same-direction revisit, both sequence matching strategies reach similar Recall@1 (94.1% vs. 91.5%), but recall at 100% precision rises from 50.9% (single-frame MegaLoc) to 71.6% in score space and falls to 36.5% in descriptor space. The remaining context representations provide no consistent improvement over the appearance-based baseline. Same-place captions show limited place-specific discrimination, reranking is constrained by the initial candidate shortlist, and stem-graph matching remains weak even with LiDAR depth.

title: Fundamental physics with quantum sensors in space
abstract: Quantum sensors such as atomic clocks, atom interferometers, and atomic magnetometers can be used as sensitive probes of physics beyond the Standard Model. Space offers microgravity, long baselines, low environmental noise, access to varying gravitational potentials, and unique opportunities involving the Sun, Moon, planets, and asteroids. These proceedings of the Aspen Center for Physics workshop on "Fundamental physics in space with quantum sensors," held February 22-27, 2026, summarize the scientific case, current capabilities, and space mission concepts for investigating dark matter, testing general relativity, and detecting gravitational waves in frequency bands inaccessible from the ground.

title: KV-LTM: Persistent Per-Session KV Caches as Long-Term Memory for Personal Assistants
abstract: Personal assistants accumulate months of conversations, but today's long-term memory stacks put derivation or selection between a question and its evidence. In a system-level comparison on LongMemEval, two commercial assistants scored well below the same model reading the history offline [1], consistent with, but not isolating, content loss between write and read. We propose KV-LTM: a memory tier storing each session's raw text plus its KV cache under a fixed reader model, answering by restoring cached sessions and appending the question. KV-LTM is complementary to, not a replacement for, retrieval and indexing. Text is the memory of record; the cache is a recompute-free prefill accelerator, degrading gracefully to text. We specify the design: storage record, budget-derived retention, append-only read path, and bounded aggregation. We size it analytically: across pinned BF16 full-attention (GQA) and latent-cached MLA configurations, per-token state spans approximately 31K-328K bytes (the pinned KDA+MLA hybrid differs: approximately 8.1K bytes/token plus a fixed per-session recurrent term), giving approximately 0.34-3.6 TB per user-year at a declared 30K-token/day scenario, against approximately 49 MB of raw text; per-query cost is modelled as regime-conditional transfer, attention, decode, aggregation, and compute. We define an evaluation protocol needing no persistent-cache implementation for logical QA evaluation: per-session prefill emulates valid cache reuse under the same model/input-state contract and ideal arithmetic, with named arms, controlled baselines, and a preregistered reader-model gate; a separate minimal real-cache replay tests numerical equivalence and measures the cost axis, with outcomes not assumed. KV-LTM trades storage for avoided re-prefill compute and write-time fidelity, within a declared retention budget.

title: Transient Synchronization and Entanglement through Shared Dissipation in Circuit QED
abstract: We propose a superconducting circuit in which two resonators couple through DC-biased SQUIDs to a common lossy auxiliary mode. Adiabatic elimination yields collective damping and correlated noise with an overlap $ξ$ whose magnitude is tuned by the flux biases and whose sign follows the relative sign of the couplings. The full three-mode dynamics confirm this reduced description. For detuned resonators, we derive the exceptional-point condition, above which the mean amplitudes lock to a common frequency. For resonant modes, unequal collective decay produces transient synchronization, antiphase or in phase depending on the relative sign of the couplings, with an analytical synchronization time set by the collective decay splitting and the initial mean amplitudes. For initially separable squeezed states, the same relaxation converts local squeezing into transient entanglement, quantified by logarithmic negativity. We obtain closed-form expressions for the squeezing threshold above which entanglement appears and for the time at which it disappears. Thermal noise suppresses entanglement without changing the mean-amplitude synchronization time at fixed parameters. For realistic circuit parameters, these effects occur within a few hundred nanoseconds and are accessible through output-field measurements. A single tunable shared channel thus produces an exceptional point, transient synchronization, and transient entanglement, and provides a controllable source of correlated noise for superconducting circuits.

title: How Much Distribution Shift Can a Clustering Withstand? Exact Split and Merge Certificates for Structured Transports
abstract: In clustering, the distribution of the population being clustered is often uncertain or changes over time, so the true distribution may shift away from the nominal distribution used to form the clustering. Once the clustering is committed and each member is assigned to a cluster, such shifts may change the distribution of each cluster. They can make a cluster too spread out for one representative at a given resolution, motivating a split, or bring distinct clusters close enough to share a representative at that resolution, motivating a merge. We make these split and merge events precise using a local stability criterion built on the phase-transition analysis in deterministic annealing. This notion of stability enables us to quantify how robust a clustering is against such events. Furthermore, motivated by applications in which uncertainty and population change are structured, we study shifts whose displacements are restricted to a prescribed subspace. The smallest structured shifts that reach the respective thresholds define the split and merge radii, for which we obtain exact semidefinite programming (SDP) reformulations. The split SDP has only two scalar decision variables. These convex reformulations enable us to combine the radii into a robustness certificate for the full clustering that gives the size of the smallest structured shift that reaches any monitored split or merge threshold.

title: DreamFAR: Real-Time and Long-Horizon Interaction with Diverse Objects
abstract: World models have shown great potential in serving as a simulator for robot manipulation. However, existing models are either fit to a single environment or lack ability to simulate long-horizon contact-rich events. We present DreamFAR, a world model whose dynamics model is trained from scratch on a large robot-native teleoperation dataset, with no internet-video pretraining. We present an architecture and learning recipe designed for training on robot-native data. DreamFAR is significantly smaller than the high-performance video generation models, yet shows better understanding of contact and causality, and runs 10 FPS on a commercial GPU. Experimentally, DreamFAR significantly outperforms existing models in predicting the long-horizon future. We further demonstrate various applications where DreamFAR can be used, including policy evaluation and mixed-data co-training. Project page: https://www.yimingdou.com/DreamFAR/

title: Multiplicity of Solutions for a Class of Logistic Problems
abstract: The present paper investigates the existence and multiplicity of positive solutions to a class of degenerate logistic problems by combining the Nehari manifold {method} with nonlinear generalized Rayleigh quotients. The quotient associated with the Nehari constraint determines the threshold $λ_*$ at which the fibering structure and the Nehari manifold geometry emerge, while a second quotient identifies the zero-energy threshold $λ^*$ associated with the minimizing solution. Together with the threshold $\barλ$ for the existence of nontrivial solutions, these results yield the strict ordering \( 0<λ_*<\barλ<λ^*<λ_1(Ω)<λ_1(Ω_0), \) showing that the Nehari geometry becomes available before nontrivial solutions {exist} and that the zero-energy transition occurs only afterwards. In the variational range, we obtain a positive minimizing solution on $\mathcal N_λ^+$ and a second positive solution via the Mountain Pass Theorem. Complementary sub-supersolution and truncation arguments extend the multiplicity result to the remaining parameter range. We also establish the sign change of the minimizing energy, the blow-up and normalized asymptotic profile of the minimizing solutions as $λ\uparrowλ_1(Ω_0)$, and the convergence of the mountain-pass level $c_λ^m$ to zero as $λ\uparrowλ_1(Ω)$.

title: Finite-Time Blow-up for the Radial Mass-Critical Fractional Nonlinear Schrödinger Equation
abstract: We prove that radial negative-energy strong solutions to the focusing mass-critical fractional nonlinear Schrödinger equation \[ i\partial_tu=(-Δ)^su-|u|^{4s/N}u, \quad N\ge2,\quad \frac12<s<1, \] blow up in finite time. This resolves the finite-time blow-up versus infinite-time grow-up alternative left open by Boulenger, Himmelsbach and Lenzmann in the mass-critical regime. The argument uses an exponentially localized virial field together with a dyadic resolvent estimate that transfers the resulting weighted Balakrishnan energy to localized fractional Sobolev norms. When $s\ge N/(2N-1)$, we extend the conclusion to radial $H^s$ solutions by establishing the integrated virial identity at energy regularity. As a consequence, mass-critical ground-state standing waves are strongly unstable by finite-time blow-up.

title: VLA Observations of the Ionized Jet IRAS 16562-3959
abstract: We present new high-resolution, high-sensitivity Karl G. Jansky Very Large Array (VLA) A-configuration observations of the high-mass protostellar jet system IRAS 16562-3959 at 3.1 and 6.1 GHz. Our images resolve the five previously known jet components (OE, IE, C, IW, OW) into 21 distinct knots and sub-components, and reveal a new off-axis source, MW. Based on the dynamical timescales from previous works ($τ_{jet} \approx 620$ yr), the spacing and structure of the knots suggest episodic accretion with a mean interval between ejections of $\sim$32 yr. We find that source MW has a substantial increase in peak brightness relative to its marginal detections in previous observations. MW exhibits a spectral index of $α\approx -0.7$, characteristic of synchrotron emission from shock-accelerated relativistic electrons. Equipartition analysis yields a minimum-energy magnetic field strength $B_{me} \approx 0.4$ mG, and a minimum total energy $E_{me} \approx 4.4 \times 10^{42}$ erg. Archival 2MASS Ks data imply a total outflow dynamical age of $\sim$1400 yr, and together with a HST [FeII] 1.64 $μ$m map, the NIR data indicate that the fast jet is embedded in a wide-angle wind with a $\sim 36^\circ$ opening angle.

title: Where Should the Lamp Go? Ambient-Aware Lamp Placement for Portraits
abstract: Portraits shape first impressions, and lighting is an important factor. Prior work, such as lighting estimation and portrait relighting, edits lighting after capture but does not guide where to place a light before the shot. This leaves an open question: where should a light go to best light a face? Therefore, we propose LightMatch, a preference-grounded inverse lighting framework that disentangles the controllable light from ambient illumination and optimizes its placement. We first learn a Bradley-Terry quality model from pairwise human judgments. A perception head then regresses spherical-harmonic lighting from frozen self-supervised features via cross-attention. Finally, a placement solver isolates the light via spherical-harmonic linearity and optimizes its reachable position. On held-out environments, LightMatch attains 87.8% of the oracle improvement, outperforming the conventional solver that ignores ambient light by a relative 28.4% and the same pipeline with the widely used DPR estimator by a relative 70.5%. It reaches 73.2% on real OLAT faces of unseen identities and, on our real captures, cuts lamp-direction error by 37.7%.

title: Supporting Researcher Control in AI-Assisted Social Media Analysis: A Mixed-Methods Study of AI4OSN
abstract: High-quality annotated datasets are critical for advancing computational social science (CSS) research, yet collecting, curating, and analyzing large-scale data from dynamic sources such as online social networks (OSNs) remains a persistent bottleneck. Researchers must also translate substantive questions into queries, relevance criteria, and defensible interpretations. Large language models (LLMs) can assist, but they can also obscure the judgments, potentially reducing researcher oversight and critical evaluation. We present AI4OSN, a mixed-initiative platform that keeps researchers in control of data collection, relevance labeling, and sensemaking while making AI assistance available as an inspectable advisory resource. In a systematic user study (N=18) using X/Twitter data, participants reported above-benchmark perceived usability (mean SUS score of 79.7), increased confidence in LLM-assisted annotation and analysis tasks, and low cognitive workload during AI-supported sensemaking. Notably, novice participants showed descriptively greater alignment and higher reported agreement with AI output than experienced participants, underscoring the need to support differentiated verification practices across expertise levels. Overall, this work contributes both a human-centered system for social data analysis and empirical insights into how AI-assisted interfaces shape researcher behavior, trust, and decision-making. Our findings highlight design opportunities and tensions in building accessible, transparent, and agentic AI systems for social media and web research.

title: The interplay between ionized and warm molecular gas in the turbulent intragroup medium of Stephan's Quintet
abstract: Using JWST MIRI spectroscopy, we explore the multi-phase intergalactic gas in the hot halo of the Stephan's Quintet compact group. Unlike the coolest H2 emission, which commonly shows double- peaked profiles corresponding to the velocity of the intruder and the intragroup gas, the ionized Neon emission-lines are often systematically shifted redwards in radial velocity away from the lowest H2 peak, and into the region corresponding to gas decelerated by the collision of the intruder galaxy with intragroup gas. The majority of the brightest clumps of ionized gas are spatially correlated with the brightest H2 clumps, suggesting they are coherent structures caught up in the opposing gas flows. Gas that is progressively heated, is shifted in velocity further from the velocity of the coldest H2 peaks. Larger and larger shifts in velocity are seen as one progresses from cool to warm molecular hydrogen, to lower-excitation (Neon lines) ionized and strongly shocked heated ionized gas (gas-phase Iron). The majority of the ionized Neon in the intergalactic medium is consistent with excitation in low-velocity shocks. We suggest that this behavior is the result of gas of progressively lower densities being shocked and accelerated by the interaction of pre-existing clouds with a hot flow created by the blast-wave from the collision between the intruder and the intragroup gas. One exception is the extragalactic star forming region, SQ-A, which shows higher-excitation ionized emission lines consistent with heating from a young starburst, consistent with previous photometry of young star clusters in the region.

title: Stokes flow in a wedge with a moving contact point: well-posedness with a fixed contact angle and Navier slip
abstract: We study 2D Stokes flow in a wedge-like region bounded by a solid substrate with Navier slip and by a free surface driven by surface tension. The two meet at a moving contact point with a fixed contact angle. This is the model of a moving contact line at scales below the slip length, in its simplest setting. The slip length is the only length scale, and nothing is prescribed at the contact point beyond the angle: no relaxation law for the angle, and no contact-point dissipation. Slip removes the paradox found by Huh and Scriven, the infinite dissipation at a contact line that moves without slip, but in this model a weaker singularity remains. We give, to our knowledge, the first rigorous characterisation of this singularity for solutions of the free-boundary problem near the stationary state. For small contact angles and small initial data satisfying two compatibility conditions, we prove local existence, uniqueness and Lipschitz dependence on the data. The compatibility conditions are the price of the fixed angle for solutions regular in time up to the initial time. Rather than hiding the singularity, the solution class carries it explicitly in corner expansions. The velocity is continuous up to the contact point. The pressure has a logarithmic singularity, the slip-regularised version of that of Huh and Scriven. Its coefficient is proportional to the contact-point velocity. The slope of the free boundary has a corresponding logarithmic correction, the slip-scale counterpart of the Cox-Voinov relation. The linearised problem combines terms of different scaling, which prevents a direct treatment by the Mellin transform. We solve it by a Lax-Milgram argument, and an auxiliary test function problem shows that the variational solution satisfies the equations.
