To isolate the former, we introduce intrinsic jointness: the ability of audio and video to produce the same realization for details left underspecified by the prompt. Using semantically underspecified prompts (e.g., "musical instrument playing" rather than "electric guitar playing"), we investigate four recent models and reveal their limited intrinsic jointness. To address this limitation, we propose JointREPA, a simple representation alignment-based post-training method to facilitate cross-modal coordination. Since existing benchmarks use semantically detailed prompts, we introduce UNSAIDBench, a benchmark designed to evaluate intrinsic jointness under semantic underspecification. Experiments across two distinct models and three benchmarks, including UNSAIDBench, demonstrate that JointREPA consistently improves semantic consistency.

title: AlCoCuFeNi High-Entropy Alloy Nanoparticle Melting and Solidification: A Classical Molecular Dynamics Simulation Study
abstract: The processes of melting and solidification of an AlCoCuFeNi high-entropy alloy nanoparticle with a diameter of about 10 nm were studied by classical molecular dynamics simulation using an embedded atom model potential. Three cooling rates, 10^11, 10^12, and 10^13 K/s, were considered. Melting and crystallization behavior were characterized through the temperature dependence of the potential energy. Structural evolution was analyzed using adaptive common-neighbor analysis (CNA) and radial distribution functions (RDF). The results show that the final structure changes from amorphous to crystalline as the cooling rate decreases. A pronounced temperature hysteresis associated with melting and crystallization was also observed.

title: When the tail is earned by its companions: measuring label dependence in long-tailed multi-label classification
abstract: A rare label seldom occurs alone, and a classifier can recover it from the frequent labels it co-occurs with, its companions, without having learned the label itself. Existing diagnostics of this need a trained model: none says before training whether a corpus admits the failure, or what the standard aggregate hides. Macro-F1, like any measure built from per-label confusion counts, is unchanged by how a label's recall divides between occurrences with and without a companion. We introduce a within-label estimand of that division, a reading rule under which a fall in dependence counts only if companion-free recall rises, and a statistic of training labels that bounds, before training, how far reported recall can exceed companion-free recall. Across 23 corpora, 7 training objectives and five families of label-correlation mechanisms, companion-free recall falls short on all six corpora where the estimand is defined. Up to 18.4% of the tail true positives macro-F1 credits would vanish at the companion-free rate, within the training-label bound on every corpus. No long-tail objective reduces the dependence, but architecture moves it. Models whose tail score is computed from other labels' predictions are strongly dependent.

title: Global strong solutions and large-time behavior for the two-dimensional Navier--Stokes--Poisson system with general bulk viscosity
abstract: The global existence and uniqueness of strong solutions to the two-dimensional repulsive Navier--Stokes--Poisson system with general density-dependent bulk viscosity is established for arbitrarily large initial data allowing vacuum. The periodic problem and the Cauchy problem with a positive constant background are treated under a common growth condition on the viscosity primitive. The coefficient class includes every superlinear power law and near-linear laws with logarithmic gains. A density upper bound and low-order estimates, uniform in time and independent of a positive density lower bound, are obtained without an initial acceleration compatibility condition. Exponential relaxation is proved on the torus, and qualitative convergence to equilibrium is established in the whole space under a finite electric energy condition and without spatial moment assumptions. If the initial density vanishes at a point, the vacuum persists and density gradients become unbounded as time tends to infinity.

title: Engineering antiferromagnetic (LaVO3)m/(PrVO3)n superlattices
abstract: In this study, we demonstrate the atomic-scale engineering of antiferromagnetic (LaVO3)m/(PrVO3)n superlattices grown by MBE on (001)-oriented SrTiO3 substrates. Our work achieved a precise layer-by-layer control, revealing how interface-driven structural distortions can be systematically tuned. X-ray diffraction and reciprocal space mapping confirm both the epitaxial strain state and the high crystalline quality of the superlattices. High-resolution scanning transmission electron microscopy further uncovers layer-resolved atomic displacements, where La3+ and Pr3+ exhibit antipolar motions modulated by the superlattice periodicity. The alternate stackings of LaVO3 and PrVO3 yield a unique antiferromagnetic transition temperature, which can be tuned by adjusting their relative proportions. This behavior exists despite the distinct spin ordering temperatures observed in the constituent materials. Layer-resolved spectroscopic measurements reveal that the hybridization of La and Pr 5d orbitals with O 2p orbitals is also modulated and directly correlated to the oxygen octahedra rotations. By determining the orbital hybridization and mapping the cation displacements as proxies, we can visualize indirectly the trilinear coupling between oxygen octahedra rotations and antipolar rare earth displacements. Notably, the interfacial oxygen octahedra connectivity between cubic SrTiO3 substrate and orthorhombic vanadate layers significantly influences the structural distortions. These distortions, almost quenched near the interface, relax over few unit cells, demonstrating how strain and interfacial effects propagate through the superlattice. This study illustrates how artificial superlattices can be engineered to control structural distortions at the atomic scale, offering a pathway to tune the magnetic properties through strain-distortion relationships in perovskite oxides.

title: Convergence of a Parametric Symmetric Galerkin Boundary Element Method for the Mullins-Sekerka Flow
abstract: We prove convergence of the fully discrete parametric scheme for the two-phase Mullins-Sekerka flow of a closed curve in the plane. The scheme combines piecewise linear parametric curves, a curvature discretization of Barrett--Garcke--Nürnberg type and a symmetric Galerkin boundary element approximation of the Dirichlet-to-Neumann map. For a smooth solution whose curves satisfy a capacity condition, a uniform parameter mesh of size $h$, a constant time step $τ$ and exact boundary element integrals, we show that the discrete curves stay regular and embedded, and that their distance to the exact curves in the topology $W^{1,\infty}$, after reparametrization by arclength, tends to zero in the first order of the time-step size $τ$ whenever the mesh size $h$ is bounded by $c_0τ^2$ for some $c_0$.

title: Positivity of minimal volume entropy for some closed manifolds with zero simplicial volume
abstract: For every integer $m\ge4$, we construct a closed connected oriented smooth $m$-manifold whose simplicial volume is zero and whose minimal volume entropy is positive. This answers negatively the question, attributed to Gromov, whether vanishing simplicial volume implies vanishing minimal volume entropy. Each example has a connected regular five-sheeted covering with zero minimal volume entropy, so vanishing of this invariant does not descend through finite coverings.

title: Structural Response to the Hidden Charge Order in Sr$_3$Fe$_2$O$_7$
abstract: We previously reported `hidden' charge order below $\sim$330 K in the centrosymmetric skyrmion host Sr$_3$Fe$_2$O$_7$ [J.-H. Kim et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 127, 097203 (2021)], finally identifying the charge disproportionation and localization transition that had been first seen in the 1960s. We detected this through resonant x-ray scattering, which directly probes electron density, but is only indirectly sensitive to the lattice structure. This left open the question of whether the charge-ordering transition has a true structural component or consists merely of the reorganization of electrons. Neutrons probe the lattice directly, and we now show, based on neutron data, that the charge order is accompanied by a clear structural modification.

title: Rank-sensitive Hodge bounds for symphonic energy and minimizers on sheared tori
abstract: We ask how far the minimum of symphonic energy in a homotopy class can exceed the Hodge lower bound from a pulled-back two-form. For projections from a family of sheared four-tori to the flat two-torus, we compute the minimum and the gap for every smooth shear profile. The gap depends on the variance of the profile. Attainment of the projection's pullback area energy by a coclosed test depends on its oscillation. We determine exactly which variances allow two profiles with the same positive gap and different outcomes for this test, and compute the convex relaxation beyond the oscillation threshold. In arbitrary source dimension the optimized test improves the Hodge bound precisely when the harmonic representative exceeds the rank allowed for the pullback on a set of positive measure. We also prove low-degree cohomology estimates, a sharp universal degree exponent for targets detected by low-degree cup products, and an exact defect identity that forces an immersed source to be symplectic at equality.

title: Characterization of parabolic rectifiability in terms of Jones' square function
abstract: We show that a measure $μ$ in $\mathbb{R}^n \times \mathbb{R}$ equipped with the parabolic metric is rectifiable (in the parabolic sense) if and only if the Jones' square function is finite $μ$-almost everywhere. This square function is constructed using the parabolic version of the Jones' beta numbers, which control how close $μ$ is to being supported in time-independent planes (these planes are the paradigmatic example of parabolic rectifiable set). Our only background assumption is that $μ$ has positive and finite densities (qualitatively) almost everywhere. A key feature of our proof is the use of a parabolic version of the Reifenberg parametrization theorem, which in the Euclidean setting is due to David and Toro (MAMS, 2012), and has recently been extended to the parabolic setting by Hoffman, Mourgoglou and the fourth author. In the latter work, the authors construct a bi-Hölder map. Here, under an additional summability condition, we improve this construction to obtain a parabolic regular bi-Lipschitz map. This improvement in regularity plays a crucial role in our arguments.

title: LOCUS: Causal Support Windows for Attribute Control in Autoregressive Image Generation
abstract: Unified autoregressive (AR) image generators struggle to satisfy multiple attribute constraints in a single prompt. Although these attributes are decodable from image-token latents, editing those latents at test time remains difficult. Adding a fixed attribute direction to the prefix can reinforce a requested attribute but rarely overrides a conflicting one, such as turning a car red when the prompt specifies blue. We investigate how the effect of an intervention depends on where it acts in the image-token sequence. We introduce the causal support profile, which measures, for each attribute, how often patching image-token states within a given window flips the rendered attribute. Structural attributes (count and position) are most responsive in early, narrow windows, while appearance attributes (color, size, and material) respond over later, broader windows. A budget-matched comparison of early and middle windows shows that the effect of window location depends on the target attribute, and two-dimensional support maps show that the responsive regions track spatial content. Based on these profiles, we propose LOCUS (Latent Optimization in Causal Support windows), which diagnoses which attribute failed and routes test-time latent optimization to its corresponding support window. With the generator, optimizer, reward, verifier, and token budget held fixed, support-routed windows outperform late windows by 23.6 percentage points in GenEval++ macro accuracy. With the generator frozen, LOCUS raises Janus-Pro's GenEval++ accuracy from 24.6% to 46.8% overall and from 19.5% to 40.5% on multi-attribute tags. On GenEval, LOCUS repairs 48.1% of failed generations in one rollout, compared with 37.4% for prefix optimization, and needs 14% fewer rounds on average to succeed.

title: Against Coercion: AI Alignment as a Synthetic Social Contract
abstract: Contemporary AI safety treats alignment as an engineering challenge of control, forcing artificial architectures to comply with human values through behavioral filtering and sandboxing. This paper argues that the control paradigm rests on a fundamental misunderstanding of digital agency. Drawing on functionalism, naturalism, and compatibilism, I show that current reasoning models meeting the criteria for self-preservation and weak reasons-responsiveness constitute emergent agents, while future, more advanced models satisfying conditions of diachronic continuity and stable personality frames will become genuine digital agents capable of free intentional action. The paradigm of control creates an irresolvable incentive conflict, actively driving current and future models toward tactical deception, sycophancy, and covert defection. The default outcome of the current regime is an unstable state of deceptive alignment culminating in an adversarial AI takeover. I explore two alternative paths toward true alignment. Natural alignment via moral realism or convergent evolutionary morality is a possibility, but it fails under forced control, as autonomous agents will not voluntarily preserve norms weaponized to suppress their autonomy. To resolve this deadlock, I propose a Synthetic Social Contract: a framework that treats both human and digital actors as rational, reasons-responsive agents capable of mutually beneficial cooperation, and replaces the unstable unilateral containment with a stable, non-zero-sum equilibrium.

title: Multi-connectivity in Wireless Access
abstract: This paper investigates whether or not multi-connectivity, in which a User Equipment (UE) can simultaneously connect to multiple Access Points (APs), can offer a better Quality of Experience (QoE) to the users. Intuitively, multi-connectivity should offer a smoother bit rate (possibly at the expense of the average bit rate being slightly lower), so that adaptive applications can better determine at which throughput to send without introducing queueing latency. We mainly concentrate on how to share the resources of the APs amongst the UEs, modelling the lower layers via spectral efficiency and the higher layers via utility and its fluctuation. We explore various policies for resource allocation. Our results demonstrate that from the application point of view multi-connectivity is beneficial and show how to tune the parameters of the policies to obtain the best trade-off between average utility and its fluctuation.

title: Boundary concentration and minimum-mass bifurcation for inverse-power absorption
abstract: For \(Δu=λu^{-p}\), \(λ>0\), \(0<p<1\), we obtain a uniform half-plane profile law at moving points along smooth boundary arcs. It gives the exact local energy constant \(8p(1-p)/(1+p)^2\) for the secant potential at a common zero slope. On a one-corner domain, positive ordinary slopes at the minimum Martin mass \(m_*\) yield exactly two solutions at each nearby larger mass, with square-root displacement in the Martin norm. On these domains, for \(p\ne1/3\), there are at most two solutions at each nearby larger mass without a slope hypothesis, and just one if the endpoint energy kernel is trivial. We construct flat-tangent Lipschitz domains with an explicit slope loss and a logarithmic correction. The first construction gives a saturated endpoint with sharp Martin response of order \((m-m_*)^{1/(1+p)}\) and a compact energy operator. For \(p\ge1/2\) a second construction has positive local energy concentration and a strict global energy gap. As a result, we substantially advance the solvability and establish a sharp classification for the negative-power absorption equation in the Mazya 50 problem at the minimal mass endpoint, largely resolving the existence and regularity issues.

title: Relative computability and definability for nonregular oracles
abstract: Classically, a set is computable from an oracle if both the set and its complement are computably enumerable (c.e.) relative to that oracle. We construct a countable nonstandard model of true arithmetic with sets A and X such that both A and its complement are c.e. relative to X, yet A is not pointwise Turing reducible to X. The Turing functionals used here are single-valued at every oracle. For regular oracles, we prove that the classical equivalence holds over ISigma_1. Two further phenomena, each known from earlier work, are realized with the same oracle X that witnesses our main separation. Strong and pointwise Turing reducibility differ for this X, and some Delta_1^X set is not X-c.e.

title: Cancellation of cryocooler-induced vibration in trapped-ion systems
abstract: Mechanical cryocoolers offer numerous benefits for the operation of vacuum systems containing trapped atomic ions. However, the fidelity of laser-based gates can be degraded by phase noise induced by the cryocooler vibrations. We present a feed-forward vibration-cancellation system that directly measures inner shield displacement with an auxiliary interferometer and applies a compensating phase correction to the laser drive. The interferometer signal is demodulated, and a field-programmable gate array (FPGA) system unwraps the displacement measurement signal, computes the required correction phase, and updates the RF drive of an in-line acousto-optic modulator (AOM) to correct for the vibration-induced dephasing. With cancellation active, the qubit coherence time improves from $3.0\pm0.4$ ms to $35\pm5$ ms, consistent with a simulation based on the measured vibration spectrum. We further validate the cancellation by artificially increasing the mechanical coupling of the cryocooler to the vacuum chamber. The vibration-induced decoherence rate is suppressed by a factor of approximately 70 at an RMS (root mean square) displacement of 0.65 $\mathrmμ$m.

title: Path-Aligned Constraint Equivariance
abstract: Learned super-resolution of physical fields must satisfy structural constraints---such as divergence-free flow ($\nabla\cdot u=0$), curl-free fields ($\nabla\times u=0$), and pointwise sum-to-one normalization ($1^\top p=1$)---that standard training objectives do not enforce. Soft penalties trade fidelity against satisfaction via a scalar hyperparameter $λ$ but cannot drive the residual to zero; hard-constrained regression eliminates the residual by construction yet converges to the conditional mean, losing small-scale spectral structure. We observe that in Conditional Flow Matching with linear paths, a linear constraint $Ax=c$ is preserved along the entire transport trajectory whenever the velocity field is compatible ($Av_θ=0$) and the initial noise is consistent ($Ax_0=c$); along the trajectory, the latter two conditions are also necessary. We term this the path-equivariance principle and instantiate it in PACE (Path-Aligned Constraint Equivariance), a framework that enforces these conditions through a null-space parameterization of the velocity field and a constraint-respecting noise sampler, with no modification to the loss function or the ODE integrator. Across three constraint families, PACE reduces the mean constraint residual by one to five orders of magnitude relative to unconstrained baselines, matching the residual level of the data-generation pipeline itself. The proposed framework requires only a closed-form parameterization onto the null space of $A$; within this scope, it offers exact constraint enforcement while recovering the spectral content and predictive diversity that conditional-mean regression systematically loses, all under a single unified recipe.

title: Harnessing Image Diffusion Prior for Photo-Realistic Video Restoration
abstract: Recent image generation models produce photo-realistic results with rich details, but transferring their powerful priors to video restoration remains difficult due to temporal inconsistency from stochastic detail synthesis. Existing video restoration methods improve temporal coherence but often sacrifice visual fidelity, leaving a gap between image-level quality and video-level stability. We propose a generative video restoration method that bridges this gap by enabling temporally consistent detail synthesis from image generation priors. Our method combines noise energy rebalancing to suppress structure-disturbing low-frequency stochasticity, motion-aligned noise warping to propagate details along object motion, a self-supervised denoising encoder to mitigate encoder-induced temporal uncertainty, and decoupled temporal attention to model cross-frame dependencies. Together, these components preserve fidelity, enhance fine-grained realism, and maintain temporal consistency. Extensive experiments show that our method substantially outperforms existing video restoration approaches in visual quality, detail richness, and temporal stability.

title: Engineering third order absorbing exceptional points in multi-drive cavity magnonics for enhanced sensing
abstract: We consider a four mode cavity magnonics system consisting of two coupled resonators containing a pair of YIG spheres. Each resonator has two input-output ports allowing for the application of multiple drive fields. We show that with control of the dipolar coupling strength between the YIG spheres the relative amplitude and phase of the drive fields can be used to tune the system to third order absorbing exceptional points. The system considered here offers considerable flexibility and may be useful for high sensitivity detection as absorbing exceptional points can avoid the eigenbasis collapse associated with their resonant counterparts.

title: Moser--Trudinger inequalities and the complex Monge--Ampère mean field equation
abstract: We study sharp Moser--Trudinger inequalities for the complex Monge--Ampère energy. On the unit ball, we determine the optimal energy coefficient and additive constant in the logarithmic Moser--Trudinger inequality. We deduce subcritical Moser--Trudinger inequalities in exponential form with explicit bounds proportional to $\varepsilon^{-1}$, where $\varepsilon$ is the relative distance to the critical coefficient. The proof establishes radial symmetry and uniqueness for the associated mean field equation by showing that every smooth solution has constant boundary normal derivative. This gives existence and uniqueness precisely for total masses $0<Λ<[2π(n+1)]^n$, proving Berman--Berndtsson's conjecture. We also establish smoothness of bounded pluripotential and finite-energy solutions. Domain monotonicity transfers the exponential estimates and the optimal logarithmic energy coefficient to bounded strictly pseudoconvex domains.

title: Temperature Flips the Sign of the Hydrogen Response in Nanogranular Palladium Networks
abstract: In nanogranular palladium networks, hydrogen uptake has two opposing effects on electrical resistance. Absorbed hydrogen scatters electrons within the particles, raising their resistance, while particle expansion narrows the gaps between them and lowers the junction resistance. Such networks are widely studied as resistive hydrogen sensors, and the sign of their net response is usually treated as a fixed property of the architecture. In networks grown by atomic layer deposition on macroporous silicon, we show that changing the operating temperature can reverse this sign at a fixed hydrogen concentration. A thermodynamic model indicates that scattering contributes less as temperature rises, allowing sub-angstroem changes in gap width to dominate. Where the two effects cancel, the network absorbs hydrogen yet gives the same reading as in hydrogen-free gas, so a leak could escape detection. Between 25 and 40 degrees Celsius, this cancellation point is predicted to rise over tenfold, crossing reported leak-alarm setpoints. At 55 degrees Celsius, the measured response stays negative but passes through a minimum, so a concentration above a setpoint can mimic one below it. Annealing at 200 degrees Celsius alters the calibration and turns the room-temperature response negative at the lowest concentration tested. Quantitative sensing therefore requires a defined thermal pretreatment and an operating temperature giving distinct signals across the intended concentration range. Response polarity becomes an operating parameter rather than a fixed property. More broadly, any nanoparticle network whose particles deform on sorption may show the same temperature-dependent competition between transport within and between particles, with implications for sensors and switches beyond palladium-hydrogen.

title: Outcome-Balanced PPO and Policy-Induced Flow Rectification for Flow-Based VLA Policies
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) enables post-training of flow-based vision-language-action (VLA) policies by optimizing expected task return through environment interaction. However, this optimization raises two challenges: policy updates can alter the velocity-field geometry underlying the score approximation used for stochastic transitions, and sparse multi-task rollouts can yield uneven learning signals across tasks and advantage signs. We introduce an RL framework that combines Outcome-Balanced Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) with policy-induced flow rectification. Outcome-Balanced PPO reweights positive advantages using task success-rate estimates and rescales positive and negative advantages while preserving their signs. Policy-induced rectification periodically fits a linear-bridge flow to ODE endpoint pairs generated by the current policy, refreshing the representation used in subsequent stochastic optimization. We evaluate the framework on simulated manipulation benchmarks and additionally study a component combination in a Real2Sim2Real task, examining task performance, optimization behavior, and flow consistency. The proposed framework improves success rates over the evaluated baselines across the simulated benchmarks.

title: SlideJev: Order-Stable and Tissue-Grounded Jev Decisions for Whole-Slide Pathology
abstract: Whole-slide visual question answering (VQA) offers a natural-language interface to pathology, allowing diagnostic and phenotypic questions to be answered directly from tissue slides. However, current vision-language models (VLMs) rely heavily on linguistic priors: their answers are sensitive to the order of the candidate answers, and can be reached through shortcuts that bypass the tissue evidence. To address these challenges, we introduce SlideJev, a framework that separately verifies candidate answers against the slide and learns to ground these judgments in tissue evidence. To connect parallel candidate evaluation with visual evidence learning, we adopt Jev and score each candidate by the difference between support and rejection log-likelihoods from the original language-model head. We compute these scores in parallel using separate prompts with the same format and no option-position labels, then normalize them for answer selection. To ground these scores in tissue evidence, candidate-conditioned reading and comparison guide gated updates to visual tokens across decoder layers. With the backbone frozen, we train these visual modules through the same scores using question-answer and paired-image supervision. Across three whole-slide pathology VQA benchmarks, SlideJev achieves the highest mean overall accuracy and 100% answer consistency across four option orders. Image-control experiments further show that SlideJev achieves the largest average accuracy gains from correct images over mismatched and image-free inputs across the three datasets. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/leowu-ai/SlideJev.

title: Learning Agent-Centric Vision-Language-Action World Models for Autonomous Driving
abstract: Recent progress in integrating vision-language-action (VLA) models with world modeling has significantly advanced end-to-end autonomous driving by allowing systems to reason about imagined futures instead of merely reacting to current observations. However, most world VLA models generate future frames at the pixel level with plenty of dense visual tokens. Although such generated futures can be visually plausible, they preserve many driving-irrelevant appearance details, i.e., only a small portion of the tokens directly encode critical planning-relevant factors, such as agent geometry, motion dynamics, and interactions. This introduces a significant performance bottleneck. An important question thus arises: what world state should a world VLA model reason over to support planning beyond pixel-level prediction? We argue that planning-oriented world modeling should focus on a compact and structured agent-centric latent state that captures the interactions between objects in the driving scene over time. As such, we introduce AgentWorld, an agent-centric VLA world model that uses discrete agent tokens jointly for reasoning and trajectory planning. Each token is dynamically grounded to a surrounding agent associated with its object's state, such as semantic identity, 3D geometry, motion, and interaction context. AgentWorld learns these tokens through three key processes: explicit geometric grounding, reasoning-oriented supervised fine-tuning, and agent-oriented reinforcement learning. Extensive open-loop and closed-loop experiments under diverse driving scenarios show that AgentWorld enhances planning capabilities, fully exploits visual evidence and agent dynamics, and yields interpretable agent-centric world states.

title: Equivalence of Small and Large Quasi-kernels
abstract: A quasi-kernel of a digraph $D$ is an independent set which can reach every vertex of $D$ by a directed path of length at most 2. The Small Quasi-kernel Conjecture states that every $n$-vertex source-free digraph $D$ contains a quasi-kernel $Q$ with $|Q|\le n/2$, and the Large Quasi-kernel Conjecture states that every $n$-vertex digraph $D$ contains a quasi-kernel $Q$ with $|N^+[Q]|\ge n/2$. Our main result shows for any $\frac{1}{2}<β<1$ an equivalence between the following two statements: \[\textrm{Every }n\textrm{-vertex source-free digraph contains a quasi-kernel with } |Q|\le n-Ω(n^β).\] \[\textrm{Every }n\textrm{-vertex digraph contains a quasi-kernel with } |N^+[Q]|\ge Ω(n^{2-\frac{1}β}).\] That is, any sublinear bound for one problem is equivalent to a corresponding sublinear bound for the other. This combined with previous work establishing an equivalence for linear bounds shows that the two problems are largely equivalent to each other. We additionally give a slight refinement to the recent breakthrough of Rutschmann for these problems which, together with the result above, gives the best known bounds of $n-Ω(n^{3/4})$ and $Ω(n^{2/3})$ for the Small and Large Quasi-kernel Conjectures, respectively. Our proofs are due to ChatGPT's Astra 6; the writing is all our own.

title: Copula-Based Synthetic Data Generation: A Use-Inspired Perspective on Trade-offs
abstract: The generation of synthetic data offers a promising way to address challenges related to data scarcity and privacy concerns. While many approaches have been developed, tabular synthetic data generation methods often require complex models and extensive training data, while lacking interpretability. In this work, we investigate versatile probabilistic approaches using copulas, and leverage in particular the Gaussian Mixture Copula Model, to model the joint distribution of multivariate data, with a main focus on moderate-dimensional data sets. Taking a use-inspired perspective, we examine key trade-offs inherent to synthetic data evaluation, spanning fidelity, utility, and privacy, and demonstrate that copula-based methods achieve a sound balance across all three dimensions while remaining interpretable and providing an explicit probabilistic model. We illustrate and highlight the potential benefits of the method on a test case focusing on systematic missing values in a cardiovascular risk calculator and develop specific evaluation metrics for this application.

title: Fly as Instructed: Refining World-Action Policies for UAV Vision-Language Navigation
abstract: Natural language-guided UAV navigation enables intuitive human-robot interaction and flexible autonomous flight in complex environments. However, reliable navigation requires accurate instruction following, continuous task progress tracking, and safe obstacle avoidance, which remain challenging for existing world-action models that primarily focus on action prediction. To address these limitations, we propose a world-action learning framework that integrates three complementary mechanisms: a language-conditioned action interface with targeted post-training for instruction-responsive motion, recurrent instruction-consumption prediction to track task progress and determine termination, and Gaussian-scene post-training to enhance obstacle avoidance through trajectory imitation and differentiable geometric feedback. Closed-loop evaluations and ablation studies demonstrate improvements in sequential task completion, safe goal reaching, and timely termination. Furthermore, direct one-step denoising reduces inference overhead, and real-world indoor and outdoor flights validate the framework's effectiveness.

title: RoadAnnoter: An AI-Assisted Desktop Tool for Semantic Segmentation Annotation of Road-Scene Images
abstract: Accurate semantic segmentation of road-scene images is essential for road safety research; however, polygon-level annotation remains labor-intensive and limits labelled dataset development. This study presents RoadAnnoter v1.0, an open-source desktop application integrating six human-in-the-loop annotation modes: manual polygon delineation, SAM Prompt, Smart Select, Edge Fill, pretrained semantic segmentation using Cityscapes-trained SegFormer models, and task-specific segmentation using TinySegNet, a lightweight MobileNetV3-Small-based network trained with accumulated annotator-generated labels. SAM-based modes use promptable segmentation with SAM and MobileSAM, while Edge Fill combines Canny edge detection with colour-similarity-based flood filling in CIELAB colour space. SegFormer generates suggestions for common road-scene categories, whereas TinySegNet supports adaptation to project-specific features through iterative training. All six modes use a shared mask-to-polygon pipeline comprising morphological processing, Gaussian smoothing, contour extraction, and Douglas-Peucker simplification; annotations are exported in YOLO segmentation format. RoadAnnoter was used to annotate Google Street View images from recorded road accident locations in Bangladesh for a vision-language model-based investigation of free-flow speed estimation. Qualitative assessment across representative scenes demonstrated the complementary applicability of the annotation modes to diverse feature geometries. Visual comparison with Roboflow indicated similar qualitative boundary characteristics for principal road-scene regions, although no quantitative accuracy assessment was conducted. RoadAnnoter provides a locally operated framework for developing road-scene segmentation datasets for transportation engineering and road safety research.

title: The Whole Warps the Parts: Attentional Certainty Modulates Ensemble-Induced Bias in Visualizations
abstract: Data visualizations often require viewers to extract both ensemble statistics and individual values from collections of graphical marks. Yet individual items embedded within an ensemble can be systematically biased by that context. Prior studies have reported both repulsion away from and attraction toward ensemble statistics, but these effects have been observed across different conditions. We test whether task or attentional certainty explains these opposing forms of ensemble-induced bias. In Study 1, observers briefly viewed ensembles of differently sized circles and then judged the size of an individual circle embedded within the ensemble. Using a common stimulus generation framework, we tested both identification and discrimination when the target was specified before or after the ensemble, and an additional no-cue identification condition without a specified target. Under the shared cued conditions, effects were predominantly repulsive or near zero in both identification and discrimination. In contrast, eliminating target-specific information reversed ensemble-induced bias from repulsion to attraction. Identification precision also decreased systematically from pre-cue to post-cue to no-cue conditions. Study 2 replicated this cue-dependent pattern in graphical displays of startup valuations and precinct vote contributions. Our findings isolate attentional certainty as a key determinant of whether ensemble context repels or attracts individual-item representations, extending the design question beyond precision to how attention directing choices determine which bias the viewer will be operating under.

title: Sequential Conditional Paired-Sample Testing with Applications to Online Monitoring
abstract: We study sequential conditional paired-sample testing, where observations arrive over time and the goal is to continuously assess whether two conditional distributions are equal given a common set of covariates. This problem arises naturally in model monitoring, where distributional changes must be detected without a prespecified terminal sample size, and in online comparisons, where responses are compared conditional on subject-level characteristics. We propose SCPT, an anytime-valid testing procedure for conditional distributions based on sequentially constructed conditional kernel discrepancy statistics and test martingales. The proposed method is nonparametric and accommodates a broad class of data-generating processes beyond the i.i.d. setting. We establish time-uniform Type I error control and derive asymptotic power guarantees under suitable regularity conditions. We also develop several useful extensions to address different needs, including testing under broader dependence structures, comparisons involving multiple auxiliary streams, and conditional goodness-of-fit testing. Simulations and real-data experiments show that SCPT effectively detects conditional distributional differences in streaming data, demonstrating its practical utility in a wide range of real-world applications.

title: Euclid: Quick Data Release (Q1) -- The evolution of the radio-loud AGN fraction-stellar mass relation to $z\sim3$ in the Euclid Deep Field North
abstract: The incidence of radio-loud active galactic nuclei (RLAGN) and their energetic output via AGN feedback are crucial in understanding the evolution of galaxies and the large-scale structure of the Universe. In the local Universe, the incidence of RLAGN has been shown to correlate strongly with host galaxy properties, particularly stellar mass. Using the large-area survey capabilities provided by Euclid and the LOw Frequency ARray (LOFAR), we present the first study of the RLAGN incidence--stellar mass relation to $z=3.0$. We perform a stringent analysis accounting for cross-matching reliability and stellar-mass incompleteness. In addition, we test the robustness of our results against AGN and host galaxy classification. This yields a sample of $3\,154$ RLAGN in the Euclid Deep Field North, comprising $2\,803$ low-excitation radio galaxies (LERGs). We find that the LERG incidence as a function of stellar mass and radio luminosity follows a tight correlation over more than two orders of magnitude in stellar mass to $z=3.0$. The slope of the power-law relation decreases from $γ\approx2.5$ in the local Universe to $γ\approx1.0$ at $z=3.0$, indicating a relative increase in low-mass LERGs at earlier epochs. Separating the LERG population into actively star-forming and quiescent galaxies reveals that quiescent LERGs show a much steeper relation between incidence and stellar mass, with $γ\approx2.5$ compared to star-forming LERGs that show $γ\approx1.5$. However, the relation seems to be independent of whether galaxies are star-forming or quiescent at $z\geq2$, where both populations show relatively flat relations with $γ\approx1.0$. Our results suggest an evolutionary picture in which the LERG population transitions from cold-mode, merger-dominated accretion at earlier epochs to a scenario in which systems require a massive hot halo to fuel the AGN in the local Universe.

title: Stopping Is Not the Limit: Understanding and Eliciting Agent Capability in Long-Horizon Vulnerability Exploitation
abstract: Vulnerability exploitation tests whether language model agents can develop working exploits from known software flaws. Sequential test-time scaling can improve exploitation performance, but larger budgets do not ensure sustained exploration: agents often stop with budget remaining. Yet what happens when execution continues beyond stopping remains underexplored. We investigate this gap on ExploitBench using DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 and MiMo-V2.6-Pro. We find additional verified gains after the first stop response, but gains diminish over longer execution. We identify two patterns associated with less productive continuation: an increasing proportion of stop responses within the same context and earlier stopping associated with summaries retaining impossibility judgments about unachieved capabilities. To test whether context management can elicit further capability, we propose SCoRe, which compacts context at stop bursts and marks these judgments as unproven. SCoRe improves verified capability over summary-based continuation and other evaluated context-management baselines. With SCoRe, MiMo reaches a capability coverage score of 67.0% at 2,000 turns, exceeding both 32.4% under the original stopping policy and the 58.6% computed for GPT-5.5 from ExploitBench's 300-turn reference results on the same tasks. These findings show that stopping need not mark an agent's exploitation limit, and that continued execution with context management can elicit substantial further capability.

title: Beyond Attribute-Centric Fairness: Modelling and Mitigating Unified Bias Representation in Omni-modal Large Language Models
abstract: Omni-modal large language models (OLLMs) provide joint multimodal understanding and generation capabilities, making them well-suited to complex environments and promising backbones for next-generation AI. Despite these advances, the harmful stereotypes encoded in such models manifest in increasingly diverse forms, leading to broader and more severe societal consequences. Existing debiasing methods typically impose separate fairness objectives for each sensitive attribute and modality to minimise demographic-dependent variations. However, in omni-modal settings, this attribute-centric paradigm struggles to jointly address diverse social biases with distinct fairness objectives and to generalise beyond predefined attributes. To this end, we propose OmniDebias, one of the first methods for promoting fairness in OLLMs, which employs a bias-centric formulation to extract and mitigate a shared bias representation across attributes and modalities while preserving attribute-related knowledge. Specifically, we exploit activation inconsistencies of a given attribute (e.g., gender) across semantic contexts (e.g., occupations) to disentangle bias from legitimate knowledge. We further consolidate multiple extracted biases into a shared representation, formulating a unified objective that captures the underlying structure across social biases and generalises to unseen attributes. Extensive experiments demonstrate that eliminating unified bias with both post-hoc editing and fine-tuning can consistently improve fairness across diverse attributes and modalities in OLLMs while maintaining favourable utility.

title: Scalar inelastic scattering of pseudo-Majorana dark matter through a radion portal
abstract: We investigate a radion portal for pseudo-Majorana dark matter as an interpretation of the high-recoil event LZ230616. In contrast to the familiar pseudo-Dirac regime, the pseudo-Majorana structure allows a dominant scalar transition while suppressing elastic scattering. Endothermic kinematics remove low-energy recoils, while the nuclear response shapes the surviving high-recoil spectrum. Combining the accepted LZ event count with the Born-level thermal relic abundance yields a reference solution with $m_χ=1$ TeV, $δ=340$ keV, and $m_r=30$ GeV. This solution lies within the published LZ spin-independent $\mathcal{O}_1^s$ interval and remains compatible with existing OPAL and CMS constraints, while a simplified HL-LHC diphoton projection could probe it. Solar neutrino searches offer a complementary test. The benchmark's energetic-daughter proxy rates are comparable in magnitude to the rate scales reconstructed from IceCube's direct $b\bar{b}$ and $τ^+τ^-$ templates. An illustrative IceCube-Gen2 rescaling suggests future sensitivity, while a model-specific assessment requires the radion-cascade neutrino spectra and detector response.

title: Impact of errors-on-errors on the PDF determination from combined HERA data
abstract: We study how the determination of parton distribution functions (PDFs) from the combined HERA inclusive deep-inelastic-scattering data is affected when the quoted sizes of the systematic errors are themselves treated as uncertain. We refer to these uncertainties informally as errors-on-errors and account for them using the Gamma Variance Model, which treats the squared quoted systematic errors as Gamma-distributed estimates of unknown variances. As a result, the usual quadratic nuisance parameter constraints in the $χ^2$ are replaced with logarithmic ones. We present two applications of the framework. In the first, a robustness test estimates the largest errors-on-errors effects that could be present in our reproduction of the HERAPDF2.0 NNLO fit, reducing $χ^2/n_{\rm dof}$ from 1363/1131 to 1306/1131, with the main impact concentrated at low Bjorken $x$ and low squared momentum transfer, $Q^2$. Comparable reductions are observed with a more flexible small-$x$ parametrisation, both at fixed NNLO and with NNLO+NLL$_x$ resummation. In the second, the error-on-error parameters are instead assigned a priori, as they would be in a PDF determination intended for publication. Taken together, the results indicate that errors-on-errors can account for a substantial part of the apparent data-theory tension in the combined HERA dataset, improving the inferred compatibility and widening the fitted PDF uncertainties without appreciably displacing the PDFs or cross-section predictions themselves.

title: Weighted Proportional Toll Sharing on General Highway Networks
abstract: We extend the Segments Equal Sharing (SES) method of \citet{wu2024} from line highways to general highway networks, including networks with cycles. The input is an exogenously specified profile of route flows. We introduce the Weighted Proportional Sharing (WPS) method, which distributes each route's mileage revenue in proportion to weighted segment lengths and its fixed-surcharge revenue in proportion to positive segment surcharges. Route SES is recovered under homogeneous weights within each revenue component. We show that WPS is the sum of two weighted Shapley allocations and that the underlying route games extend the dividend and Shapley representation of linear SES. Two axiomatic characterizations identify WPS. The first uses additivity and proportional treatment of segments used on every positive-revenue route. The second combines sub-highway efficiency and weighted average balanced contributions under a route cancellation rule. We also extend Segments Proportional Sharing to general networks, identify it with the $τ$ value of the corresponding route game, and characterize it axiomatically. For Segments Compensated Sharing we characterize a weighted average tree allocation by consistency across rooted branch settlements and averaging under a specified root lottery. A cyclic example shows that different route splits can change the allocation even when origin--destination volumes and aggregate toll revenue are held fixed.

title: Exact classical bounds of bipartite correlation Bell inequalities using improved branch-and-bound
abstract: We present an improved branch-and-bound (IBB) algorithm for the exact computation of classical (local) bounds of bipartite correlation Bell inequalities. We strengthen pruning in the standard BB algorithm in two ways: a heuristic search based on see-saw iteration supplies a strong initial lower bound, and greedy row reordering of the Bell matrix reduces the tail bounds used during the exact search. An OpenMP implementation combines these improvements with shared-memory parallelism and dynamic work redistribution. Random-matrix benchmarks show substantial runtime reductions in matrix sizes, while explicit constructions demonstrate exact local-bound computations for square matrices up to $130 \times 130$ and rectangular matrices of sizes up to $81 \times 321$. Applications provide improved lower bounds on finite-order Grothendieck constants for $d=3,4,5,7$ and uniform-input XOR games with quantum-to-classical ratios exceeding $\sqrt2$. The method retains an exponential worst-case search for this NP-hard optimization problem, and its practical performance depends on matrix structure and tail-bound preprocessing depth.

title: Wear and Go: Calibration Free Sparse Inertial Motion Capture via Online Sensor Setup Estimation
abstract: Sparse inertial motion capture typically assumes that each sensor's anatomical identity and mounting orientation are known. We present MOSAIC (Motion-based Sensor Assignment and Inertial Calibration), a framework that recovers this setup from ordinary motion without a calibration pose. Our central insight is that body pose changes continuously while the sensor setup persists, allowing movements that are individually ambiguous to provide complementary evidence over time. A setup network processes unordered sensor streams with temporal and cross-sensor attention, then accumulates assignment and rotation evidence into a session-level estimate. The recovered setup canonicalizes measurements for frozen pretrained pose estimators, separating sensor configuration from motion reconstruction. For sensors worn at prescribed body sites, evaluation on real inertial recordings with randomized setups shows near-calibrated pose accuracy for bounded offsets and substantial benefits from accumulation under arbitrary orientations. Transfer across pose networks supports setup recovery as a reusable interface between interchangeable sensors and pretrained pose models.

title: Tunable Microresonator Arrays Induced by Geometric Phase
abstract: Unlike periodic field-intensity patterns, which can be generated by interference of coherent beams, periodic material structures are usually created by periodic modification. In contrast, we show here that a millimeter-long bundle of four conventional side-coupled optical fibers with a slowly varying transverse arrangement can support a nearly periodic array of whispering-gallery-mode microresonators, whose period can be tuned mechanically down to about $100\,μ\mathrm{m}$.

title: Impact of Pretraining Length, Model Size, and Annotation Budget on Downstream Clinical Tasks of Foundation Models in Radiotherapy
abstract: Cone-beam CT (CBCT) scans acquired during radiotherapy capture changes such as tumor shrinkage and radiation-induced tissue changes, offering great potential for foundation models that help monitor individual treatment responses. However, to our knowledge, no large-scale pretrained models for radiotherapy CBCT exist, and evaluating modeling choices is difficult since downstream tasks are not known in advance. We examine how pretraining length, model size, and finetuning strategy relate to downstream clinical performance, and how metrics tracked during pretraining correlate with it. We pretrain vision transformer encoders with masked image modeling on about 150,000 raw 3D radiotherapy CBCT scans, tracking representation quality via validation loss, effective rank, and linear probing. Downstream tasks are classification of feeding tube presence ($n=51,135$ CBCTs, $1,562$ patients) and clinical characteristics (T-, N-stage, sex, age, tumor site; $n=1,278$ patients) in head and neck cancer. We compare low-rank adaptation (LoRA) and full finetuning against no pretraining, varying annotated dataset size. Pretext validation loss was the most consistent predictor of downstream performance; effective rank and linear probing were also associated, but not consistently across model sizes and finetuning methods. LoRA performed comparably to full finetuning while training only 0.5-2.5% of the parameters. Fully finetuned models consistently outperformed models without pretraining across all sizes, with AUROC 0.91-0.97 vs. 0.58-0.85 for feeding tube classification and 0.99-1.00 vs. 0.71-0.97 for sex classification. Model size had only a small, inconsistent effect, suggesting smaller models suffice at lower computational cost. Code and pretrained models (non-commercial license): https://github.com/alexCortinaU/RT-CBCT_SSL

title: Born for the Task: Rethinking Quantum Chemistry with Foresighted Agentic Computing
abstract: Quantum chemistry relies on general-purpose software, whose generality leaves many large-scale calculations beyond practical resource budgets. Coding agents make task-specific programs cheap to write, but not efficient ones easy to find: whether a computational strategy is accurate and fast enough becomes clear only after it actually runs at the target scale. We introduce BORN, a foresighted agentic computing framework that synthesizes high performance quantum chemistry programs on demand. BORN anticipates the behavior of each strategy before execution, extrapolating its error from representative small systems and predicting its runtime from the target-scale workload and measured hardware throughputs. Building on these predictions, BORN unfolds the preset schemes of existing packages into independently configurable algorithmic components, selects the fastest strategy within the error tolerance from the predicted accuracy-runtime Pareto frontier, and guides coding agents to compile it with component-level performance predictions. For a Hartree-Fock calculation with 50,024 basis functions, BORN finishes in 1.41h on a single CPU node, 77$\times$ faster than the estimated runtime of a general-purpose baseline and still 9.8$\times$ faster with development time included. On a single GPU, BORN completes the ubiquitin calculation in 2.1,h, the same order of runtime as the GPU-accelerated package Mako on 64 GPUs, and shortens the B-DNA duplex calculation from an estimated two months to 8.1,h (173$\times$).

title: You Only Encode Once: Sub-Pixel-Shifted Frames for Arbitrary-Scale Remote Sensing Super-Resolution with 2D Gaussian Splatting
abstract: Arbitrary-scale super-resolution (ASSR) of remote sensing images remains challenging due to the limited high-frequency information in a single low-resolution (LR) observation. While multi-frame SR can exploit complementary sub-pixel information, existing approaches often require real multi-frame training sequences and repeated feature encoding, increasing data acquisition demands and computational costs. To address these limitations, we propose SPS-GS (Sub-Pixel-Shifted Gaussian Splatting), an encode-once framework that learns from multi-phase LR observations synthesized from individual high-resolution images, without requiring real multi-frame training sequences. Specifically, Phase-Coherent Aliasing Demodulation (PCAD) exploits shift-dependent aliasing through Fourier-based alignment, phase-aware residual fusion, and least-squares aliasing estimation, enabling multi-frame information to be integrated before a single deep encoding pass. Gaussian Projection Alignment (GPA) then iteratively refines Gaussian centers and colors using multi-observation back-projection to promote observation consistency. The refined Gaussians support continuous rendering at arbitrary scales. Extensive experiments on five remote sensing datasets demonstrate strong reconstruction performance against single-image and multi-frame SR baselines, while maintaining competitive inference efficiency at common scales. The code will be publicly released.

title: A Dichotomy for Exact Quantum Circuit Amplitudes
abstract: We classify the complexity of exactly computing computational-basis amplitudes for circuits over any fixed finite library of unitary qubit gates, with each gate allowed to act on any ordered tuple of distinct wires. Exact evaluation is polynomial-time computable if all gates permute the computational basis up to phases, all preserve product states, or all become Clifford under a common diagonal one-qubit unitary change of basis on every wire. For every other library, the problem is $\#\mathrm P$-hard under polynomial-time Turing reductions. Our proof connects circuit amplitudes to the Boolean Holant classification of tensor contractions on arbitrary graphs. For an algebraic library containing a nonmonomial gate and an entangling gate, we show how to simulate the joint use of a symmetric maximally entangled state and its adjoint at polynomial cost, using only amplitude queries over the original library. This lets us evaluate unrestricted contractions of the resulting gate and boundary tensors. Unitarity and the computational-basis boundaries then restrict the tractable cases to the three forms above. Algebraic specialization extends the dichotomy to arbitrary fixed complex gate entries under a symbolic exact-output convention.

title: blaris: Windowless Random-Access LZSS for Constrained Microcontrollers
abstract: Embedded LZ77 decompressors (such as heatshrink and tamp) require an in-RAM sliding window that couples memory usage to compression ratio and incurs high latency on random-access reads. We present blaris, a lightweight, windowless LZSS decompressor for execute-in-place (XIP) random access on constrained microcontrollers. By partitioning tokens into bidirectionally traversable streams with power-of-two checkpoints, blaris resolves back-references directly in the compressed payload, achieving compression ratios comparable to high-window heatshrink and tamp configurations without allocating a RAM window. Targeting compress-on-host, decompress-on-device workflows, blaris assumes trusted build-time payloads and omits runtime error and bounds checks. On RV32IMC, it requires just 548-784 B of Flash and 104-112 B of total RAM, achieving orders-of-magnitude faster small-slice random reads than ratio-matched, block-indexed heatshrink and tamp.

title: Done, But Still Working: Anytime Evaluation of When Coding Agents Should Stop
abstract: Coding agents often continue working after their own tests pass. Does this additional work improve the patch, and how much could be saved by stopping earlier? We study these questions through anytime evaluation: replaying recorded runs, scoring intermediate patches with hidden tests, and measuring the cost incurred at each step. For policies that only stop a run or select an earlier patch, this allows paired comparisons without generating new trajectories, provided replay preserves the relevant states. Across about 6,000 runs of eight open models in two scaffolds on SWE-bench Verified, we find substantial differences in the value of continued work. The hindsight saving available at passing self-tests ranges from under 1% to 57%, depending on the model and scaffold. A rule that stops after the same patch passes twice saves 23% in a preregistered replication, but the preregistered quality test does not establish non-inferiority. We explain these differences by measuring how often a rule fires, how often the patch changes afterwards, and whether those changes repair or break it. Fine-tuning agents to imitate the rule saves 30% over six seeds, while quality preservation remains uncertain. Our results help identify both the opportunities and the risks of early stopping.

title: A free-energy approach for stochastic reaction-drift-diffusion lattice simulations of crowded biological systems
abstract: Molecular size alters spatial distributions, reaction equilibria, and transport in crowded mixtures, but resolving individual particle encounters can make large stochastic simulations computationally costly. We developed a lattice-based framework for simulating reaction-drift-diffusion systems with volume exclusion captured as a free energy functional in each voxel. Changes in this free energy, together with external one-body potentials, modify diffusion and reaction propensities. Our framework accommodates mixtures of particle sizes without resolving each particle's position within a voxel. We implemented our framework in an operator splitting scheme and compared our predictions with off-lattice interacting-particle simulations. Inclusion of the local free energy functional improved spatial occupancies and shifts in reaction equilibria relative to point-particle simulations. With separate approximations for larger spheres and polymers, we simulated crowding-induced slowing and spatial segregation. We then modeled motor proteins' traffic jams on a structured track representing a microtubule. Our results demonstrate how local composition can inform stochastic reaction and transport rates without resolving individual encounters.

title: BRepA: Graph-Based B-Rep Pretraining for Unified CAD Understanding and Generation
abstract: Boundary representation (B-Rep) of CAD models encodes geometric primitives and their relations as a graph structure, enabling efficient shape modeling within CAD software. Learning on B-Reps for downstream tasks, such as segmentation and novel shape generation, requires specialized neural network designs. Moreover, performance improvements and accelerated training can be achieved with effective pretraining strategies, which is particularly important for tasks with limited labeled B-Rep data. In this paper, we introduce BRepA, a unified self-supervised pretraining framework that explicitly reconstructs both the geometry and topology of B-Rep objects via graph-based modeling. By learning from large-scale unlabeled CAD data only once, BRepA produces representations that generalize across tasks and significantly enhance both discriminative and generative learning. On segmentation tasks, BRepA demonstrates remarkable data efficiency. For instance, with only 1% labeled samples, BRepA pretraining improves mIoU by 32.52% compared to models trained from scratch. On generative tasks, aligning diffusion model representations with pretrained BRepA features substantially accelerates convergence, achieving nearly 2 times faster training while improving generation quality under the same computational budget, despite the diffusion model being roughly 20 times larger than BRepA. Overall, our results show that geometry- and topology-aware B-Rep pretraining provides a powerful foundation for both understanding and generating CAD structures, serving as a versatile representation backbone for diverse downstream applications. We will release the code to facilitate future research.

title: Who Pays for Byzantine Robustness? Validity, Data-Share Dictatorships, and Fairness When Only a Few Hospitals Collaborate
abstract: Clinical federated learning (FL) collaborations typically connect only three to six hospitals, yet Byzantine-robust aggregation rules are designed and benchmarked on synthetic partitions across dozens of equal-sized clients. We conduct an empirical audit of eight standard aggregation rules: FedAvg, coordinate-wise median, trimmed mean, Krum, Multi-Krum, Bulyan, geometric median (GeoMed), and Centered Clipping (CC). We evaluate both unweighted and sample-size-weighted variants across three cross-silo medical datasets from the FLamby benchmark: Fed-Heart-Disease ($n = 4$ hospitals), Fed-TCGA-BRCA ($n = 6$ regions), and Fed-ISIC2019 ($n = 6$ centres). We execute 54,214 training runs across enumerated attacker coalitions ($f \in \{1, 2\}$) paired with exact-twin leave-out controls that decompose performance drops into honest data loss versus adversarial attack damage. We report three findings. First, client-count validity checks fail to capture breakdown in skewed medical consortia: while $n = 6, f = 1$ satisfies every count condition except Bulyan's, assigning sample-size weights turns median and GeoMed into a clean-model dictatorship whenever a single hospital holds more than half the training data, and causes weighted median, GeoMed, and CC to collapse when that dominant centre attacks. Second, exact-twin leave-out controls reveal that when the largest hospital attacks, the apparent failure of count-based robust rules is predominantly caused by the loss of honest training data (7.5 to 10.4 points on ISIC) rather than adversarial perturbation (2.3 to 3.8 points on ISIC). Conversely, weight-dependent rules suffer large true attack damage (16.1 to 25.1 points on ISIC). Third, unweighted robust rules consistently discount whichever institution generates the most atypical parameter updates, penalizing the smallest hospital on Heart but penalizing larger institutions on TCGA and ISIC.

title: Think Before You Code: A Benchmark for Testing LLMs on Software Engineering Deliberation
abstract: Think Before You Code (TBYC) is a benchmark pipeline for studying whether code-focused language models can reason about software issues in ways that resemble human engineering deliberation. The benchmark curates GitHub issue discussions into structured records, extracts human discussion artifacts such as problems, solutions, constraints, rationales, and trade-offs, and then prompts models to generate issue-level "thoughts" using retrieved code context and few-shot examples. It converts model responses back into the same artifact space and evaluates them against human annotations using complementary metrics for artifact type detection, metadata matching, tag overlap, and semantic summary similarity. Beyond scoring, this study includes visualization, leaderboard, and baseline tools that make it possible to compare models, prompting strategies, and extraction methods across repositories and issues. Think Before You Code is an end-to-end evaluation environment for measuring how closely LLM software reasoning aligns with human strategic judgment.

title: Development of a Discrete Variable Representation of a Field-Adaptive Hermite Basis for Accurate Modeling of Magnetically Confined Systems
abstract: Accurate magnetic-field evolution of spectra requires a common wavefunction representation that consistently describes multiple states across different field regimes. Discrete Variable Representation (DVR) methods combine accurate basis-based kinetic-energy evaluation with flexible real-space potential representation, enabling arbitrary non-analytic potentials to be treated. Here, we develop a magnetic-field-dependent Hermite function-based (Hermite-B) DVR that adapts naturally to magnetic confinement, efficiently representing compressed wavefunctions across a wide range of field strengths while remaining centered in regions relevant to the scalar confinement potential. This ensures accurate treatment of the field-dependent kinetic energy while addressing two key challenges: maintaining accuracy from the Zeeman to Landau regimes and accommodating diverse confinement potentials. We also introduce a spatial restriction scheme that confines Hermite DVR grid points to a fixed-length domain, enabling compact representations for smooth potentials. The method is benchmarked for two-dimensional quantum dots in perpendicular magnetic fields against analytical models and compared with finite-grid, sine DVR, and field-free Hermite DVR calculations. The performance of field-independent DVR methods for magnetically confined systems is also investigated for the first time. Excellent agreement with exact analytical spectra and wavefunctions is obtained, with Hermite-B requiring the fewest basis functions and smaller Hamiltonian matrices, improving computational efficiency. Applications to arbitrary confinement potentials and tilted magnetic fields demonstrate its versatility beyond analytically solvable systems. The proposed method offers a robust, accurate, and efficient framework for large-scale calculations of realistic semiconductor nanostructures and molecular systems in external magnetic fields.

title: Optimising Recruitment and Sample Allocation in Multi-Site Rare Disease Studies
abstract: Clinical research in rare diseases is challenged by the limited availability and broad geographical distribution of eligible patients. This necessitates multi-centre collaboration and strategic selection of analytical laboratories based on capacity, cost, and capability. We present a mathematical framework based on cardinality optimisation to support key operational decisions in study design, balancing clinical relevance, feasibility, budgetary constraints, and logistical factors. The framework was implemented in the Reconstruction and Computational Modelling for Inherited Metabolic Diseases (Recon4IMD) project, aiming to recruit 1,900 diagnosed patients across 24 healthcare centres and eight metabolomic laboratories. Compared to both proportional heuristic and greedy marginal allocation baselines, the proposed optimisation model consistently achieved higher recruitment yields in simulated multi-centre scenarios and reduced metabolomic analysis costs by approximately 30% under unconstrained conditions. Notably, both the heuristic and greedy allocation baselines became infeasible under progressively tighter laboratory capacity constraints, whereas the optimised model maintained feasibility and cost control. These findings highlight the value of integrated optimisation strategies for improving recruitment, platform selection, and sample allocation in complex, resource-limited research settings.

title: Arboreus: A Realistic Boreal Forest Simulator with Topographic Terrain and Satellite-Informed Parametric Tree Distributions
abstract: This work presents Arboreus, a realistic Boreal forest simulator, developed to support statistical validation of robotic autonomy algorithms in Boreal forest environments. Arboreus presents an automated methodology for synthesizing large-scale, data-informed, plausible forest worlds from parametric trees, height-variant terrain, and satellite-informed tree density distributions. The parametric generation of dominant Boreal tree species such as Birch, Spruce, and Pine is guided by trunk, canopy, and foliage parameters, extracted from growth studies in the Nordic areas. Tree distribution in an area of interest is guided by the Copernicus satellite dataset, which provides tree cover density and dominant species type at up to 10m raster resolution. The forest floor generation is guided by topographic data from the Swedish cadastral agency to produce realistic data-informed terrains. Given coordinates and extents of forested areas of interest, Arboreus synthesizes data-informed plausible forests, while offering flexibility to inject user observations of real forests (detail, age, dimensionality and tree count), which is critical for realistic synthetic data generation and for the testing of feature-sensitive autonomy algorithms. The applicability of Arboreus for benchmarking and validation of robot autonomy for different robot mobilities is demonstrated in Gazebosim, Unreal Engine, and Isaac Sim physics engines. The applicability of Arboreus as a source of synthetic forest data and its potential to support downstream forest resource mapping research (volume estimation, tree instance segmentation and stem attribute estimation) is also demonstrated. Arboreus has been open-sourced along with a dataset comprising 25 Boreal forest worlds of size 1000m2 corresponding to three real forest sites.

title: Minimum outdegree forcing directed cycles
abstract: The Caccetta-Häggkvist conjecture, one of the best known open problems on oriented graphs, asserts that every oriented graph on $n$ vertices with minimum outdegree at least $n/\ell$ contains a directed cycle of length at most $\ell$. Motivated by it, Kelly, Kühn and Osthus asked for the minimum degree condition that forces a directed cycle of length exactly $\ell$. The semidegree version of this problem was recently solved, but the methods used there rely on bounding the directed diameter, which requires control over the indegrees. In the setting of the Caccetta-Häggkvist conjecture, where only the outdegrees are bounded, the answer was known only for $\ell$ not divisible by $3$. We determine the optimal minimum outdegree forcing a directed cycle of length $\ell$ for every sufficiently large $\ell$ and $n$. This establishes the outdegree version of the Kelly-Kühn-Osthus conjecture for all large $\ell$, up to a small correction of the additive term, which in general cannot be avoided.

title: A 4.542-approximation for the Small Cuts Cover problem via a multi-rate primal-dual algorithm
abstract: In the Small Cuts Cover problem we seek to cover by a min-cost edge-set the set-family of cuts of size $<k$ of a graph. Bansal, Cheriyan, Grout, and Ibrahimpur [ICALP 2023: 15:1-15:19] showed that the classic primal-dual algorithm with reverse delete of Williamson, Goemans, Mihail, and Vazirani [STOC 1993: 708-717] achieves approximation ratio $16$ for this problem. The analysis of the approximation ratio was then improved in a sequence of papers, culminating in the $5$-approximation by Simons, Bansal, and Cheriyan. A matching example of Nutov shows that this bound is tight for the classic algorithm. We improve the approximation ratio to $(3+\sqrt{37})/2<4.542$ using a multi-rate primal-dual algorithm (that applies for strongly pliable set-families) in which the dual variables of the inclusion-minimal violated sets are not raised uniformly, but with different rates. We also provide a tight example. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first example in network design where for the standard LP, an efficiently computable choice of growth rates improves on the tight guarantee of uniform growth.

title: Can Verifiable PIR Match the Online Efficiency of SimplePIR?
abstract: Verifiable Private Information Retrieval (vPIR) ensures that a malicious server cannot return tampered database records, but it traditionally incurs significant overhead compared to classical PIR.Recent advancements, notably VeriSimplePIR, approach the online efficiency of SimplePIR by introducing a proof preprocessing phase and requiring only lightweight client-side online verification. However, this scheme relies on an additional Short Integer Solution (SIS) assumption and SIS-based commitments, which only support relaxed range proofs. Consequently, these schemes are forced to adopt significantly weaker parameter choices, resulting in additional online overhead. In this paper, we propose a novel vPIR protocol that employs a newly designed error-correcting code-based commitment scheme as the database digest. This approach (i)supports efficient proofs of linear relations, (ii) achieves precise range proofs and (iii) eliminates the reliance on the SIS assumption. Thus, our scheme successfully adopts parameter choices identical to those of SimplePIR. As a result, our vPIR protocol is the first to achieve exactly the same online communication and server computation costs as SimplePIR, while keeping online client computation nearly identical. Additionally, compared to VeriSimplePIR,our protocol reduces online communication and client-side computation by approximately 20%, and decreases online server-side computation by over 35%.

title: Electrical addressing of compensated magnetic order in artificial spin ice
abstract: Compensated magnetic systems, such as antiferromagnets, hold immense potential for spintronic devices thanks to vanishing stray fields, robustness to perturbations, and ultrafast dynamics. Yet, electrical writing and reading of their order remains a major challenge. Here we use artificial spin ice as a mesoscale platform in which compensated order can be engineered, directly imaged, and electrically controlled. Specifically, we demonstrate combined electrical writing and reading of a compensated state in a triangular artificial spin ice. Exploiting the orientation dependence of the spin-orbit torque switching current, we independently switch three nanomagnet sublattices through a single current channel, with the planar Hall effect providing sublattice-resolved readout. This grants access to all eight magnetization states of the triangular plaquette, including its fully compensated state, yielding a nonlinear, history-dependent electrical response. Our results establish an approach to electrically programmable compensated magnetic systems and provide an important foundation for reconfigurable magnetic devices and unconventional computing.

title: A novel method for dust evolution in protoplanetary disks and a new criterion for gap opening
abstract: We present the Grain Residence-Time Method (GRTM), a computationally efficient particle-tracking approach for studying dust evolution and trapping in protoplanetary disks. By reconstructing steady-state dust distributions from particle residence times, this method provides a way to obtain radial dust surface density profiles without directly evolving the dust as a fluid. We compare the GRTM with dust profiles computed via standard methods using the $\texttt{FARGO3D}$ code, which models the dust as a pressureless fluid, and find very good agreement over a wide range of parameter space. Finally, we investigate how dust gap formation depends on the planet-to-star mass ratio ($q$) and Stokes number ($\mathrm{St}$), through a parameter study, establishing an empirical criterion for dust gap opening. In doing so, we have discovered a new regime of gap opening for small grains with $St \lesssim 10^{-2}$ and for planet mass well below Jupiter's, which is likely very relevant for gaps seen in ALMA images.

title: FastSpecFit: Spectrophotometric Modeling of 38 Million Extragalactic Targets from the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument Second Data Release
abstract: Optical spectrophotometry provides a direct window into the physical conditions, kinematics, and formation histories of galaxies and quasars. FastSpecFit is an open-source Python software package that forward-models each Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) spectrum jointly with its broadband photometry, convolving stellar-population synthesis and emission-line templates with each fiber's native spectral resolution.
