These findings suggest that SBC captures structural characteristics that are largely distinct from those reflected by other measures, while RC exhibits distinct structural associations and shows significant potential for identifying vertices critical to network connectivity.

title: Fine-Tuning Gemma 4 Edge Models for MATLAB Signal-Processing Code with SFT and QLoRA on a Laptop iGPU
abstract: Small language models that run on a laptop are attractive for writing signal-processing code offline, but they make systematic errors on digital signal processing (DSP) conventions. We apply supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to the Gemma 4 edge models E2B and E4B with 66 checked examples covering 11 signal-processing MATLAB subtasks, using low-rank adaptation (LoRA) and quantized LoRA (QLoRA) on the integrated GPU (iGPU) of a laptop, and deploy the 8-bit integer (int8) models with the adapters through OpenVINO. On held-out variants scored by deterministic checkers, the pass rate rises from 18/66 to 37/66 (LoRA) and 37/66 (QLoRA) for E2B and from 32/66 to 47/66 for E4B (QLoRA). Reading all 159 failing programs shows that the adapters remove most errors of convention, such as the sign of a lag, units and array shapes, but few errors in building signals and noise. Applied at run time, the adapter costs 17-19% of the generation speed.

title: Reading Scene States: Uncovering Safety Failures in Vision-Language Models
abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) can provide harmful assistance by interpreting visual events, even without an explicit request for the underlying harmful objective. We identify this \textbf{scene-state safety vulnerability} and introduce \textbf{SceneSafetyBench}, comprising 375 image--question pairs spanning Initial, Medium, and Ultimate scene states and five visual presentations. Across eight VLMs, scene-state inputs elicit harmful assistance with attack success rates (ASRs) of 45.6--72.3\%. Comparative analysis across three VLMs shows that scene-state inputs most closely resemble QR-related images in their layer-wise safety-related signal profiles, while exhibiting lower average late-layer readouts and distinct signal dynamics during generation. To turn this vulnerability into a systematic attack, we propose \textbf{S3TA}, which translates harmful objectives into scene states, queries image--question pairs independently, and assembles the responses. On seven MM-SafetyBench categories across eight open-weight and commercial VLMs, S3TA achieves a model-average ASR of \textbf{71.2\%, exceeding the strongest baseline by 6.1 percentage points}. Text-side filters and visual moderation provide limited protection. These findings highlight the need to safeguard the assistance models infer through scene-grounded reasoning, beyond screening input content.

title: Local interference algorithms for observables in large random circuits
abstract: In quantum dynamics, it is generally believed that interference effects lead to a sign problem for classical Monte Carlo sampling methods, rendering sampling ineffective. In this paper we show that this is generically not the case for the task of simulating the evolution of observables in random instances of circuit dynamics. Specifically, we consider two examples of observables which give large signals despite the randomness of the dynamics: first order out-of-time-ordered correlators (OTOCs) in unstructured random circuits without conservation laws and time-ordered charge-charge correlators (TOCs) in particle number-preserving random circuits. We show that these observables can be approximated by classical stochastic processes and that these approximations can be systematically improved with a series expansion that incorporates coherent corrections associated with clusters of gates. We design and implement algorithms that combine Monte Carlo sampling and tensor network methods to approximate the series. We observe numerically that the computational complexity of approximating TOCs and OTOCs scales polynomially in the circuit size and in the target precision. We study the accuracy of these algorithms by directly mapping their ensemble-averaged errors to partition functions of replica statistical models, allowing for perturbative analysis and numerics in $1$d brickwork geometries. Our theoretical analysis explains the empirical observation of polynomial complexity of these algorithms and is consistent with polynomial complexity extending to arbitrarily small precision and to the thermodynamic limit.

title: Distortion-Free Semantic Watermarks for Black-Box Generative Models
abstract: We present a provably distortion-free semantic watermarking algorithm that requires only black-box sampling access to a generative model and black-box access to a semantic embedding. A watermark is called distortion-free if, averaged over its secret detection key, it leaves the generator's output distribution unchanged; this provides a formal guarantee that watermarking does not reduce output quality. Conventional such watermarks are often brittle to transformations. This is especially problematic for images, where benign operations such as compression, cropping, or resizing change the entire pixel representation. Semantic watermarks therefore require detection to be robust to content-preserving transformations. Previous methods combining these properties rely heavily on specific white-box properties of the underlying model: either to autoregressive text generation or to diffusion-specific access, such as control of the initial noise or diffusion inversion. In contrast, our construction is fully generic: It only interacts with the generative model and the semantic embedding, a function that determines the notion of "preserving content" under which detection should be robust, via sample and query access. We then instantiate this framework for image generation. We characterize the two competing properties required of the semantic embedding: it should remain stable under transformations that preserve an image's content, but should distinguish independent generations from the same prompt. We train an image encoder directly for this tradeoff. The resulting encoder improves separation while maintaining stability over off-the-shelf alternatives and enables strong aggregate detection while remaining robust to various transformations. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our watermark scheme on both open-source and closed models, which is possible only due to restriction to black-box access.

title: Learning Grounded Reasoning from Human Gaze
abstract: Human visual reasoning is driven by systematic exploration and extraction of task-relevant visual evidence. Human gaze provides a window into this process, making gaze a useful source of guidance for visually-grounded reasoning in vision-language models (VLMs). However, human gaze also includes noise and redundancies that may transfer poorly to VLMs. In this work, we investigate how human gaze data can be effectively leveraged to improve visual reasoning in VLMs, while maintaining alignment with human behavior. We collect 7,109 human gaze trials from a diverse and challenging set of visual reasoning tasks, and train grounded reasoning models with different forms of gaze guidance. Across evaluations in chart understanding, visual search, and counting, we find that using human gaze as a prior for grounded reasoning consistently outperforms supervision using the full gaze sequence. Based on these findings, we introduce GGR (Gaze-Guided Reasoner), which achieves greater human alignment and more reliable visual grounding while matching or outperforming leading grounded-reasoning baselines in accuracy. Reinforcement learning further improves task accuracy, gaze alignment, and grounding quality despite using no gaze supervision. Behavioral analyses show that gaze supervised models exhibit more visual exploration before arriving at an answer. Our results suggest that the value of human gaze lies in guiding spatial exploration and shaping reasoning behavior without requiring complete imitation of human behavior.

title: Non-homogeneous parabolic conormal boundary problem with singular-degenerate coefficients
abstract: We study non-homogeneous conormal boundary value problems for a class of divergence-form parabolic equations whose volumetric heat-capacity coefficients belong to a Muckenhoupt class of weights. Consequently, the equations exhibit singular, degenerate, or simultaneously singular-degenerate behavior. Under smallness conditions on the partial mean oscillation of the diffusion coefficients and the weighted mean oscillation of the volumetric heat-capacity coefficient, we establish regularity estimates, existence, and uniqueness results in appropriate weighted Sobolev spaces. To obtain these results, we employ the level-set argument introduced by Caffarelli and Peral. We also establish weighted parabolic cylinders, weighted inequalities, and a weighted Aubin-Lions compactness theorem, which are essential tools in our analysis.

title: Multimodal Masked Diffusion Autoencoder for Modeling Impaired Driving
abstract: Human cognitive state (e.g., distraction, stress), gaze, and behavior interact with the driving environment in subtle ways that AI could use to assist drivers, but ground-truth labels for human cognitive state levels are costly to obtain at scale. We propose a multimodal masked-diffusion autoencoder, ID-MAE, that adds a self-supervised objective to impairment prediction: alongside predicting the impairment label as a masked token, it reconstructs masked gaze and trajectory. To probe the effects of different modalities and types of impairments on model inference, we introduce DIVERT, a driving-simulator dataset containing 103 hours of driving data (n = 109) with ten impairment inductions spanning cognitive, visual, and emotional states, recorded with gaze, vehicle state, and scene video. We demonstrate how ID-MAE affords significant improvements in impairment inference results on both the DIVERT dataset and existing datasets, and enables strong results in additional tasks, such as trajectory and gaze prediction. For location-matched pairs, our model achieves a paired AUC of 0.706 for impairment detection on DIVERT, compared to 0.590 without reconstruction loss, improving over existing baselines. We probe the design space in terms of input modalities, masking scheme, positional encoding, attention mechanism, and decoding. We also investigate the interaction between various impairments in training and inference, demonstrating that visually demanding distractions are separable from cognitive distractions. Code and data will be available upon acceptance.

title: EviSlide-MIL: Multi-Query Pooling and Shared Prediction for Class-Incremental Whole-Slide Image Classification
abstract: Histopathological analysis of whole-slide images (WSIs) plays a critical role in cancer diagnosis, and multiple instance learning (MIL) is widely adopted for WSI analysis under weak supervision. As new tumor subtypes are introduced, extending existing MIL models requires learning new classes while retaining knowledge of previously learned ones. This presents a class-incremental learning challenge, where models must acquire new classes with limited access to historical training data and recognize all learned classes without task identifiers at inference. A major obstacle is forgetting, as updates to feature aggregation and prediction modules can degrade performance on previously learned classes. To address this challenge, we propose \textbf{EviSlide-MIL}, a class-incremental WSI framework that integrates multiple learnable queries per class with a shared prediction module. The queries aggregate frozen patch features into class-specific representations, while the shared prediction module limits parameter growth across incremental stages. By freezing queries associated with previously learned classes, EviSlide-MIL preserves their attention patterns for identical inputs, while experience replay and knowledge distillation further mitigate forgetting as shared parameters are updated. Experiments on eight tumor subtypes from The Cancer Genome Atlas demonstrate that EviSlide-MIL achieves improved performance and reduced forgetting compared with competing methods across most learning settings, demonstrating its potential for scalable and knowledge-preserving WSI classification. Code and pretrained models will be released.

title: Modeling quantum information scrambling in realistic protein NMR experiments
abstract: Out-of-time-order correlators (OTOCs) are important probes of operator spreading and information scrambling, and have recently been proposed as a means of extracting molecular structural information through nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR). Realizing this potential requires accurate modeling of OTOCs in complex molecular environments within experimentally relevant settings. Here, we develop an end-to-end computational pipeline connecting molecular structures to OTOC dynamics in protein systems. Our framework incorporates molecular motion through molecular dynamics simulations, orientational averaging appropriate for powder samples, and spin-network truncation, using an experimentally realizable double-quantum effective Hamiltonian. We apply this framework to a dataset of over 350 carbon-carbon spin pairs across 10 protein systems, spanning interspin distances of 5-17 A. We find that OTOC arrival times scale approximately linearly with interspin distance, revealing system-dependent operator-spreading velocities that enable correlations to propagate over extended distances within milliseconds. Our sensitivity analysis further shows that individual OTOCs predominantly constrain a single structural parameter, primarily associated with interspin distance. Together, these findings highlight the potential of OTOCs to probe spatially extended spin correlations on timescales compatible with solid-state NMR experiments.

title: Asymptotics of Gibbs Posterior Measures on Infinite-Dimensional Hypothesis Spaces
abstract: We prove almost sure contraction rates and consistency for Gibbs posterior measures on arbitrary hypothesis spaces, in general infinite dimensional, under dependent data, nonadditive and time-dependent losses and learning rates, misspecified models, and unattainable minimisers of the limiting objective. In particular, we develop a novel proof approach in contraction rate theory by studying the asymptotics of Gibbs measures through Lorentz spaces, real interpolation theory, and Laplace transforms dispensing with testing or variational formulations which are unavailable in the considered generality. As a consequence we obtain almost sure contraction rates for dominated Bayes and fractional Bayes posterior measures in the same generality, extending existing theory on misspecified Bayesian inference. Furthermore, we demonstrate our theoretical results on novel applications to Gibbs posteriors for Dirichlet process priors with a nonadditive Wasserstein metric loss function under ergodic, non-Markovian observables.

title: Feedback-Linearised Trajectory Tracking via Model-Informed Robust Geometric DDPC
abstract: Data-driven predictive control (DDPC) predicts system responses from recorded trajectories, but nonlinear dynamics can limit the accuracy of fixed linear predictors. This paper studies geometric robust DDPC for trajectory tracking of a fully actuated manipulator using model-based feedback linearisation. A mechanical model maps virtual acceleration commands into joint torques, while recorded data capture residual dynamics arising from imperfect model parameters. The controller minimises worst-case prediction error over an open Grassmannian ball centred at the fitted trajectory subspace. Simulations on a planar 2R manipulator under gravity compare the proposed method with double-integrator model predictive control (MPC) and direct regularised data-enabled predictive control (DeePC). Results show improved tracking over double-integrator MPC despite increased torque effort, while performance relative to DeePC depends on the reference trajectory.

title: Higher-Scoring Coding Models Did Not Get More Work Done
abstract: New coding models advertise themselves on score improvements of coding benchmarks. Yet no study has tested if a model that scores higher on these benchmarks gets more real work done. On June 12, 2026, a U.S. export control directive banned access to Claude Fable 5 for 19 days, which forced users to switch to other models. During this time, most former Fable 5 users switched to Opus 4.8 (11 points lower on SWE-Bench Pro compared to Fable 5). We treat this suspension as a natural experiment, where the people and projects stayed the same and only the model changed, so we could isolate the effect of Fable 5 on user productivity. We tracked GitHub pull requests of 297 Fable 5 users before, during, and after the suspension. We used 8,908 developers who stayed on Opus 4.8 all the time as the control group. We also repeated the comparison across five model upgrades before and after the suspension in 2026 (1,208 developers, 15,442 pull requests). Fitting a difference-in-differences model with developer and date fixed effects, we found that having access to Fable 5 increased the 7-day merge rate of pull requests by only 1.4 percentage points [-1.4; +4.3], which was not statistically significant. Similarly, no significant increases of merge rates were found with the upgrades (weighted mean: -0.9 percentage points [-1.9; +0.2]); all five estimates were negative (95% intervals included 0, did not differ from each other). We also did not observe a significant increase in the number of pull requests merged per week (+2.4% [-4.9%; +10.2%]).

title: Near Resonance, Less Ordered: Radius and Mass Ordering in Compact Multi-planet Systems
abstract: Compact multi-planet systems exhibit a tendency for planetary radii to follow ordered sequences with orbital position, suggesting that these non-random patterns preserve a fossil record of their formation. Here, we investigate whether ordering of planet radii and masses with orbital period is related to proximity to mean-motion resonances. We compare near-resonant and non-resonant systems using complementary rank- and inversion-based measures of ordering, while accounting for differences in planet multiplicity and uncertainties in the measured planetary properties. We find that radii and masses are less monotonically ordered in near-resonant systems than in non-resonant systems, with the primary radius analysis providing stronger evidence than the mass analysis. This result is opposite to the naive expectation that dynamical instabilities should erase the primordial ordering of initially resonant systems and leave non-resonant systems in a more disordered state.

title: What Does a Bias Head Measure? Non-Identifiability in Head-Level Bias Attribution
abstract: Methods that localise social bias in large language models to individual attention heads and remove it by ablation are validated by their effect on a fairness metric, never by evidence that the statistic selecting the heads measures bias. We audit this on Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. The head map correlates at $ρ= -0.950$ and $-0.768$ with a label-blind response-length map, apparently identifying a surface confound. An intervention that breaks the length-label coupling rejects this reading: with the prompt held fixed, response length explains 1% of the statistic's variance. What does explain it is prompt identity, at 64% of variance, in an ordering that is not monotonic in length. Within any fixed prompt the fairness label, response length and the presence of a protected-group token are collinear at $ϕ= 0.95$, partly by definition of the labelling rule, so no observational analysis can attribute the map to any of them, and no method in this family performs an experiment that could. The substantive claims fail independently: bias selectivity is not late-layer-concentrated on either model under either reference reading, and no head set we tested reduces the unfairness rate when ablated. Its complement, scored on the opposite label, reliably destroys refusal behaviour ($p = 2.7\times10^{-5}$), demonstrating that the pipeline detects effects at this scale.

title: Do LLM Agents Still Need to Be Told How to Self-Improve?
abstract: LLM agents increasingly drive their own learning. Self-improvement methods delegate various components of model optimization to the models themselves. As models become more capable, this motivates a basic question: do these increasingly capable models still need us to specify how they should self-improve? In this paper we study an autonomous paradigm in which, given basic primitives, resources, and a general goal for self-improvement, agents construct their own self-learning algorithm for context-based optimization. Using the setting of gameplay as a testbed, a frozen LLM agent is given a compute budget and tools for collecting experience and updating text documents, and allowed to freely experiment without an externally imposed loop or access to real-world data. We find that sufficiently capable models do self-improve under these conditions, demonstrating strategies that align with classic cognitive frameworks for self-regulated learning and constructs from machine learning literature on self-generated curricula. Furthermore, we study the extent to which the learned text artifacts transfer to external benchmarks, observing improvement across different game horizons, mechanics, and 3D navigation.

title: Complete Cosmological Collider Signatures from Right-handed Neutrino Loops
abstract: We study the complete cosmological collider (CC) signatures from right-handed neutrino loops with chemical-potential enhancement. These CC signals are induced by the inflaton-right-handed-neutrino interaction and can be extracted in the collinear squeezed configuration, which allows the right-handed-neutrino triangle loop to be factorized into the hard and soft parts. We precisely compute the soft part of the fermion loop for the first time by using the complete mode functions and the full loop integral, and treat the hard part as a tree-level subdiagram. We subtract the large-momentum asymptotic terms of the soft loop integrand and retain their finite contributions to the oscillation. We then evaluate the full spinor-helicity and Schwinger-Keldysh sums to obtain a finite, closed analytic formula for the complex clock coefficient. We further derive a compact formula for the leading CC signals in the large-chemical-potential expansion. We analyze the structure of the soft-part contribution by examining the sum of residues of the Mellin poles of the fermion propagators. For this, we demonstrate that the first local pole on each soft line contributes half of the asymptotic coefficient on one Schwinger-Keldysh path and the remaining local poles on the second soft line supply the other half.

title: An inexact stochastic variance-reduced gradient method for constrained convex finite-sum optimization
abstract: In this paper, we study a class of constrained convex finite-sum optimization problems. In many practical applications, all or some of the constraints are hard constraints that represent imperative requirements. Consequently, any desirable approximate solution must (nearly) satisfy these constraints. Motivated by this, we focus on computing an $ε$-$surely\ feasible\ stochastic\ optimal$ ($ε$-SFSO) solution, in which the constraint violation is deterministically bounded by $ε$, and the expected optimality gap is at most $ε$. While a recently proposed stochastic variance-reduced first-order penalty method can compute an $ε$-SFSO solution, there remains a significant gap between its first-order oracle complexity for computing an $ε$-SFSO solution and that for computing an $ε$-$expected\ feasible\ stochastic\ optimal$ solution, where both the expected constraint violation and the expected optimality gap are bounded by $ε$. To narrow this gap, we propose an inexact stochastic variance-reduced gradient (SVRG) method that significantly improves the previously best-known first-order oracle complexity for computing an $ε$-SFSO solution. Furthermore, when the objective consists of a single function, the proposed method reduces to a novel deterministic first-order method for solving standard convex conic optimization. It achieves a significantly lower gradient evaluation complexity with respect to the objective function compared to existing methods, and can outperform them when computing constraint gradients and projections onto the associated cone is cheaper than evaluating the objective gradient. Preliminary numerical results are presented to illustrate the performance of the proposed method.

title: Sidorenko Inequalities in Oriented Graphs
abstract: We introduce relative Sidorenko and relative anti-Sidorenko inequalities for oriented graphs, strengthening the corresponding well-studied notions for tournaments by allowing arbitrary host graphs. An orientation $\vec H$ of a graph $H$ is relatively Sidorenko if $\hom(\vec H,\vec G) \ge 2^{-e(H)}\hom(H,G)$ for every oriented graph $\vec G$ with underlying graph $G$, and relatively anti-Sidorenko if the reverse inequality holds. We provide a complete characterisation of the class of connected relatively Sidorenko graphs in terms of weakly norming graphs, and exhibit several families of relatively Sidorenko and relatively anti-Sidorenko oriented graphs. Despite the substantially stronger definitions, many known tournament Sidorenko and anti-Sidorenko examples satisfy the relative inequalities, suggesting a broader theory of these phenomena in arbitrary host graphs and motivating several new structural and classification problems.

title: Equilibrium Statistics and Stability in Random Two-Population and Three-Population Evolutionary Games
abstract: Multi-population matrix evolutionary games provide a framework for studying adaptation and strategic interactions among heterogeneous agents. When payoffs are uncertain, however, analysing a specified game does not reveal how frequently different evolutionary outcomes occur or how their probabilities depend on modelling assumptions. We study two- and three-population games with two strategies per population and both within- and between-population pairwise interactions, with payoffs fixed during each evolutionary trajectory. For two populations, we derive equilibrium-existence probabilities and analytical stability results for generic games and three structured classes: diversity, exclusive, and avoidance games. For generic two-population games, independent Gaussian sampling of payoff entries and of replicator coefficients produces different equilibrium statistics. Interaction structure further distinguishes coexistence from attraction: diversity and exclusive games share the same interior-existence probability, but only exclusive games admit asymptotically stable interior equilibria. Avoidance games admit transversely attracting equilibrium families without locally asymptotically stable individual points. For generic three-population games under independent payoff sampling, we obtain existence probabilities for all equilibrium types and joint existence-and-stability probabilities for boundary equilibria. Monte Carlo simulations support the analytical predictions and quantify multistability, while phase portraits illustrate initial-condition dependence. Under the same Gaussian payoff-sampling protocol, simulations show a lower frequency of fully mixed equilibria but a higher frequency of multistability for three populations than for two.

title: From nonlocal correlations to local symmetry breaking: Asymmetry dynamics of crosscap states
abstract: Under unitary dynamics preserving a global symmetry, bipartite entanglement typically grows while an initially broken symmetry is locally restored. Here, we show that this conventional scenario can be reversed when symmetry-breaking coherence is initially encoded in long-range entanglement. We investigate this phenomenon in a family of charge deformed crosscap states, characterized by antipodal entangled pairs with tunable entanglement and symmetry breaking. We first characterize their static properties, finding a Page-like entanglement profile and an entanglement asymmetry that vanishes for subsystems smaller than half the system size, but grows logarithmically for larger subsystems. For symmetric subsystems, we also analyze the symmetry-resolved entanglement and investigate how it evolves as the subsystem is continuously deformed away from a symmetric partition. Following a quench to a free-fermion tight-binding chain, we uncover an unconventional dynamics in which the entanglement entropy decreases whereas the entanglement asymmetry increases, so that initially symmetric subsystems dynamically develop local symmetry breaking. This behavior is quantitatively captured by a quasiparticle picture describing the propagation of antipodal correlations. Our results reveal how symmetry-preserving dynamics can redistribute globally encoded symmetry-breaking coherence, making it locally accessible, and establish the initial entanglement structure as a key ingredient in determining the fate of local symmetries out of equilibrium.

title: StringQFT: A Multiuse Textbook Resource for AI-Assisted Theoretical Physics
abstract: We present StringQFT as a textbook collection for string constructions of quantum field theory and as infrastructure for AI-assisted theoretical physics. The collection comprises 18 volumes, 190 chapters and 3,795 pages, covering brane probes, brane webs, geometric engineering, F-theory constructions, wrapped M5-branes and exact worldsheet constructions. Its open-book benchmark inventory contains 1,073 items, including 499 with automatic finite-answer checking. For retrieval-augmented generation, it provides 1,371 section records linked to textbook sources and PDF locations, together with a local lexical retriever. Training-data preparation is illustrated by 21 private, source-linked examples. For agents, it exposes 19 calculation tools with specified inputs and finite domains, connecting tool use to textbook derivations. We illustrate these uses through specific questions, retrieved passages and finite calculations. The textbook collection and accompanying resources are available at https://github.com/xingyang-yu/StringQFT.

title: FastFrames: Video Generation at Interactive Latency
abstract: Autoregressive video diffusion models generate frames based on new observations and inputs, making them a promising medium for interactive visual experiences. However, existing models are orders of magnitude too slow for fluid interaction. This paper introduces FastFrames, a family of fast autoregressive video diffusion models that achieves interactive latency without compromising quality. We profile the inference pipeline of state-of-the-art models and find that operations often treated as fixed implementation details, such as VAE decoding and KV cache updates, in fact account for over half of end-to-end inference latency. We challenge the assumption that these components are indispensable and replace them with lightweight alternatives. Our 1.3B variant runs at 36 ms per frame, or 28 responses per second (RPS), on a single B200 GPU while matching the generation quality of a state-of-the-art model that is nearly 8x slower. Our 14B variant runs at 45 ms per frame, or 22 RPS, on an 8x B200 GPU node and yields significantly better visual quality and realism. We show that FastFrames enables real-time interaction in applications such as camera-conditioned and physics-conditioned video generation.

title: Expressivity of two-dimensional Gaussian fermion tensor network states
abstract: Tensor network states (TNS) provide a family of efficiently compressed approximations to physically relevant many-body quantum states. An important quantity that characterizes the computational resources required by a TNS is its bond dimension. While in one dimension an area law for the Renyi-0 entropy guarantees an exact matrix product state representation with a bond dimension independent of the system size, an analogous statement does not hold for general states in two dimensions (2D). This leaves open the question of how the expressivity of 2D TNS is related to the entanglement properties of the states they represent. In this work, we focus on two families of 2D translation-invariant Gaussian fermionic states: single-band BCS superconductors and half-filled two-band insulators (including semimetals). For each family, we prove that an area law for the Renyi-0 entropy is equivalent to having an exact Gaussian fermionic TNS representation with a finite bond dimension determined by the Renyi-0 entropy. We also establish equivalent characterizations in terms of compactly supported Wannier-type orbitals and the momentum-space wavefunction, relating the spatial extent of these orbitals and the structure of the wavefunction to the required bond dimension.

title: Spool: Low-Latency Streaming Inference for Hybrid Vision-Language Models
abstract: Applications such as visual accessibility agents and robotics require answering questions about recent video content promptly, over a bounded window of past frames (e.g., the last two minutes). Hybrid vision-language models (VLMs), which interleave attention with linear recurrent layers such as Gated DeltaNet (GDN), are attractive for this setting, but maintaining a sliding window is expensive. The reason is that recurrent layers combine all past frames into a shared state, so expiring old frames normally requires re-running the entire window through the model. We observe that the recurrent update is affine in the state with input-dependent coefficients, so the effect of each frame can be captured as a transformation that composes associatively. We present Spool, a training-free framework that caches per-frame state transformations and composes them efficiently as the window advances, removing expired frames from each recurrent layer's state without replaying frames through the backbone. Removal is exact within each layer; as with key-value eviction in attention, expired frames can retain residual influence through the cached inputs computed by earlier layers. We design a dedicated data structure and GPU kernels to achieve low caching and composition overhead. Across five open-source hybrid VLMs and four video reasoning benchmarks, Spool achieves the lowest p95 time-to-first-token in all 20 model-benchmark tests, reducing it by a geometric mean of $6.6\times$ over the faster of two recent vLLM baselines, while improving accuracy by 2.3 percentage points on average.

title: Ambient LLMs: Data-Efficient Supervised Fine-tuning via Temperature Matching
abstract: Collecting large-scale, diverse, and high-quality post-training datasets for autoregressive language models is challenging. Consequently, Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) is typically applied to datasets significantly smaller than those used for pre-training, which leads to overfitting and the catastrophic forgetting of the tails of the data distribution. To prevent this collapse, we introduce Ambient SFT, a principled framework for leveraging imperfect predictions to augment the fine-tuning set. In our method, a "frozen" version of the pre-trained model serves as a noisy teacher that the fine-tuned model must match at a coarse level. In particular, we require that the high-temperature versions of the conditional distributions produced by the post-training model should match the high-temperature versions of the pre-training ones. The temperature hyperparameter controls the level of trust in the pre-trained model, with the limit $T\to \infty$ reverting back to regular SFT and $T=1$ to knowledge distillation. We demonstrate that our approach outperforms standard SFT across domain adaptation, instruction-tuning, and reasoning, leading for up to $21\%$ average relative improvement to standard SFT.

title: On the multiplicity of crossing limit cycles of double diagonalizable piecewise linear vector fields
abstract: We consider planar piecewise linear vector fields with two zones separated by a straight line and having two diagonalizable components, which we call the \emph{double diagonalizable configuration}. In this configuration, the Poincaré half-maps correspond to separatrices of saddle points in the foliations of symmetric differential forms $ω_r(x)-ω_r(y)$, where $ω_r$ is a rational $1$-form with exactly three simple poles. Limit cycles correspond to non-diagonal intersections of two such separatrices, and the multiplicity of a limit cycle is precisely the order of contact at the intersection point. We prove that two distinct separatrices which are not nested segments of the same straight line have a contact of order at most $4$ at a diagonal point and at most $2$ at a non-diagonal point. As a consequence, we obtain that the multiplicity of limit cycles in the double diagonalizable configuration is at most two, this bound being sharp.

title: CFTs with Large Virasoro Primary Gaps
abstract: We construct the first explicit examples of compact unitary bosonic full conformal field theories (CFTs) in two dimensions with a unique vacuum and an all-spin Virasoro-primary gap greater than two. Our constructions use asymmetric orbifolds of lattice CFTs built from even unimodular lattices of sufficiently large minimum norm, ensuring that no charged state lies below the desired gap. The gauged symmetries combine a common orthogonal action on the left- and right-moving currents with independent sign reversals; the latter project out the dimension-two scalar primary $\sum_i J_L^iJ_R^i$ that survives when the symmetry acts identically on both chiral halves. We prove that the gauging is anomaly-free and determine the exact gaps by analyzing the invariant untwisted spectrum and all twisted sectors. From lattices constructed using ternary quadratic-residue codes, we obtain an infinite family with gap three at $(c_L,c_R)=(p+1,p+1)$ for primes $p\ge71$ with $p\equiv23\pmod{24}$. From Barnes-Wall lattices, we obtain an infinite family with gap four at $(c_L,c_R)=(2^m,2^m)$ for odd $m\ge7$. We also obtain two additional examples, with gap three at $(c_L,c_R)=(48,48)$ and gap four at $(c_L,c_R)=(512,512)$.

title: Emergent Attraction and Competing Orders near the Van Hove Singularity in Rhombohedral $n$-layer Graphene
abstract: Unconventional superconductivity in rhombohedral $n$-layer graphene exhibits a rich phase diagram with multiple distinct superconducting regions, whose microscopic origins remain unclear. Here, we investigate the competition between charge-density-wave (CDW) and pair-density-wave (PDW) instabilities near the inner van Hove singularities (VHSs), using a patch renormalization-group approach with the realistic band structures incorporated. We identify two key findings. First, we find an effective attractive interaction emerging from purely repulsive interactions through RG flow in the presence of $C_3$ symmetry breaking. The resulting interaction structure, with two repulsive couplings and one attractive coupling, gives rise to competing CDW and PDW instabilities. Second, the competition is controlled by the detuning from the VHS. While CDW dominates near the VHS filling and at higher temperatures, PDW becomes the leading instability on either side of the VHS and at lower temperatures. This mechanism naturally produces two superconducting regions separated by a CDW-dominated regime, providing a possible qualitative explanation for the experimentally observed separation between SC1 and SC2.
